teile.einleitung: Salt water is water with salt dissolved in it, like the water of the seas. Because the salt makes the water heavier, salt water carries things better than fresh water. That is why an egg can float in it and people almost float by themselves in the Dead Sea.
wichtigste: Seawater tastes salty because a lot of salt is dissolved in it.
Salt water has a higher density than tap water, so a litre of it is heavier.
A fresh raw egg sinks in tap water but floats in very salty water.
If you pour in a lot of tap water, the water is diluted and the egg sinks again.
You float more easily in the sea than in a lake, and in the Dead Sea you even bob like a cork.
When salt water evaporates, the salt is left behind.
Salt water only freezes at lower temperatures than fresh water.

abschnitte.text: Salt water contains dissolved **salts**, above all table salt, that is sodium chloride. The water of the oceans contains on average about 3.5 per cent salt, around 35 grams per litre. Rivers and lakes such as Lake Constance or Lake Geneva, on the other hand, contain only very little salt and are therefore called **fresh water**. The salts come from rocks that have been washed out by rain over millions of years and carried to the sea by rivers.

Put a fresh raw egg into a glass of tap water: it sinks to the bottom. If you now stir lots of spoonfuls of salt into the water, at some point the egg starts to float. This is because of **density**: salt water is heavier than the same amount of tap water and pushes the egg up more strongly. If you pour in a lot of tap water again, the egg sinks again. An old egg often stands up or floats even in tap water, because a larger air bubble forms inside it over time.

All water pushes things upwards with a force called **buoyancy**. The denser the water, the stronger this buoyancy. That is why you float a little more easily in the sea than in a Swiss lake. The **Dead Sea** between Israel and Jordan is almost ten times as salty as ordinary seawater. There you can lie on your back and read a newspaper without sinking.

If you let salt water evaporate in the sun, the salt is left behind as a white crust. This is how sea salt is obtained in warm countries, in shallow pools called **salt pans**. In Switzerland, salt lies deep underground as rock salt. The Swiss salt works pump water down deep, dissolve the salt in it and bring the **brine** back up. Then the water is boiled off, and what is left is table salt or road salt.

Salt in water lowers its freezing point. Seawater only freezes at about minus 2 °C, which is why salt is spread on roads in winter. You cannot use salt water as drinking water, because the body has to get rid of the large amount of salt with extra water. That is why shipwrecked people at sea can die of thirst despite all the water around them. In some dry countries, drinking water is made from seawater in **desalination plants**.

begriffe.erklaerung: How heavy a substance is compared with its size.
The force with which a liquid pushes an object upwards.
Water with very little salt, as in rivers and most lakes.
Water in which a great deal of salt is dissolved.
A plant in which salt is produced.

gewusst: If you took all the salt out of the seas and spread it on land, it would form a thick layer over all the continents.
Because of all the salt, hardly any fish or plants can live in the Dead Sea, which is how it got its name.
The salt mine at Bex in the canton of Vaud can be visited, and you can ride through it on a small train.

teile.einleitung: A pumped storage power station is a huge battery made of water. It pumps water up into a high lake when there is plenty of electricity, and lets it flow back down when electricity is needed. Some of the largest plants of this kind in Europe are in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: A pumped storage power station needs two reservoirs at different heights.
When there is surplus electricity, water is pumped up; when it is needed, it flows back through turbines.
The energy is stored as the potential energy of the water.
Many plants use a pump turbine, which pumps or generates electricity depending on which way it turns.
The overall efficiency of modern plants is about 75 to 80 per cent.
Pumped storage power stations balance out fluctuations in the power grid.
The Linth-Limmern power station with the Muttsee lies in the canton of Glarus.

abschnitte.text: A pumped storage power station has an **upper reservoir** and a **lower reservoir**, connected by pipes or tunnels. When there is more electricity than is needed at the moment, electric motors drive pumps that move water upwards. When a lot of electricity is needed later, the water flows back down and turns turbines on the way. These drive generators, which produce electricity again.

The pumped-up water has **potential energy** because it is high up. It is calculated with the formula mass times gravitational field strength times height. If 1000 kg of water is pumped 100 m up, that is exactly 1,000,000 joules at 10 N/kg. If one cubic metre of water falls 600 m, it theoretically contains about 1.64 kilowatt-hours. The greater the difference in height and the more water, the more energy fits into the store.

When pumping and when running the turbines, some energy is always lost as heat and through friction. If the pumps have an **efficiency** of 88 per cent and the turbines 90 per cent, about 79 per cent is left at the end. So if 100 MWh are used for pumping, with 80 per cent efficiency only 80 MWh come back and 20 MWh are lost. It is still worth it, because cheap surplus electricity is turned into valuable electricity for peak times.

Many modern plants use a **pump turbine**. If it turns one way, it pumps water upwards. If it turns the other way, it is driven by the water and produces electricity. This means you do not need two separate machines, which saves space and money.

The **Linth-Limmern** power station in the canton of Glarus uses the high Muttsee as its upper reservoir and the Limmernsee as its lower reservoir. It started operating around 2016 and, with around 1000 megawatts of power, is one of the most powerful plants in Europe. In Valais, the **Nant de Drance** power station has been working since 2022 between the Emosson and Vieux Emosson reservoirs. In the Grimsel area in the Bernese Oberland, water is also pumped back and forth.

In the power grid, production and use must be equal at all times. But solar and wind power stations deliver sometimes a lot and sometimes little electricity, depending on the weather. Pumped storage power stations can switch from pumping to generating within a few minutes. This makes them an important **balance** for fluctuations, helping to prevent power cuts.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy an object has because it is high up.
The high lake into which the water is pumped.
A machine that pumps or generates electricity depending on which way it turns.
The share of energy that comes out again in usable form at the end.
A device that turns turning motion into electric current.

gewusst: For 100 MW of power with a 400 m drop, about 28 cubic metres of water per second must flow through the turbines.
The dam wall at the Muttsee is at around 2500 metres above sea level and is one of the highest dam walls in Europe.
The first pumped storage plants were built in Switzerland and Italy as early as the end of the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: The threshold of pain is the loudness at which sound is no longer just loud but hurts the ear. In people it is at a sound level of around 130 decibels, about as loud as a jet aircraft at very close range. But even far below this limit, noise can permanently damage your hearing.
wichtigste: The threshold of pain for hearing is around 130 dB.
A sound level of 120 dB corresponds to an intensity of 1 W/m² and a sound pressure of 20 Pa.
According to Suva, noise of 85 dB(A) or more over a working day is a danger to hearing.
An extremely loud, short bang can cause acoustic trauma.
Destroyed hair cells in the cochlea do not grow back in people.
A whistling or rushing sound in the ear is called tinnitus.
Ear protection with 25 dB of damping reduces 110 dB, by calculation, to 85 dB.

abschnitte.text: The **sound level** is measured in decibels, shortened to dB. 0 dB is the **threshold of hearing**, the quietest sound a young, healthy person can only just hear. The scale is logarithmic: every 10 dB more means ten times the sound intensity, and we feel this as roughly twice as loud. At 120 dB the intensity is 1 watt per square metre, and the effective sound pressure about 20 pascals.

Rustling leaves are about 20 dB, a normal conversation around 60 dB. Heavy road traffic reaches about 80 dB, a pneumatic drill close up over 100 dB. At a loud rock concert right in front of the speakers it can be 110 dB or more. From around 130 dB the **threshold of pain** is reached, and sound is felt physically as pain.

Deep in the inner ear lies the **cochlea**, which is lined with thousands of fine hair cells. These cells turn vibrations into nerve signals that the brain understands as sounds. Too much noise bends and destroys the fine hairs. In people, destroyed **hair cells** do not grow back, which is why noise damage is permanent.

A very short, extremely loud burst of sound, for example a firecracker close to the ear, can cause **acoustic trauma**. Afterwards you often hear less well or have a whistling in your ear. Such a whistling, humming or rushing sound with no outside cause is called **tinnitus**. It can also happen after a very loud concert and sometimes stays.

Suva, Switzerland's accident insurer, states that noise at work averaging 85 dB(A) or more over a day is a danger to hearing. Then ear protection must be worn, for example earplugs or **ear defenders**. Ear protection that damps by 25 dB reduces 110 dB, by calculation, to 85 dB. When listening to music with headphones, too: better to turn it down and give your ears breaks, and wear earplugs at concerts or on New Year's Eve.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of measurement for sound level, in other words how loud something is.
The quietest sound a person can only just hear.
Sensory cells in the inner ear that turn sound into nerve signals.
Whistling, humming or rushing in the ear with no outside cause.

gewusst: Between the threshold of hearing and the threshold of pain, the sound intensity differs by around ten million million times.
Noise damage often does not hurt at all; it develops slowly and unnoticed over many years.

teile.einleitung: A precision balance is a balance that can measure very small masses very accurately. The finest models, analytical balances, measure to a ten-thousandth of a gram. For this to work, even draughts, heat and vibrations must be avoided.
wichtigste: Precision balances measure masses very accurately, often to a milligram or even better.
An analytical balance in the laboratory often weighs to 0.0001 g.
A glass case around the weighing pan protects the measurement from draughts.
A spirit level with an air bubble shows whether the balance is level.
Warm objects give false readings, because warm air rises.
With a test weight of known mass, you check whether the balance is measuring correctly.
Precision balances are needed especially in laboratories and pharmacies.

abschnitte.text: A **precision balance** measures the mass of an object much more accurately than a kitchen scale. Many precision balances still show thousandths of a gram. Even more accurate are **analytical balances**, which often weigh to 0.0001 g, a tenth of a milligram. That is about the mass of a tiny grain of sand.

In the past, fine balances worked with a balance beam and **weights**. Today most precision balances are electronic. Many use the principle of **electromagnetic force compensation**: an electromagnet holds the weighing pan exactly in place, and the current needed for this reveals the mass. A computer converts the value and shows it on the display.

Even a slight **draught** can change the reading, which is why many precision balances have a glass case with sliding doors. You should not weigh warm objects, because rising **warm air** makes the pan seem lighter. Vibrations also disturb the measurement, which is why the balance is placed on a heavy, vibration-free **weighing table**. A **spirit level** with an air bubble shows whether the balance is level; the bubble must be exactly in the middle.

Electronic balances actually measure the **weight force** and convert it into a mass. But the Earth's pull is not equally strong everywhere; it depends, for example, on altitude and latitude. That is why a precision balance must be **adjusted** again after a move, for example from Bern to Zermatt. The balance is checked regularly with a **test weight** whose mass is known exactly.

In **laboratories**, chemists and biologists weigh out tiny amounts of substances. In **pharmacies**, they are used to measure out active ingredients for ointments and capsules. Goldsmiths, jewellers and food inspectors also work with precision balances. The company Mettler, now Mettler-Toledo, was founded in Switzerland in 1945 and is one of the best-known makers of such balances in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: An especially accurate laboratory balance, often accurate to a ten-thousandth of a gram.
A small glass tube with an air bubble that shows whether something is level.
To set a measuring device so that it shows the correct value.
A piece of metal with an exactly known mass for checking a balance.

gewusst: A very accurate balance can even show a fingerprint on an object as a change in weight.
Test weights are only handled with tweezers or gloves, because grease and sweat from fingers make them heavier.
If you weigh something on a high mountain, a balance that has not been adjusted shows slightly less than in the valley.

teile.einleitung: In the photoelectric effect, light knocks electrons out of a metal. At the beginning of the 20th century, this effect showed that light consists of individual packets of energy, and so it became a cornerstone of quantum physics.
wichtigste: In the photoelectric effect, light frees electrons from a surface.
Heinrich Hertz was the first to observe the effect, in 1887.
Albert Einstein explained it in 1905 with his light quantum hypothesis.
Electrons are only freed at all above a certain threshold frequency.
Brighter light frees more electrons, but not faster ones.
Even with very weak light, the electrons come out practically without delay.
Solar cells and light sensors in cameras are based on related effects.

abschnitte.text: In 1887, **Heinrich Hertz** noticed that UV light makes it easier for sparks to jump between two electrodes. A year later, Wilhelm Hallwachs showed this with a **zinc plate** that was negatively charged and lit with UV light: the plate discharges because electrons fly out. With ordinary visible light, on the other hand, nothing happens. Philipp Lenard studied the effect more closely around 1902.

According to the classical idea, light is a wave whose energy increases with brightness. Then bright light of any colour should knock out electrons, and with weak light it should take a while. But the experiments showed something else. Below a **threshold frequency**, no electrons come out at all, however bright the light is. Above it, they come out immediately, even with very weak light.

In 1905, **Albert Einstein** explained that light consists of small packets of energy, light quanta, which today are called **photons**. Each photon has the energy E = h · f, where h is Planck's constant and f is the frequency. A photon can only free an electron if its energy is greater than the **work function** W of the metal. The electron gets the rest as kinetic energy: E kin = h · f minus W. Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this explanation.

With the **retarding field method**, the electrons are slowed down with a voltage. If the current just becomes zero at 1.5 volts, the fastest electrons had 1.5 electronvolts of kinetic energy. If you plot this energy against the frequency of the light, you get a straight line whose gradient is Planck's constant. An example: light of 400 nanometres has about 3.1 eV; with a work function of 2.3 eV, around 0.8 eV is left for the electron.

Today the photoelectric effect is used in many devices. A **photomultiplier** can detect single photons and is used in research and medicine. In the internal photoelectric effect, the electrons stay in the material but make it conductive. **Solar cells**, light barriers and the image sensors in mobile phone cameras are based on this.

begriffe.erklaerung: The minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal.
The lowest frequency of light at which electrons are just freed.
The smallest packet of energy of light.
A small unit of energy, abbreviated eV, often used for particles and photons.

gewusst: Albert Einstein did not get his Nobel Prize for the theory of relativity but for explaining the photoelectric effect.
Einstein wrote his paper on the photoelectric effect in 1905, while he was working at the patent office in Bern.
Zinc needs UV light for the photoelectric effect, whereas caesium reacts even to visible light.

teile.einleitung: A slide is a piece of play equipment on which you glide down a smooth, sloping surface from the top. On it you can experience a lot of physics: gravity, friction, momentum and even electricity. Slides are found in playgrounds, swimming pools and theme parks.
wichtigste: You slide down because the Earth pulls you with its gravity.
Your momentum comes from the height at the top, which is turned into movement as you slide.
On a steep slide you get faster than on a gentle one.
The friction between you and the slide slows you down a little.
You can brake best with rubber soles, because rubber produces a lot of friction.
Water makes the sliding surface smoother, which is why you often slide faster when wet.
On plastic slides, your hair can stand on end because of electric charge.

abschnitte.text: A **slide**, called a Rutschbahn in Switzerland, consists of a ladder or steps and a sloping, smooth chute. It is usually made of **metal**, plastic or polished wood. There are straight slides, wave slides and twisting tube slides. At the end, the chute becomes flat so that you can come to a gentle stop.

The Earth's **gravity** constantly pulls you downwards. On the sloping chute, part of this force becomes the force that pushes you along the slide. The steeper the slide, the larger this part and the faster you go. At the top you have **potential energy** because you are high up, and at the bottom it has turned into kinetic energy. At the flat end there is no slope, so friction slows you down and you get slower.

**Friction** acts between your body and the sliding surface. Smooth fabrics such as waterproof trousers slide better than rough jeans. With rubber soles you can brake hard, because rubber grips well. If there is water on the slide, it forms a thin film that reduces friction. That is why water slides at the swimming pool are so fast.

When you slide on plastic, your clothes and hair rub against the chute. Tiny charged particles, the electrons, are passed from one material to the other. Your body becomes **electrically charged**, and hairs with the same charge push each other away. That is why your hair stands on end. If you then touch something made of metal, you may get a small spark or a slight shock.

A metal slide can get very hot in blazing summer sun, because metal takes in and conducts heat well. So check with your hand whether it is too hot. It is best to slide sitting down, feet first. Wait until the child in front of you has moved out of the way at the bottom. Cords on jackets or hoods can get caught and are therefore dangerous.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the Earth pulls everything down towards it.
A force that arises when two surfaces rub against each other and that slows down movement.
Energy an object has because it is high up.
A property of tiny particles that makes things attract or repel each other.

gewusst: If a slide had no friction at all, you would arrive at the bottom just as fast as if you had fallen from the same height.
Many water parks have slides with an almost vertical start, called free-fall slides.
The same slide feels much faster in waterproof trousers than in woollen trousers.

teile.einleitung: Rolling friction is the force that slows down a rolling wheel or a rolling ball. It is much smaller than the friction when dragging, which is why we move heavy loads on wheels.
wichtigste: Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, which is why loads roll easily on wheels.
It is caused mainly by the wheel and the surface changing shape.
Soft, badly pumped bicycle tyres change shape more and roll less easily.
Steel wheels on steel rails have especially low rolling friction.
The rolling friction force is the coefficient of rolling friction times the normal force: 0.01 times 1000 N gives 10 N.
On soft sand, it is harder going, because the ground gives way a lot.
Larger wheels roll more easily with the same load.
Rolling friction is often also called rolling resistance.

abschnitte.text: When a wheel rolls, it is squashed a little flat where it touches the ground, and the surface also gives way slightly. As it rolls on, the wheel has to climb a small hill again and again, as it were, and energy is lost as heat as things change shape. This braking effect is called **rolling friction** or **rolling resistance**. It always acts against the direction of movement.

The rolling friction force is calculated from the **coefficient of rolling friction** times the force with which the wheel presses on the ground, the **normal force**. If a cart presses on the road with 1000 N and the coefficient of rolling friction is 0.01, that gives a rolling friction force of 10 N. For car tyres on tarmac, the figure is roughly in this range. For steel wheels on rails, it is about ten times smaller still.

Because steel is very hard, the wheel and rail hardly change shape, which is why a train needs especially little energy per tonne of load. That is one reason why the railway is considered a very energy-efficient means of transport. On a bike, rolling friction depends strongly on **tyre pressure**. A firmly pumped, narrow tyre on smooth tarmac rolls much more easily than a soft tyre.

On soft sand, in deep snow or on wet grass, wheels sink in and change the shape of the ground a lot. Then rolling friction becomes very large, and it is hard going. That is why vehicles for sand or snow have especially wide tyres or tracks that spread the weight. Larger wheels sink in less and roll more easily over bumps.

If you push a heavy box across the floor, **sliding friction** arises and you need a lot of force. If you put the same box on a trolley, a small fraction of that is enough. That is why we use wheeled suitcases, shopping trolleys and ball bearings. But it does not work entirely without friction, because without static friction between the tyres and the road a car could neither start nor brake.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that tells you how strongly a wheel is slowed down on a particular surface.
The force with which an object presses at right angles on the surface below it.
Friction when one surface slides over another.
Another word for the braking force when rolling.

gewusst: A loaded goods wagon can be pushed on level rails by a few people, because rolling friction is so low.
In bike races, professionals choose their tyres and tyre pressure very carefully, because rolling resistance can decide by seconds.

teile.einleitung: A fictitious force is a force you only feel when you are yourself in an accelerating or rotating system, for example in a bus that is braking or on a roundabout. Seen from outside, this force does not exist at all; it comes from the inertia of bodies. Even so, fictitious forces are very important, for example for understanding wind and ocean currents on the rotating Earth.
wichtigste: Fictitious forces only appear in accelerating or rotating frames of reference.
They are also called inertial forces, because they come from the inertia of bodies.
On a roundabout, the centrifugal force seems to push you outwards.
The Coriolis force only acts on bodies that are moving within the rotating system.
Gaspard Gustave de Coriolis described this force in 1835.
In 1851, Léon Foucault demonstrated the Earth's rotation with his pendulum in the Panthéon in Paris.
At the equator, the horizontal deflection by the Coriolis force is zero.

abschnitte.text: If a bus brakes suddenly, the passengers lurch forwards as if someone were pushing them. In reality, because of **inertia**, their bodies simply want to carry on at the same speed. But for someone sitting in the bus, it feels like a real force. Such forces, which only appear in an accelerating **frame of reference**, are called fictitious forces or inertial forces.

On a chair-swing ride, the seats fly outwards. Anyone riding feels a force pulling them outwards, the **centrifugal force**. Seen from outside, each body actually wants to fly on in a straight line, and the chains force it onto the circular path. A spin dryer uses the same effect: the water is flung outwards through the holes in the drum.

In a rotating system, the **Coriolis force** acts on bodies moving within it and is proportional to their speed. The French scientist Gaspard Gustave de Coriolis described it in 1835. In the northern hemisphere it deflects moving bodies to the right, in the southern hemisphere to the left. If a projectile is fired southwards from the North Pole, from the Earth's point of view it drifts westwards, because the Earth keeps turning eastwards beneath it.

Because the Earth rotates, air does not flow straight from high pressure to low pressure. It is deflected and circles around the areas of low pressure, anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere. That is why tropical storms in the two hemispheres also turn in different directions. High up, the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force often balance each other, which gives the **geostrophic wind**. At the equator the horizontal deflection disappears, which is why tropical storms do not form right there.

In 1851, Léon Foucault hung a heavy ball on a wire about 67 metres long in the Panthéon in Paris. The **Foucault pendulum** swung back and forth, and its plane of swing slowly turned relative to the floor. This made it visible to everyone that the Earth is turning beneath the pendulum. At the North Pole, the plane of swing would make a full turn in about one day; in Switzerland it takes longer, about 33 hours.

begriffe.erklaerung: The viewpoint from which a movement is observed and measured.
The property of every body to keep its motion as long as no force acts on it.
A fictitious force that seems to pull outwards in a rotating system.
A fictitious force that deflects moving bodies sideways in a rotating system.

gewusst: The idea that water in a washbasin always swirls in a particular direction because of the Coriolis force is a myth, because the force is far too weak for that.
Today, a Foucault pendulum swings in many museums around the world, showing visitors the Earth's rotation.

teile.einleitung: A saucepan lid is the lid you put on a pan or cooking pot when cooking. It looks ordinary, but it is full of physics. With it, water boils faster, you save energy and in an emergency you can even put out a fire.
wichtigste: Water boils faster with a lid on.
Cooking with a lid saves energy.
Drops of water collect on the inside of the lid because the steam cools down there.
A metal lid gets hot itself from the hot steam.
A small hole in the lid lets steam escape.
Through a glass lid you can look into the pot.
You smother burning oil in a pan with a lid, never with water.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, a cooking pot is often called a “Pfanne” (pan), which is why its lid is called a **Pfannendeckel**. Lids are made of metal such as stainless steel, of glass or of cast iron. They usually have a handle or knob that is not supposed to get so hot. A good lid fits exactly on the rim of the pan.

Without a lid, hot **steam** is constantly rising and carries a lot of heat away into the kitchen. The lid keeps the steam and the warm air in the pot. This keeps more heat in the water, and it comes to the boil faster. As a result, you need less electricity or gas, so you save **energy** and money.

When the hot steam hits the cooler lid, it cools down and turns back into water. This process is called **condensation**. That is why lots of drops of water collect on the inside of the lid and drip back into the pot. At the same time, the steam gives off its heat to the lid, which is why a metal lid is very hot after cooking.

Sometimes the steam lifts the lid and makes it rattle, because **pressure** builds up under the lid. Some lids have a small hole through which the steam can escape so that nothing boils over. A glass lid is practical because you can see whether it is boiling without lifting it. In a **pressure cooker**, on the other hand, the lid is sealed tight, the pressure rises and the water only boils at about 120 degrees, so the food cooks faster.

Always lift the lid off a hot pot away from your body so that the steam does not rise into your face. It is best to use an oven glove for this. If oil in a frying pan catches fire, simply put a lid on it and switch off the hob. Without **oxygen**, the fire goes out. You must never pour water onto burning oil, because it turns to steam instantly and throws burning fat out.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water in the form of a gas, which rises when cooking.
When steam cools down and turns back into liquid water.
The temperature at which a liquid boils; for water about 100 degrees.
A fire of burning oil or fat, for example in a frying pan.

gewusst: On high Swiss mountains, water boils below 100 degrees because the air pressure is lower.
When boiling water, a lid often saves more energy than you think, because evaporation needs a particularly large amount of heat.
The rattling of the lid shows that steam can exert a force, as in a steam engine.

teile.einleitung: Oxygen is a chemical element and an invisible gas without which people and animals could not live. It makes up about a fifth of the air and also makes it possible for a fire to burn. Its chemical symbol is O.
wichtigste: Oxygen is a colourless, odourless gas with the chemical symbol O.
Air consists of about 21 per cent oxygen.
A flame needs oxygen from the air to burn.
People and animals breathe in oxygen to get energy from their food.
Plants produce oxygen during photosynthesis.
Oxygen is the most common element in the Earth's crust.
In water, oxygen is bound together with hydrogen.

abschnitte.text: Oxygen is a **chemical element** with atomic number 8 in the periodic table. In the air it usually occurs as a pair of two atoms, written O2. You can neither see, smell nor taste it. If it is cooled to minus 183 degrees Celsius, it becomes liquid and has a pale blue colour.

A fire needs fuel, heat and **oxygen**. When something burns, the fuel combines with oxygen, producing heat and light. This process is called **oxidation**. If you put a glass over a burning candle, the flame goes out after a short time, because the oxygen in the glass has been used up. In pure oxygen, things burn much more fiercely than in normal air.

When we breathe in, oxygen gets into the **lungs** and from there into the blood. The red blood cells carry it to all the cells in the body. In the cells, it helps to get energy from sugar and other nutrients. This produces **carbon dioxide**, which we breathe out again. Fish get the oxygen dissolved in water with their gills.

Almost all the oxygen in the air comes from plants, algae and bacteria. They use sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide, giving off oxygen as they do so. This process is called **photosynthesis**. A large part comes from tiny algae in the sea, the **plankton**. Switzerland's forests also play their part.

Oxygen was discovered independently by two researchers in the 18th century. The Swedish-German pharmacist **Carl Wilhelm Scheele** found it around 1771, and the Englishman **Joseph Priestley** in 1774. The Frenchman Antoine Lavoisier recognised the part the gas plays in burning and gave it its name. Both the name oxygen and the German word “Sauerstoff” mean something like acid-maker, because people at the time wrongly believed it was found in all acids.

In hospitals, sick people are sometimes given extra oxygen through a mask. Mountaineers often take oxygen bottles with them on very high mountains, because the air is thin there. In industry, oxygen is needed for **welding** and for making steel. High up in the atmosphere, oxygen forms the **ozone layer**, which protects us from the Sun's harmful UV rays.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance made of only one kind of atom.
A chemical reaction in which a substance combines with oxygen, for example when burning or rusting.
The process in which plants make sugar with sunlight and give off oxygen.
A form of oxygen made of three atoms, which protects against UV rays high up in the air.

gewusst: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and is attracted by magnets.
Almost half the weight of the Earth's crust consists of oxygen bound in rocks.
Rust also forms because iron slowly combines with oxygen.

teile.einleitung: Sound is everything we can hear: voices, music, birdsong or thunder. It is produced when something vibrates and travels as a wave through air, water or solid materials. We perceive it with our ears.
wichtigste: Sound is produced when an object vibrates.
Sound needs something to travel through, such as air; in airless space you hear nothing.
In air at 20 °C, sound travels at about 343 metres per second.
The number of vibrations per second is called the frequency and decides the pitch.
The sound level is measured in decibels.
An echo forms when sound is reflected by a wall or rock face.
Sound above 20,000 hertz is called ultrasound and cannot be heard by people.

abschnitte.text: If you pluck a guitar string, it moves back and forth very quickly; it **vibrates**. As it does, it nudges the air particles near it. These pass the push on to their neighbours, and so a **sound wave** is formed. Your vocal cords in your throat also vibrate when you speak or sing.

abschnitte.titel: Sound needs something to travel through
abschnitte.text: Sound can only spread if there are particles that can vibrate. In **space** there is no air, so you cannot hear any noises there. In water, sound is about four times faster than in air, and in steel even more than ten times faster. In air at 20 °C, it covers about 343 metres per second, roughly one kilometre in 3 seconds. That is why you hear the thunder of a storm one kilometre away about 3 seconds after the lightning.

The **frequency** tells you how often something vibrates per second, measured in hertz. Many vibrations give a high note, few give a low note. People hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz; older people often hear high notes less well. How loud something is, is given as the sound level in **decibels**: a whisper is about 30 decibels, a rock concert over 100 decibels.

Sound waves travel through the ear canal to the **eardrum** and make it vibrate. Three tiny bones, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, pass the vibration on into the inner ear. In the cochlea, hair cells turn it into nerve signals, which the brain understands as sound. Very loud noise can permanently damage these hair cells, which is why **ear protection** protects the ears.

If you shout loudly at a rock face in the mountains, your call comes back as an **echo**. **Bats** use the echo of their very high calls to fly in the dark and find insects. These sounds are often in the range of **ultrasound** above 20,000 hertz, which people cannot hear. In hospitals, ultrasound is used to make pictures of the inside of the body, for example of a baby in its mother's tummy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
The unit for the loudness of a sound.
Reflected sound that you hear again after a delay.
Sound with such a high frequency that people cannot hear it.

gewusst: Elephants communicate with such low notes that people cannot hear them; this is called infrasound.
When an aircraft flies faster than sound, a loud sonic boom is produced.
Whales can hear each other under water over hundreds of kilometres.

teile.einleitung: A reflector, also called a retroreflector or cat's eye, throws light back exactly where it came from. It does not shine by itself, but it makes bikes, pedestrians and vehicles visible from far away in the dark.
wichtigste: A bicycle reflector is also called a cat's eye.
A reflector does not shine by itself; it only throws light back.
It throws the light back to the lamp it came from.
You see it best when light falls on it, for example from car headlights.
At the back of a bike the reflector is red, at the front white.
A high-visibility vest with reflectors helps you to be seen better in the dark.
The name cat's eye comes from the fact that cats' eyes shine in the light.

abschnitte.text: A **reflector** is a part made of plastic or glass that throws back the light falling on it. Unlike a normal mirror, it does not send the light off at an angle but straight back towards the **light source**. That is why a driver sees the reflector light up brightly as soon as the headlight falls on it. Without light, the reflector stays dark; it has no battery.

A typical bicycle reflector consists of many small **prisms** shaped like the corner of a cube. In them, light is reflected by three surfaces one after the other and then travels back exactly parallel. Such a part is also called a **retroreflector**. Reflective strips on clothes, on the other hand, often contain tiny glass beads that work in a similar way.

In Switzerland, a bike needs reflectors: a red one at the back and a white one at the front. Many bikes also have yellow reflectors on the pedals and reflective strips on the tyres or spokes. But they do not replace the **bike lights**, which must be switched on in the dark. Red at the back and white at the front also applies to cars and lorries, by the way.

At night, a driver often only sees pedestrians in dark clothing a few dozen metres away. With reflectors on their body, the driver can see them from much further away. That is why experts recommend **high-visibility vests**, reflective bands on arms and legs or school bags with reflective strips. Reflectors that move, for example on the ankles or wrists, work especially well.

abschnitte.titel: Cat's eyes in nature and technology
abschnitte.text: Cats have a reflective layer behind the retina that throws light back, which is why their eyes shine in headlights. The **cat's eye** gets its name from this effect. On some roads there are reflectors set into the road surface that mark the edge of the road at night. In 1969, astronauts even set up retroreflectors on the Moon, which researchers still use today to measure the distance to the Moon by laser.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part that throws light straight back to the light source.
A transparent object with flat surfaces that bends or reflects light.
A vest in a striking colour with reflective strips.
Something that produces light itself, for example a lamp.

gewusst: With the reflectors on the Moon, the distance to the Earth can be measured to within a few centimetres.
A reflector that shines brightly for a driver looks almost dark to someone standing beside it.
Road signs are coated with reflective film so that they can be read in headlights at night.

teile.einleitung: A shadow play or shadow theatre is a theatre in which you do not see the figures themselves, only their shadows on a bright screen. All you need is a lamp, a white sheet and figures. This old art has existed in Asia and Europe for many centuries, and you can easily try it yourself.
wichtigste: For a shadow theatre you need a lamp, a white sheet and figures.
The audience sits on the other side of the sheet and only sees the shadows.
A shadow forms where an object blocks the light.
Figures are easy to make from card and are moved with thin sticks.
With coloured clear film you get coloured patches.
Wayang from Indonesia is a famous old shadow theatre with leather figures.
With your hands you can make animal shadows such as a rabbit.

abschnitte.text: Light travels in straight lines. If something is in the way, no light arrives behind the object, and a **shadow** forms there. If you hold a figure close to the lamp, its shadow becomes big and a little blurred. If you hold it close to the screen, the shadow becomes smaller and sharper. With several lamps, a dark **umbra** and lighter penumbras form.

abschnitte.titel: How to build a shadow theatre
abschnitte.text: Stretch a white sheet or tracing paper in a frame, for example in an open doorway. Put a bright lamp behind it, and darken the room so that the shadows can be seen clearly. The players stand between the lamp and the sheet, and the audience sits on the other side. Figures are cut out of **card** and stuck onto thin wooden sticks.

If you cut holes in a card figure and stick coloured **clear film** over them, bright patches glow on the screen. Movable arms and legs are attached with split pins and guided with their own sticks. You can also make shadows with your hands alone: two fingers spread apart become a rabbit's ears, and folded hands a flying bird. This is called **hand shadow play**.

The best-known traditional shadow theatre is **Wayang Kulit** from Indonesia, especially from the islands of Java and Bali. Its finely perforated and painted figures are made of buffalo leather, and one player, the dalang, often tells old hero stories for a whole night. China also has a long tradition of shadow play. In Turkey, the funny shadow figure Karagöz is famous.

In the 18th and 19th centuries, shadow theatres were popular in Europe too, for example in Paris. In 1926, the German artist **Lotte Reiniger** created “The Adventures of Prince Achmed”, one of the oldest surviving feature-length animated films, made entirely of paper-cut silhouettes. To this day, shadow theatre groups perform in shows and use their bodies to form whole landscapes. In many Swiss schools and kindergartens, children love to make their own shadow plays and perform them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark area behind an object that no light reaches.
The darkest part of a shadow, where no light from the light sources falls at all.
Traditional puppet theatre from Indonesia; in Wayang Kulit you see the shadows of leather figures.
The dark outline of a figure against a bright background.

gewusst: Wayang Kulit was honoured by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
A shadow can be much bigger than the figure itself if you hold it very close to the lamp.

teile.einleitung: Snowshoes are wide frames that you strap under your shoes so that you do not sink into deep snow. They spread your body weight over a large area. That makes them a fine example of how the physics of pressure helps in everyday life.
wichtigste: Snowshoes increase the contact area and so reduce the pressure on the snow.
Pressure is force divided by area and is measured in pascals.
With a weight of 600 N and a 0.04 m² sole, the pressure is 15,000 Pa; with 0.3 m² snowshoes it is only 2,000 Pa.
Traditional snowshoes consisted of a wooden frame with a web of straps.
Modern snowshoes have spikes for grip and a climbing aid under the heel.
With a heavy rucksack you sink in deeper, because the force gets bigger but the area stays the same.
In Switzerland, snowshoers should respect wildlife quiet zones.

abschnitte.text: **Pressure** tells you how strongly a force presses on an area. It is calculated with the formula pressure equals force divided by area. A person with a weight of 600 N in winter boots with an area of 0.04 m² produces a pressure of 15,000 **pascals**. With snowshoes of 0.3 m² it is only 2,000 Pa, about seven times less, and the snow holds them up much better.

Snowshoes are among the oldest inventions for life in winter. In particular, the **Indigenous peoples** of North America built skilful snowshoes from wooden frames and webs of rawhide straps. In the Alps, too, farmers, hunters and mule drivers used simple snow rings made of bent wood. Long before skiing, they were an important aid there for getting from farm to farm in winter.

Today's snowshoes are usually made of plastic or aluminium. Under the foot there are **spikes** or claws that grip on hard or icy snow. A fold-up **climbing aid** under the heel lifts the foot so that the calves are spared on steep climbs. Poles with large snow baskets are usually used as well.

In winter, animals such as chamois, red deer and black grouse have little food and have to save energy. If they are startled and run away, they use up a lot of strength. That is why Switzerland has **wildlife quiet zones**, which you may not enter, or only on marked routes. You can check where these zones are on the federal government's map portal.

Some animals have built-in snowshoes. The **mountain hare** of the Alps has wide, very hairy hind paws that carry it on powder snow. The ptarmigan also has thickly feathered toes in winter. The principle is always the same: a large area spreads the weight.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force acting on a particular area.
The unit of pressure; 1 Pa is 1 newton per square metre.
A fold-up bar under the heel that helps when walking uphill.
An area where wild animals should be left in peace in winter.

gewusst: In North America there is a hare that is called the snowshoe hare because of its wide paws.
Snowshoeing is a very popular winter sport in Switzerland, because you do not need pistes for it.
Snowshoes come in different sizes, and heavier people need bigger models.

teile.einleitung: Rotational energy is the kinetic energy an object has because it is turning. A spinning wheel, a top or even the whole Earth stores rotational energy. It can be used to store energy and give it back later.
wichtigste: Rotational energy is the kinetic energy of turning.
It is calculated with E = ½ · J · ω².
J is the moment of inertia, ω the angular velocity.
If the angular velocity doubles, the rotational energy quadruples.
A flywheel is a rotating mass that stores energy.
In 1953, the first gyrobus went into regular service in Yverdon-les-Bains.
The Earth's rotational energy is slowly decreasing because of tidal friction.

abschnitte.text: An object that moves has **kinetic energy**. If it turns around an axis, this energy is in the turning and is called **rotational energy**. It is calculated with E = ½ · J · ω². Here ω is the angular velocity, that is how fast the object turns, measured in radians per second. So an object with J = 2 kg·m² turning at 3 rad/s has ½ · 2 · 9 = 9 joules.

The **moment of inertia** J tells you how hard it is to set an object turning. It depends not only on the mass but also on how far the mass is from the axis of rotation. Mass far out counts much more than mass near the axis. That is why a ring has a larger moment of inertia than a disc of the same weight.

A rolling object has both kinetic energy of forward movement and rotational energy. For a rolling **solid cylinder**, a third of the total kinetic energy is rotational energy. If you let a solid ball and a hollow ball of the same weight and size roll down an inclined plane, the **solid ball** reaches the bottom first. The hollow ball has to put more energy into turning, because its mass is on the outside. A solid cylinder rolling down from a height of 0.3 metres is going at about 2 m/s at the bottom.

A **flywheel** is a heavy wheel that stores energy in its turning. In the past, steam engines and sewing machines had large flywheels so that they ran smoothly. A disc with J = 0.5 kg·m² turning at 600 revolutions per minute stores about 990 joules. Because the energy grows with the square of the speed, modern flywheel stores spin very fast, often in an airless casing.

**Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon** developed a bus that ran without overhead wires and without a diesel engine: the **gyrobus**. In its floor, a heavy flywheel turned, which was recharged electrically at every stop. In 1953, the first gyrobus went into regular service in Yverdon-les-Bains. Later, gyrobuses also ran in Belgium and the Congo, but the technology did not catch on.

The Earth also has an enormous amount of rotational energy because of its daily turning. But the **tides**, caused mainly by the Moon, slow the Earth down very gradually. As a result, days are getting longer over millions of years. Hundreds of millions of years ago, a day therefore had clearly fewer than 24 hours.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how hard it is to set an object turning.
Tells you how fast an object turns, measured in radians per second.
A heavy wheel that stores energy in its turning.
The braking effect of the tides on the Earth's rotation.

gewusst: A figure skater spins faster when she pulls her arms in, because her moment of inertia gets smaller.
A gyrobus could travel a few kilometres on one charge of its flywheel.
Because of the tides, the Moon moves a few centimetres further away from the Earth every year.

teile.einleitung: A reversible process is one that can be completely reversed without leaving a trace anywhere. In reality there is never quite such a thing, but the idea is very important in thermodynamics because it shows what is possible at best.
wichtigste: A reversible process can be reversed without any changes remaining in the surroundings.
A process that runs so slowly that the system is always in equilibrium is called quasi-static.
In a reversible process, the total entropy of the system and its surroundings stays the same.
Heat conduction between objects at different temperatures is irreversible.
If an ideal gas flows freely into a vacuum, its temperature stays the same but its entropy rises.
A change of state that is both adiabatic and reversible is called isentropic.
All real processes in nature and technology are more or less irreversible.
The conversion of work into heat, for example by friction, is called dissipation.

abschnitte.text: The word **reversible** means able to be turned back. A process is reversible if you can let it run backwards and afterwards everything, including the surroundings, is exactly as before. A process for which this is not possible is called **irreversible**. A broken glass never puts itself back together by itself; that is a typical irreversible event.

For a process to be almost reversible, it has to run very slowly. The system is then in **equilibrium** at every moment; such a process is called **quasi-static**. If, for example, you push a piston infinitely slowly and without friction into a cylinder of gas, you could pull it out again in just the same way. In practice this is never quite possible, but you can come close to the ideal.

abschnitte.titel: Entropy and the direction of time
abschnitte.text: **Entropy** is a quantity that, put simply, tells you how spread out energy is. According to the second law of thermodynamics, total entropy always increases in irreversible processes and stays the same in reversible ones. That is why heat always flows by itself from the warm object to the cold one and never the other way round. This idea was worked out in the 19th century, among others by Rudolf Clausius.

If a gas flows out of a container into an empty space, it spreads out by itself but never comes back of its own accord. A drop of ink in water also spreads out irreversibly. **Friction** also makes processes irreversible, because kinetic energy is turned into heat; this is called **dissipation**. A frictionless pendulum in a vacuum, on the other hand, would swing almost reversibly.

In 1824, the French engineer Sadi Carnot described an ideal, reversible heat engine, the **Carnot cycle**. It shows the highest efficiency that can be reached at given temperatures. Real engines, refrigerators and power stations always stay below it, because friction and heat losses occur. Engineers try to bring their machines as close as possible to this limit.

begriffe.erklaerung: Able to be turned back without leaving any traces.
A quantity in thermodynamics that describes how spread out energy is.
So slow that the system always stays in equilibrium.
The conversion of kinetic energy or work into heat, for example by friction.

gewusst: Because almost all processes are irreversible, you can tell at once from a film played backwards that something is wrong.
The term entropy was introduced by Rudolf Clausius in 1865.

teile.einleitung: Sound intensity tells you how much sound energy flows through an area of one square metre per second. It is a measure of the strength of sound and the basis for the well-known decibel scale.
wichtigste: Sound intensity is sound power per area.
It is given in watts per square metre.
If an intensity of 10^-4 W/m² falls on 0.5 m², a power of 5 · 10^-5 W arrives.
For a point source, the intensity falls with the square of the distance; at three times the distance it drops to one ninth.
If the vibration amplitude of the air particles doubles, the intensity becomes four times as large.
Two equally loud, independent sound sources together double the intensity.
An effective sound pressure of 2 Pa corresponds to about 0.01 W/m² in air.

abschnitte.text: Sound is a wave in which air particles vibrate back and forth and pass on energy. **Sound intensity** tells you how much energy flows through an area of one square metre per second. It is measured in **watts per square metre**. It is closely linked to **sound pressure**, the small changes in pressure that our ears detect.

A small sound source sends its sound out in all directions, and the energy spreads over an ever larger spherical surface. If it gives out 1 watt, the intensity at a distance of 2 metres is about 0.020 W/m². If you double the distance, the intensity falls to a quarter; if you triple it, to a ninth. This is called the **inverse square law**.

Our ears can hear a huge range, from about 10^-12 W/m² at the **threshold of hearing** up to about 1 W/m² near the threshold of pain. That is a difference of a million million times. That is why the logarithmic unit **decibel** is used: every tenfold increase in intensity gives 10 decibels more. If the intensity doubles, for example through a second equally loud source, the level only rises by about 3 decibels.

The further the air particles swing back and forth, the larger the **amplitude** of the sound wave. Intensity grows with the square of the amplitude. So double the amplitude means four times the intensity. That is why a loudspeaker with slightly stronger cone movement can send much more energy into a room.

Very high sound intensities can permanently damage the fine hair cells in the inner ear. Long and frequent exposure is especially dangerous, for example from loud music through headphones or at concerts. That is why Switzerland has limits on sound levels for concerts and parties. **Ear protection** such as earplugs clearly reduces the intensity that reaches the ear.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy given out by a sound source per second, measured in watts.
Small changes in air pressure produced by a sound wave.
Unit for sound level that makes large differences easy to compare.
The quietest sound a person can only just hear.

gewusst: A whisper and a pneumatic drill differ in sound intensity by more than a million times.
We only feel a sound is twice as loud when its intensity is about ten times as great.

teile.einleitung: Relative humidity tells you how much water vapour there is in the air compared with the largest amount the air can hold at that temperature. It is given as a percentage and helps to decide whether fog, dew or mould forms.
wichtigste: Relative humidity is the ratio of the actual vapour pressure to the saturation vapour pressure.
At 100 per cent, the air is saturated with water vapour.
Warm air can hold much more water vapour than cold air.
If the temperature rises by 10 kelvin, the saturation vapour pressure roughly doubles.
When cold winter air is heated up indoors, its relative humidity falls.
The dew point is the temperature at which the air is saturated and water condenses out.
Hygrometers such as the hair hygrometer or the psychrometer measure humidity.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains some invisible **water vapour**. How much it can carry at most depends on the temperature; this is called the **saturation vapour pressure**. Relative humidity compares the amount present with this maximum. So 50 per cent means that the air contains half as much water vapour as it could hold at that temperature.

At 20 degrees, a cubic metre of air can contain about 17 grams of water as vapour; at 0 degrees, only around 5 grams. Roughly: 10 degrees warmer means about twice as much room for water vapour. This relationship is often calculated with the **Magnus formula**. That is why heated winter air in a flat is so dry, even though the weather outside is wet.

When air cools, its relative humidity rises until it reaches 100 per cent at the **dew point**. Then water condenses into tiny droplets, and dew forms on the grass or fog in the air. In the Swiss Plateau in autumn, the air near the ground often cools so much on clear nights that thick fog forms. Glasses steaming up when you enter a warm room are also a dew point effect.

The **hair hygrometer** uses the fact that human hair gets slightly longer in damp air. The Geneva natural scientist Horace-Bénédict de Saussure developed it in 1783. A **psychrometer** has two thermometers, one dry and one wrapped in a damp cloth. The drier the air, the more water evaporates and the colder the damp thermometer gets; from this the humidity is calculated.

In living spaces, most people find about 40 to 60 per cent comfortable. If the air is very damp for a long time, **mould** can form on cold walls. If it is very dry, the eyes and mucous membranes dry out. Regularly opening the windows wide for a few minutes helps to keep the humidity in the flat in the right range.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water in the form of a gas, spread invisibly through the air.
The state in which the air cannot take in any more water vapour.
The temperature at which water vapour turns into droplets.
A device for measuring humidity.

gewusst: A glass with a cold drink gets wet on the outside because the air next to it cools below the dew point.
In the desert, relative humidity can fall below 10 per cent during the day.
Hair hygrometers are still used today in simple weather stations for the home.

teile.einleitung: A resonance disaster happens when a structure or a machine is pushed again and again in exactly its own rhythm until it breaks. Such accidents have made bridges collapse and are the reason why engineers calculate vibrations very carefully.
wichtigste: A resonance disaster is the destruction of a weakly damped system by being driven at its natural frequency.
In a completely undamped oscillator, the amplitude would in theory grow without limit.
In 1831, the Broughton Suspension Bridge in England collapsed under marching soldiers.
In 1850, a suspension bridge in Angers in France collapsed under soldiers, and more than 200 people died.
The Millennium Bridge in London was closed in 2000 because pedestrians made it sway strongly sideways.
A washing machine shakes hard for a moment as it speeds up, when the drum passes through the machine's natural frequency.
By stiffening a part, its natural frequency can be shifted and resonance avoided.
The dangerous vibration of a helicopter with its rotor running on the ground is called ground resonance.

abschnitte.text: Every structure has a **natural frequency** at which it vibrates especially easily. If it is pushed again and again in exactly this rhythm, it takes in a little energy with each push. If the **damping** is low, the vibration gets bigger and bigger. At some point the material can no longer stand the strain and breaks; that is the **resonance disaster**.

In 1831, soldiers marched in step across the **Broughton Suspension Bridge** near Manchester, and the bridge collapsed. In 1850, in **Angers** in France, the Basse-Chaîne suspension bridge collapsed under a marching battalion, and more than 200 soldiers were killed. Storm and rusty cables probably also played a part in this disaster. Since then, many armies have had the rule of not marching in step on bridges.

In 1940, the **Tacoma Narrows Bridge** in the USA was set into ever more violent vibrations by the wind and collapsed; a film of it is world-famous. Physicists today explain this disaster mainly by flutter, a self-reinforcing vibration caused by the wind. London's **Millennium Bridge** swayed sideways in 2000 because pedestrians adjusted their steps to the swaying. It was closed in time and fitted with dampers.

A **washing machine** shakes especially hard for a moment as the spin cycle starts. At that point, the drum is turning at just the speed of the machine's natural frequency. Once this range has been passed, it gets calmer again. In helicopters on the ground, a dangerous **ground resonance** can arise that can destroy the machine in seconds.

Engineers calculate the natural frequencies of bridges, towers and machines while they are still being planned. By **stiffening** them or adding extra mass, the natural frequency is shifted away from dangerous excitations. **Vibration dampers** take energy from the vibration and keep it small. With machines, dangerous speeds are passed through as quickly as possible so that no large vibration can build up.

begriffe.erklaerung: The largest displacement of a vibration, that is how far it swings.
The rhythm in which an object prefers to vibrate by itself.
Anything that takes energy from a vibration.
The dangerous build-up of vibration in a helicopter with its rotor running on the ground.

gewusst: Because of its swaying, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge got the nickname Galloping Gertie even before it collapsed.
Loudspeaker boxes are also built so that their casing does not vibrate along too much with loud music.

teile.einleitung: Room acoustics studies how sound spreads in a room and how it sounds to us. Whether a gym echoes, a classroom feels calm or a concert hall sounds wonderful depends on the size, shape and materials of the room. Acousticians plan rooms so that people can speak, listen and make music well in them.
wichtigste: Room acoustics describes how sound is reflected, absorbed and scattered in rooms.
An important measure is the reverberation time, that is how long a sound keeps ringing in the room.
An open window has a sound absorption coefficient of 1; it absorbs all sound.
A flutter echo can arise between parallel, smooth walls.
Diffusers scatter sound evenly in all directions.
An anechoic chamber has walls that reflect almost no sound.
The KKL Lucerne opened in 1998 and is famous for its acoustics by Russell Johnson.

abschnitte.text: Sound travels through the air as a wave at about 343 metres per second. In a room, it hits walls, ceiling, floor and furniture. Part of it is **reflected**, part is **absorbed**, that is soaked up, and part is scattered. **Room acoustics** studies these processes and makes sure that a room sounds good for its purpose.

If you hear a reflection at least about 0.1 seconds after the original sound, you perceive it as a separate **echo**. For this, a rock face must be at least about 17 metres away, because the sound has to travel there and back. In closed rooms, the many reflections merge into **reverberation**. The **reverberation time** tells you how long it takes for a sound to become clearly quieter. A classroom needs little reverberation; a church often has a great deal.

How strongly a material absorbs sound is given by the **sound absorption coefficient**, a number between 0 and 1. A smooth concrete wall is close to 0; it reflects almost everything. An open window has the value 1, because the sound simply disappears outside. Curtains, carpets, upholstered furniture and special acoustic panels absorb a lot of sound and make a room quieter.

Between two parallel, smooth walls, sound can bounce quickly back and forth; this is called a **flutter echo**. Between parallel walls, **room modes** also form: standing waves at certain low notes. With walls 5 metres apart, the lowest such room mode is at about 34 hertz. **Diffusers** with an uneven surface scatter the sound evenly and prevent such effects; they are found in recording studios and concert halls.

In an **anechoic chamber**, the walls, ceiling and floor are covered with thick wedges of sound-absorbing material. It is so quiet in there that some people can hear their own heartbeat. Such rooms are used for testing loudspeakers and microphones. The opposite is a **whispering gallery**: along a curved wall, a whisper travels a long way and can be heard clearly at the other end, as in St Paul's Cathedral in London.

Concert halls need a lot of experience so that the music sounds clear and warm everywhere in the hall. The **KKL Lucerne** on Lake Lucerne opened in 1998, built to designs by the French architect Jean Nouvel. Its acoustics were planned by the American acoustician **Russell Johnson** and are considered among the best in the world. A famous pioneer of room acoustics was the American Wallace Clement Sabine, who studied reverberation time scientifically around 1900.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time a sound in a room takes to die away clearly.
The soaking up of sound by a material.
An uneven surface that scatters sound in many directions.
A fast, repeated echo between two parallel walls.
A standing sound wave that strengthens a particular low note in a room.

gewusst: A full concert hall sounds different from an empty one, because people and their clothes absorb sound.
That is why the seats in good concert halls are often upholstered so that an empty seat absorbs about as much sound as a person.
Many visitors can only stand being in an anechoic chamber for a short time, because the complete silence is so unusual.

teile.einleitung: Precession is the slow change in direction of the axis of a spinning object. You can see it well in a spinning top running at a slant, whose axis slowly traces a circle. The Earth's axis also precesses, but so slowly that one turn takes around 26,000 years.
wichtigste: Precession is the change in direction of an axis of rotation under a torque.
In a tilted spinning top, the axis slowly wanders round in a circle.
The faster a top spins, the more slowly it precesses.
The Earth's axis precesses once around in about 26,000 years.
That is why the pole star changes over thousands of years.
Magnetic resonance imaging is based on the precession of nuclear spins in a magnetic field.
The precession of Mercury's perihelion was only fully explained by the general theory of relativity.

abschnitte.text: A spinning object has an **axis of rotation** around which it turns. If a force acts on it in a way that wants to tip it over, it does not simply fall over. Instead, the axis moves off to the side and slowly traces a cone. This movement is called **precession**. In physics, the tipping effect of a force is called **torque**.

abschnitte.titel: The spinning top as an example
abschnitte.text: If a fast-spinning top stands tilted on the table, gravity wants to tip it over. But because it is spinning, its axis slowly wanders round in a circle instead of falling over. The faster the top spins, the **more slowly** it precesses. As friction slows it down, the circling of the axis becomes faster and wobblier, until it finally falls over. You can see something similar with a rolling bicycle wheel or a coin spinning on the table.

For a spinning top, you can calculate the speed of precession: you divide the torque by the angular momentum. The torque is mass times acceleration due to gravity times the distance to the centre of gravity, and the **angular momentum** is moment of inertia times spinning speed. For a top of 0.5 kg, a distance of 0.1 m to the centre of gravity, a moment of inertia of 0.002 kg·m² and 200 rad/s, that gives 0.49 divided by 0.4, about 1.2 rad/s. If it spins twice as fast, the speed of precession is halved.

The Earth is a little fatter at the equator than at the poles, and its axis is tilted. The Sun and Moon pull on this bulge and try to straighten the Earth's axis. That is why the **Earth's axis** traces a large cone, and one turn takes around 26,000 years. Today the axis points almost exactly at the **pole star**; in a few thousand years, other stars will take on the role of the north star. This movement was already discovered by the Greek astronomer Hipparchus in the 2nd century BC.

Tiny atomic nuclei also behave like little spinning tops with a **nuclear spin**. In a strong magnetic field they precess, and **magnetic resonance imaging** uses this movement to make pictures of the inside of the body. In space, the orbit of Mercury slowly turns around the Sun; this is called the precession of the perihelion. A small part of it could not be explained for a long time, until Albert Einstein found the solution in 1915 with the **general theory of relativity**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line around which an object turns.
The effect of a force that wants to turn or tip an object.
A measure of how much turning motion an object has.
A toy or device that spins quickly around its axis.
The star that the Earth's axis points at almost exactly today.

gewusst: In around 12,000 years, the bright star Vega will roughly take on the role of the pole star.
Because of precession, the star signs of astrology no longer match the constellations in front of which the Sun actually stands today.
An MRI scanner uses the precession of the hydrogen nuclei in our body to produce images.

teile.einleitung: The Reynolds number is a figure that tells you whether a flow is calm and orderly or wild and swirling. It helps engineers design pipes, aircraft and ships, and it even explains why bacteria swim quite differently from fish.
wichtigste: The Reynolds number describes the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces.
It is calculated as speed times length divided by the kinematic viscosity.
It has no unit; it is dimensionless.
In pipes, a flow usually stays laminar below about 2300.
In 1883, Osborne Reynolds made the change to turbulent flow visible with a thread of dye in a glass tube.
A model at a scale of 1 to 10 must be met by the same fluid at 10 times the speed for the Reynolds number to stay the same.
At a very small Reynolds number, viscosity dominates, which is why a bacterium cannot glide on after a swimming stroke.

abschnitte.text: When water, air or oil flows, two kinds of force act. **Inertia** wants to keep the movement going, and **viscosity** slows it down like inner friction. The Reynolds number tells you which of the two is stronger. If it is small, viscosity wins; if it is large, inertia wins.

You multiply the **flow speed** by a typical length, such as the diameter of the pipe, and divide by the kinematic viscosity of the fluid. If water flows at 0.5 m/s through a pipe 2 cm across, that gives a Reynolds number of 10,000. If air flows at 30 m/s around a model car 1 m long, you get about 2 million. Because all the units cancel out, the number is **dimensionless**.

At a small Reynolds number, the flow is **laminar**: the layers slide past each other in an orderly way. Above a critical value, about 2300 in pipes, the flow becomes **turbulent** and eddies form. You can see this at the tap too: a thin, slow stream is crystal clear, a fast, thick stream becomes unsteady. Turbulent flows slow things down more but mix substances and heat better.

In 1883, the British engineer **Osborne Reynolds** sent water through a glass tube and added a thin thread of dye. With slow flow the thread stayed a straight line; with fast flow it suddenly swirled and coloured all the water. Reynolds realised that this change depends on a single figure. It was later given the name Reynolds number in his honour.

In a **wind tunnel**, small models of cars or aircraft are tested. For the results to match the original, the Reynolds number must be the same, so a smaller model needs a higher speed. For bacteria, the Reynolds number is tiny; water feels to them like thick honey does to us. For a whale or an aircraft, on the other hand, it is many millions.

begriffe.erklaerung: How thick and sticky a liquid or gas is; honey has a high viscosity, water a low one.
Flowing in orderly layers without eddies.
Flowing in an unsteady, swirling way.
Without a unit; just a pure number.

gewusst: The blood in the large blood vessels usually flows laminarly; doctors can sometimes hear turbulence as a sound with a stethoscope.
Golf balls have dimples because the turbulent boundary layer they create reduces air resistance, so the ball flies further.

teile.einleitung: Iridescence is when a surface shimmers in rainbow colours and its colours change depending on the angle you look at it from. You can see it on soap bubbles, oil patches, peacock feathers or a CD. These colours do not come from dyes but from tiny structures that reflect light in a special way.
wichtigste: Iridescent colours change with the viewing angle.
They come from fine structures, not from dyes.
A thin film of oil on a puddle shimmers in many colours.
The underside of a CD shines in many colours because of its fine grooves.
Mother of pearl in shells shimmers because of many thin layers.
Peacocks, kingfishers and rose chafers shimmer thanks to structural colours.
The bright blue of some butterflies comes from tiny structures on their scales.

abschnitte.text: Normal colours, for example of a red jumper, come from **dyes** that swallow part of the light. Iridescent colours are different: they are called **structural colours**, because they come from tiny structures smaller than the width of a hair. Typically, the colour changes when you move your head or turn the object. That is why a soap bubble never looks the same twice.

Light is a wave, and white light contains all colours. When it falls on a very thin film, such as a soap skin or a film of oil on a puddle, it is reflected at the top and at the bottom. The two light waves overlap: some colours are strengthened, others cancel each other out. This interplay is called **interference**, and depending on the thickness of the film and the viewing angle, a different colour lights up.

On the underside of a CD there is a track of tiny pits running very close together. It acts like a **diffraction grating**: the light is bent at the grooves and split into its colours. That is why you see a rainbow on a CD. The security images on banknotes and credit cards, which change their appearance when you tilt them, work in a similar way.

The tail feathers of the **peacock**, with their eye patterns, shimmer in blue, green and gold. By Swiss streams you can spot the **kingfisher**, whose back shimmers a brilliant blue. The rose chafer shines a metallic green, and some tropical morpho butterflies glow a deep blue, even though their wings contain no blue dye at all. Animals use such colours to stand out, impress rivals or confuse enemies.

The inside of some mussel and snail shells shimmers delicately in many colours. This material is called **mother of pearl** and consists of a great many wafer-thin plates of lime lying on top of each other like bricks. Pearls are also built from mother of pearl. In the past it was used to make buttons and jewellery, and opals and some minerals also shimmer in a similar way.

begriffe.erklaerung: Colour produced by tiny structures and not by dye.
The overlapping of light waves, in which colours are strengthened or cancelled out.
A surface with very fine, regular grooves that splits light into colours.
The shimmering inner layer of shells, made of thin plates of lime.

gewusst: A peacock feather contains no blue or green dye at all; its colours come only from structure.
Just before a soap bubble bursts, its skin becomes so thin that it looks almost black at that spot.

teile.einleitung: Horsepower, abbreviated in German as PS (Pferdestärke), is an old unit of power, that is of how much work a machine can do in a certain time. One metric horsepower is about 735 watts. Although the kilowatt is now the official unit, many people still talk about horsepower when it comes to cars.
wichtigste: Metric horsepower is a unit of power and is abbreviated PS in German.
One PS is roughly 735 watts.
The idea for it, the English horsepower, comes from James Watt.
Today, the kilowatt is officially the unit for the power of engines.
100 PS is about 74 kilowatts, and 110 kilowatts is about 150 PS.
A cyclist producing 250 watts manages about 0.34 PS.
A real horse can briefly produce clearly more than 1 PS.

abschnitte.text: **Power** tells you how quickly work is done. A metric horsepower is defined exactly as the power needed to lift 75 kilograms by one metre in one second. Converted, that is about 735 **watts**. The name is a reminder that the strength of machines used to be compared with the work of horses.

abschnitte.titel: James Watt and the steam engine
abschnitte.text: In the 18th century, the Scot **James Watt** improved the steam engine. To sell it, he wanted to show how many horses it could replace. To do this, he estimated roughly what a mine horse could do when driving a pump or a mill and called it “horsepower”. At about 746 watts, the English horsepower is slightly larger than the German metric horsepower.

Today, the **kilowatt** is the official unit in the International System of Units, including in Switzerland. One kilowatt is 1000 watts and about 1.36 PS. So a car with 100 PS has about 74 kilowatts, and an engine with 110 kilowatts about 150 PS. That is why vehicle registration documents show kilowatts, while adverts often still give horsepower.

A cyclist who produces 250 watts over a longer time manages about 0.34 PS. A healthy **horse** can manage about one horsepower over a whole working day. For a short time, for example when starting to pull, it can produce clearly more than 1 PS. A normal car often has over 100 PS, and a large SBB locomotive even several thousand kilowatts.

With power, you can compare devices and engines. In Switzerland, the **electric motor** of an e-bike produces at most 500 or 1000 watts depending on the category, and a vacuum cleaner uses about as much as a horse can produce. Because different countries used different kinds of horsepower, the watt was introduced as a single unit. It is named after James Watt, of all people the inventor of horsepower.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much work is done in a certain time.
The unit of power, named after James Watt.
1000 watts, the official unit for the power of engines.
A machine that produces movement with hot steam.

gewusst: A trained person can produce more than 1 horsepower for a few seconds, for example when sprinting up stairs.
Formula 1 cars today reach around 1000 horsepower.
You also know the kilowatt from the electricity bill, because energy is shown there in kilowatt-hours.

teile.einleitung: The coefficient of friction, often written with the Greek letter μ (mu), tells you how strongly two surfaces rub against each other.
