It decides whether a car brakes well, whether you slip on ice or whether a sledge glides easily. The larger the coefficient of friction, the more force you need to move something.
wichtigste: The coefficient of friction μ is the friction force divided by the normal force.
It has no unit and depends on the two materials that are touching.
There is static friction, sliding friction and rolling friction.
The coefficient of sliding friction is usually smaller than the coefficient of static friction.
A car tyre on dry tarmac has a coefficient of static friction of about 0.7 to 1.
A steel runner on ice has a very small coefficient of sliding friction of about 0.01.
Guillaume Amontons formulated the classic laws of friction in 1699.

abschnitte.titel: What is the coefficient of friction?
abschnitte.text: When two objects touch, a **friction force** acts between them that works against movement. How large it is depends on how hard the objects are pressed together. This pressing force at right angles to the surface is called the **normal force**; on level ground it equals the weight. The **coefficient of friction** μ is the ratio of the two: friction force divided by normal force. It has no unit and is usually a number between 0 and about 1.

**Static friction** has to be overcome for an object at rest to start sliding at all. Once it is moving, **sliding friction** acts, and this is usually smaller. That is why you need more force to get a heavy box moving than to keep pushing it afterwards. **Rolling friction**, for example with wheels, is often the smallest. Because steel wheels on steel rails have especially little rolling friction, a train needs comparatively little energy.

For the friction force: F = μ · normal force. A 20 kg box has a weight of about 196 N, so with μ = 0.4 you need about 78.5 N to pull it along steadily. The other way round, if you need 30 N for a 10 kg block, the coefficient of sliding friction is about 0.31. You can also estimate the **braking distance**: a car at 25 m/s, that is 90 km/h, needs about 64 m to stop on a wet road with μ = 0.5. Interestingly, the size of the contact area makes approximately no difference.

abschnitte.titel: History of the laws of friction
abschnitte.text: Around 1500, **Leonardo da Vinci** was already studying friction with blocks and weights. But his notes did not become known for a long time. In 1699, the French physicist **Guillaume Amontons** formulated the classic laws of friction. Around 100 years later, Charles-Augustin de Coulomb added to these laws through many experiments. That is why people speak of the law of Amontons and Coulomb.

Friction is sometimes wanted and sometimes a nuisance. So that cars, bikes and shoes do not slip, a lot of static friction is needed, which is why tyres have **treads** and in winter there are snow chains and road salt. On wet or icy roads, the coefficient of friction drops sharply, and the braking distance becomes much longer. In ice skating, curling or skiing, on the other hand, you want as little friction as possible. In machines, oil and ball bearings reduce friction so that less energy is lost.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force between two surfaces that works against movement.
The force with which an object presses at right angles on a surface.
The friction that stops an object at rest from sliding away.
The friction that acts when an object slides over a surface.
The unit of force, abbreviated N.

gewusst: Because static friction is greater than sliding friction, a car with ABS brakes better: the wheels do not lock and do not slide.
In curling, players sweep the ice in front of the stone so that it glides further and straighter.
Without friction you could not walk, because your shoes would simply slide away on the ground.

teile.einleitung: An escalator is a staircase whose steps move like a conveyor belt and carry people up or down automatically. In stations, department stores and airports, it takes countless people comfortably from floor to floor every day.
wichtigste: On an escalator, the steps move, and you can stand still yourself.
You should hold on to the handrail, which moves along with the steps.
In Switzerland, people usually stand on the right on the escalator so that those in a hurry can walk on the left.
The yellow edges are warning markings; shoes can get trapped there.
At the top, the steps become flat and disappear under the floor.
A flat moving walkway without steps is called a travelator; you find it in airports, for example.
With a pram, it is safer to take the lift.
Escalators are often found in stations and department stores.

abschnitte.text: An **escalator** consists of many individual steps attached to two endless chains. An electric motor drives the chains so that the steps move in a loop. On the visible side they form a staircase, and underneath they run back. Most escalators move at about half a metre per second.

Each step has small rollers that run in **guide rails**. The rails are shaped so that the steps form a staircase on the sloping part and lie flat against each other at the beginning and end. At the top and bottom, the steps disappear behind a toothed comb, the **comb plate**. The **handrail** is a rubber belt that moves at the same speed as the steps.

You hold on to the handrail and put your feet in the middle of the step, not on the yellow edges. Shoes, shoelaces or long clothes could get trapped there. Children should not play on the escalator or sit on the steps. With a pram, wheelchair or large luggage, it is better to take the **lift**, and in an emergency there is a red emergency stop button at the bottom and the top.

At the end of the 19th century, several inventors in the USA were working on moving staircases, including Jesse Reno and Charles Seeberger. At the 1900 World's Fair in Paris, an escalator was shown to a large audience. Seeberger coined the English word **escalator**, which later became a common term. The Swiss company **Schindler** from Ebikon in the canton of Lucerne is now one of the largest makers of escalators and lifts in the world.

A **travelator** is a flat or slightly sloping moving walkway without steps, on which you can also ride with a suitcase or a shopping trolley. You find them in airports, long station corridors and some shopping centres. In Hong Kong, there is a whole system of outdoor escalators that takes pedestrians up a steep hill. Many modern escalators slow down or stop when no one is on them, to save electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The moving rubber belt at the side that you hold on to.
The toothed plate at the end under which the steps disappear.
A moving walkway without steps, for example at the airport.
A button with which you can stop the escalator immediately in an emergency.

gewusst: Escalator was originally a brand name but was used so often that it is now an ordinary English word.
Some underground stations are so deep that you ride the escalator for several minutes.

teile.einleitung: A fuse is a small safety component in the electricity network that protects the wires from too much current. Inside it is a thin wire that melts if the current becomes too strong. This breaks the circuit before the cables get hot and a fire can start.
wichtigste: In a fuse, a thin wire melts if the current becomes too great.
It mainly protects the wiring in the house from overheating.
A fuse that has blown must be replaced with a new one.
The rating of a fuse is given in amperes.
You must never bridge a fuse with a piece of wire.
Fuse cartridges are often filled with quartz sand, which puts out the electric arc.
A circuit breaker can simply be switched on again after it has tripped.

abschnitte.text: If too much current flows through a cable, it gets hot. This happens, for example, with a **short circuit** or when too many powerful devices are connected to the same wire. Without protection, the insulation could melt and a fire could start. The **fuse** is deliberately the weakest point in the circuit and breaks it in time.

Inside a fuse there is a fine **fuse element**, a thin wire or strip of metal. Normal current flows through it without any problem. If the current becomes too great, the thin wire heats up more than the cable and melts through. A small **electric arc** can form as this happens, which the quartz sand in the cartridge quickly smothers.

Every fuse shows the current at which it blows, measured in **amperes**. In flats, ratings such as 10 or 13 amperes are common. Many screw-in fuses have a small coloured disc at the front that falls off when the fuse has blown; red, for example, stands for 10 amperes. A fuse may only be replaced by one with exactly the same rating.

The fuses of a house are in the **fuse box**, often in the cellar or the hallway. In newer houses, instead of fuses you usually find **circuit breakers**. They also trip if there is too much current, but afterwards they can simply be switched on again with a lever. There is also the residual current device, RCD for short, which protects people from electric shocks.

You must never bridge a blown fuse with a piece of wire or kitchen foil. Then the protection is gone, and the wires can overheat and start a fire. If a fuse keeps blowing, a device is usually faulty or the wiring is overloaded. In that case an electrician should take a look. Cars, chargers and many household appliances also contain small fuses.

begriffe.erklaerung: A safety component that breaks the circuit if there is too much current.
The unit of measurement for electric current.
A bright, very hot spark that jumps through the air when current is broken.
An automatic fuse that can be switched on again after it has tripped.

gewusst: A fuse sacrifices itself: it breaks on purpose so that nothing more valuable is damaged.
A car often has dozens of small blade fuses in different colours, each for a different circuit.

teile.einleitung: The theory of relativity is one of the most important theories in physics and comes from Albert Einstein. It shows that space and time are not the same for everyone and that gravity is a curvature of spacetime. Einstein developed part of it in Bern while he was working at the patent office there.
wichtigste: The theory of relativity consists of the special theory (1905) and the general theory of relativity (1915).
Einstein published the special theory of relativity in 1905 while working at the patent office in Bern.
It is based on the fact that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for everyone.
At very high speeds, time passes more slowly; this is called time dilation.
The general theory of relativity describes gravity as a curvature of spacetime.
Without the theory of relativity, GPS would be kilometres out every day.
Gravitational waves were measured directly for the first time in 2015.

abschnitte.text: **Albert Einstein** was born in Ulm in 1879 and studied at ETH Zurich. From 1902 he worked as an expert at the Federal Patent Office in **Bern**. In 1905, his miracle year, he published several groundbreaking papers there, including the special theory of relativity. His flat at the time on the Kramgasse is now a museum, the Einstein House.

The special theory of relativity is based on one principle: the **speed of light** in a vacuum is the same for all observers moving at constant speed, around 300,000 kilometres per second. From this it follows that moving clocks run slow; this is called **time dilation**. If a spaceship flies at 80 per cent of the speed of light, for example, 6 years pass on board but 10 years on Earth. The famous formula E = mc², which links mass and energy, also comes from the theory.

In 1915 in Berlin, Einstein presented the **general theory of relativity**. It describes gravity not as an invisible pulling force but as a curvature of **spacetime** caused by mass and energy. You can picture it like a stretched rubber sheet into which a heavy ball presses a dent. Smaller balls then roll on curved paths around the dent, much like planets around the Sun.

As early as 1919, researchers observed during a solar eclipse that starlight is bent by the Sun, as Einstein had predicted. In 2015, the LIGO detectors in the USA measured **gravitational waves** directly for the first time: tiny waves in spacetime from two black holes merging. **Black holes** themselves also follow from the theory. In 2019, the first picture of the shadow of a black hole was published.

Because of relativistic effects, the clocks in **GPS satellites** run around 38 microseconds a day faster than clocks on the ground. Without correction, the position shown on your mobile phone would be around 10 kilometres out every day. Particle accelerators such as the one at **CERN** near Geneva also have to take the theory of relativity into account. There, particles fly at almost the speed of light.

begriffe.erklaerung: Space and time considered together as a single structure.
At high speed or in strong gravity, time passes more slowly.
The highest possible speed, around 300,000 kilometres per second.
A tiny wave in spacetime given off by very heavy objects.

gewusst: Einstein did not receive the Nobel Prize for the theory of relativity but for explaining the photoelectric effect.
On a high mountain such as the Jungfraujoch, time passes very slightly faster than in the valley.
Einstein was a Swiss citizen; he received citizenship of Zurich in 1901.

teile.einleitung: Reflection means that light, sound or other waves are thrown back from a surface. Without reflection, we could not see most of the things around us at all. Mirrors, bicycle reflectors and even the Moon in the night sky work thanks to reflection.
wichtigste: In reflection, light is thrown back from a surface.
The law of reflection says that the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal.
We see objects that do not give off light because they reflect light.
A reflection in a flat mirror appears reversed left to right.
On rough surfaces, light is thrown back in a disorderly way; this is called diffuse reflection.
Bicycle reflectors throw back the light from headlights and make cyclists visible.

abschnitte.text: When light hits a surface, it can be absorbed, let through or thrown back. Throwing back is called **reflection**. Bright surfaces such as fresh snow reflect a great deal of light, dark surfaces such as tarmac only a little. Sound is reflected too, which is how the **echo** in the mountains comes about.

On a smooth mirror, the **law of reflection** applies: the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal. Both angles are measured from the **normal**, an imaginary line at right angles to the mirror. If a ray hits at 35 degrees to the normal, it is reflected at 35 degrees on the other side. Between the incoming and the reflected ray there are then 70 degrees altogether.

Lamps and the Sun shine by themselves, but most things do not. We see a table or a book because they reflect light in all directions and part of it reaches our eyes. On rough surfaces such as paper, **diffuse reflection** happens: the light is spread out in a disorderly way. On smooth surfaces such as a mirror or still water, on the other hand, **specular reflection** happens, and with it a mirror image.

In a flat mirror, the image appears the same size and seems to be as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. If you raise your right hand, your reflection seems to raise its left; the image is said to be **reversed left to right**. That is why on some ambulances the word for ambulance is written in mirror writing. In a car's rear-view mirror, drivers can then read it the right way round.

**Reflectors** on bicycles, school bags and high-visibility vests throw the light from car headlights straight back to the light source. This means children on their way to school in the dark can be seen from far away. Cat's eyes on roadside posts work the same way. Periscopes in submarines and rear-view mirrors also use reflection in mirrors.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line at right angles to a surface.
The angle between the incoming ray and the normal.
Light is scattered in many directions by a rough surface.
An object that throws light back towards the light source.

gewusst: The Moon does not shine by itself; we only see reflected sunlight.
Fresh snow reflects up to about 90 per cent of sunlight, which is why you need sunglasses in the mountains.
Astronauts set up mirrors on the Moon, which are used to measure the distance to the Earth by laser.

teile.einleitung: Radiocarbon dating is a method researchers use to find out the age of things that were once alive. It works like a built-in clock in wood, bone or cloth. This is how we know, for example, how old the charcoal from a Stone Age fireplace is.
wichtigste: Radiocarbon dating uses the radioactive isotope carbon-14, C-14 for short.
C-14 forms in the atmosphere when neutrons from cosmic rays change nitrogen-14.
In living organisms, about one in a trillion carbon atoms is a C-14 atom.
After death, C-14 slowly decays; after about 5730 years only half is left.
The American Willard Libby developed the method and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1960.
It can be used to date samples up to about 50,000 years old.
With accelerator mass spectrometry, samples of just milligrams are enough.

abschnitte.text: Carbon comes in different kinds, called **isotopes**. Almost all carbon is carbon-12, and a small part is carbon-13. Only about one part in a trillion is the radioactive **carbon-14**. It forms high up in the atmosphere when neutrons from cosmic rays hit nitrogen-14 and change it.

abschnitte.titel: How does C-14 get into living things?
abschnitte.text: The new C-14 combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide. Plants take in this carbon dioxide during **photosynthesis** and build the carbon into their leaves and wood. Animals and people eat plants and so also take in C-14. As long as a living thing is alive, its share of C-14 therefore stays almost the same as in the air.

When a living thing dies, it no longer takes in new carbon. The C-14 that is there now slowly decays back into nitrogen. After about 5730 years, half has decayed; this time is called the **half-life**. If you measure how much C-14 is left, you can work out when the living thing died. After around 50,000 years, so little is left that it can hardly be measured.

In the past, the individual decays in the sample were counted with a counting tube, which needed several grams of material. Today the C-14 atoms are counted directly with **accelerator mass spectrometry**. Samples of just milligrams are enough for this, such as a tiny piece of bone or a few seeds. One such facility is at ETH Zurich, for example.

The share of C-14 in the air has not always been exactly the same. That is why the measurements are compared with wood whose age is known exactly. This is done with **dendrochronology**, in which the annual rings of trees are counted. This conversion is called **calibration**; only then do you get an age in calendar years.

Suitable materials are wood, charcoal, bone, shells, seeds, leather or cloth. The method was used, for example, to find the age of the glacier mummy **Ötzi**, who lived about 5300 years ago. The lake dwellings on Swiss lakes have also been studied this way. Stones or metal cannot be dated with it, because they were never alive.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of chemical element with a different number of neutrons in the atomic nucleus.
The time it takes for half of a radioactive substance to decay.
Very fast particles from space that hit the Earth's atmosphere.
Matching a measurement against known values so that the result is correct.
Finding out how old something is.

gewusst: The many atomic bomb tests in the 1950s and 1960s greatly increased the share of C-14 in the air.
With this bomb effect, you can even determine the age of cells in the human body.
Libby tested his method on wood from Egyptian tombs whose age was already known from historical sources.

teile.einleitung: A mercury barometer is a device for measuring air pressure in which a column of liquid mercury stands in a glass tube. It was invented by the Italian Evangelista Torricelli in the 17th century. With it, people proved for the first time that air has weight and exerts pressure.
wichtigste: A mercury barometer measures air pressure with a column of mercury.
Evangelista Torricelli was Galileo Galilei's assistant shortly before Galileo's death.
The glass tube in Torricelli's experiment was about 1 metre long.
The almost empty space above the mercury is called the Torricellian vacuum.
The height of the column does not depend on the diameter or tilt of the tube.
The unit of pressure torr is named after Torricelli.
Mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water.
Because mercury is poisonous, mercury barometers are hardly used any more today.

abschnitte.text: In 1643 or 1644, **Evangelista Torricelli** filled a glass tube about 1 metre long, closed at one end, with **mercury**. Then he turned it upside down and stood the open end in a dish of mercury. The mercury sank a little but stopped at a height of about 76 centimetres. At the top of the tube there was an almost empty space, the **Torricellian vacuum**.

The air presses from above on the mercury in the dish. This **air pressure** holds the column up in the tube. If the air pressure rises, the column rises too; if it falls, the column falls. The vertical height of the column stays the same even if you hold the tube at a slant or use a wider tube, because only the height counts for the pressure.

Normal air pressure at sea level corresponds to a column of mercury 760 millimetres high. In Torricelli's honour, the unit millimetre of mercury is also called the **torr**. Today air pressure is usually measured in **hectopascals**, with about 1013 hPa being normal. But for blood pressure, millimetres of mercury, abbreviated mmHg, are still used today.

Mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water. With water, you would therefore need a tube over 10 metres long. Mercury is also liquid at room temperature and evaporates only a little. However, mercury is **poisonous**, which is why such barometers are now replaced by **aneroid barometers** and electronic sensors.

Shortly before Galileo's death, Torricelli was the assistant of the famous **Galileo Galilei** in Florence. His experiment showed that air has weight and that a **vacuum** is possible, which many people doubted at the time. In 1648, the Frenchman Blaise Pascal had the barometer carried up a mountain, the Puy de Dôme. At the top the column was lower, because air pressure is lower at height.

A barometer can be used to forecast the **weather**: falling air pressure often announces bad weather, rising air pressure fine weather. Altitude can also be worked out, because air pressure decreases as you go up. On a high Swiss alpine summit it is clearly lower than in the Swiss Plateau. That is why water boils below 100 degrees on mountains.

begriffe.erklaerung: The pressure that air exerts on everything through its weight.
A device for measuring air pressure.
An old unit of pressure equal to one millimetre of mercury.
A space in which there are almost no particles.

gewusst: In a barometer, water would have to rise over 10 metres, as high as a three-storey house.
The word “barometer” comes from the Greek “baros” for weight.
Blood pressure is still given in millimetres of mercury today.

teile.einleitung: The pan flute is an ancient wind instrument made of many pipes fixed side by side. Each pipe gives its own note, and the longest sounds the lowest. The pan flute is a wonderful example for understanding how vibrating air turns into music.
wichtigste: A pan flute consists of many pipes of different lengths side by side.
The pipes are closed at the bottom and open at the top.
You play it by blowing across the top edge of a pipe.
Each pipe normally gives only one note.
The longer the pipe, the lower the note.
The instrument is named after the Greek shepherd god Pan.
Pan flutes used to be made mostly of reed or bamboo, and they are still very popular in the Andes of South America today.

abschnitte.text: A pan flute consists of several **pipes** arranged by length like a staircase. They are held together with string, raffia or a crosspiece of wood. The pipes are closed at the bottom, for example by a natural knot in the bamboo or a plug. In the past, reed or bamboo was mostly used; today there are also pan flutes made of wood, plastic or metal.

You hold the pipe against your lower lip and blow a fine stream of air across the **edge**. The stream of air is split at the edge and sets the air inside the pipe vibrating. This **air column** vibrates at a certain frequency, which we hear as a note. It sounds similar when you blow across the neck of an empty bottle.

The pitch depends on the length of the air column. In a long pipe, the sound wave takes longer to travel there and back, the **frequency** is lower and the note is deeper. Short pipes sound high accordingly. Because the pipes are closed at the bottom, a pipe sounds about an octave lower than a pipe of the same length that is open at both ends. By changing the angle of blowing, a skilled player can bend a note up or down a little.

The name comes from **Greek mythology**. Pan was a god of shepherds and flocks, half man and half goat. According to the legend, the nymph Syrinx turned into reeds while fleeing from him, and Pan then cut his flute from them. That is why the pan flute is also called syrinx in Greek.

Pan flutes existed thousands of years ago in many parts of the world, for example in China, Europe and South America. In the **Andes**, for example in Peru and Bolivia, it is called siku or zampoña and is part of traditional music. In Romania, a curved pan flute called the nai is played. In Switzerland, too, you often hear pan flutes from street musicians and in music schools.

begriffe.erklaerung: The air inside a pipe that vibrates when you blow.
How often something vibrates per second; it decides the pitch.
The distance between two notes in which the higher one vibrates twice as fast.
A nature spirit in the form of a young woman from the Greek legends.

gewusst: You can make a simple pan flute from drinking straws closed at the bottom with modelling clay.
In biology, the voice organ of birds is also called the syrinx, like the pan flute.
A pipe that is half as long sounds about an octave higher.

teile.einleitung: An inclined plane is a sloping surface that lets you move loads upwards with less force. It is one of humanity's simplest machines. Ramps, mountain roads with hairpin bends and wheelchair ramps are all inclined planes.
wichtigste: An inclined plane is a sloping surface, for example a ramp.
On it you need less force to bring a load up, but the distance is longer.
The force that pulls a body down the slope is called the downhill force.
The steeper the plane, the greater the downhill force.
The inclined plane is one of the simple machines, like the lever and the pulley.
The wedge and the screw work on the same principle.

abschnitte.text: An **inclined plane** is any sloping surface that connects a lower point with a higher one. Examples are ramps on lorries, wheelchair ramps and ski slopes. It counts as one of the **simple machines**, like the lever, pulley and wheel. People were already using it for buildings in ancient times.

If you lift a box straight up, you have to carry its whole weight. On an inclined plane, the surface supports part of the weight. So you need less force, but you have to cover a longer distance. This rule is called the **golden rule of mechanics**: what you save in force, you have to add in distance.

The weight of a body on a slope can be split into two parts. One part presses the body at right angles onto the surface; this is the **normal force**. The other part pulls it down the slope; this is the **downhill force**. The steeper the road, the greater the downhill force and the harder a car has to brake or pull.

Many pass roads such as the Gotthard or the Grimsel wind up in **hairpin bends**, so that the gradient is smaller. This makes the road longer, but cars and bicycles get up more easily. With gradients of up to 48 per cent, the Pilatus Railway is the steepest cog railway in the world. Stairs and zigzag hiking paths also use the principle of the inclined plane.

A **wedge**, such as an axe, is an inclined plane that is driven into wood. A **screw** is an inclined plane wound around a rod. That is why you can turn a screw deep into wood with little force. Long ramps were probably also used to build the Egyptian pyramids.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that pulls a body down a slope.
The force with which a body presses at right angles onto a surface.
How steep a road or surface is, often given as a percentage.
A simple aid that saves force, such as a lever or a ramp.

gewusst: A gradient of 100 per cent corresponds to an angle of 45 degrees, not a vertical wall.
Galileo Galilei rolled balls down inclined planes to study the laws of falling.

teile.einleitung: The cutting edge is the sharp, very narrow edge of a knife, a pair of scissors or an axe. The reason it cuts so easily has to do with physics: a small force on a tiny area produces enormous pressure. The same principle is found in drawing pins, needles and ice skates.
wichtigste: A cutting edge is the sharp, wedge-shaped edge of a tool.
Pressure is force divided by area.
The narrower the edge, the greater the pressure for the same force.
With a blunt knife you have to press harder, because the edge is wider.
Sharpening makes the edge narrow and sharp again.
Drawing pins, needles, skate blades and cheese wires also use high pressure.
Sharp edges are dangerous and must be used carefully.

abschnitte.text: A cutting edge is the very front, sharp edge of a blade. In cross section it looks like a very pointed **wedge**. Knives, scissors, hatchets, planes and razor blades all have a cutting edge. Cutting edges are usually made of hard **steel**, and some kitchen knives of ceramic.

**Pressure** tells you how strongly a force acts on an area. It is calculated by dividing the force by the area, and its unit is called the **pascal**. A knife edge 10 centimetres long and 0.1 millimetres wide has an area of only 0.00001 square metres. If you press with 20 newtons, the pressure is 2,000,000 pascals. This enormous pressure separates the fibres of a tomato or a loaf of bread effortlessly.

Over time, a cutting edge wears and becomes wider and rounder. Then the knife is **blunt**: the area is bigger, so the pressure is smaller, and you have to press harder. When **sharpening** on a whetstone, material is removed until the edge is narrow again. A sharp knife is actually safer, because it is less likely to slip.

A **drawing pin** has a wide head and a fine point: there is little pressure on your thumb and a great deal at the point. A hypodermic needle is ground at an angle so that its fine point goes in with little force. Ice skate blades are narrow and so produce high pressure on the ice. With a thin wire you can even cut up a wheel of cheese.

As early as the Stone Age, people made blades by knapping flint or obsidian. Such blades could be amazingly sharp. Later came blades of bronze and then of **iron** and steel. In Switzerland, the **Swiss Army knife** is famous; it has been made in Ibach in the canton of Schwyz since the end of the 19th century.

Always cut away from your body and keep your fingers behind the edge. On a firm chopping board, the food slips less. Carry knives with the point facing down, and do not put them in a sink where you cannot see them. Younger children should only use knives with an adult.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a force presses on a particular area.
The unit of measurement for pressure, shortened to Pa.
The unit of measurement for force, shortened to N.
A body that is thick on one side and very thin on the other.

gewusst: Blades made of obsidian, a volcanic glass, can be sharper than steel blades.
A woman in stiletto heels presses harder on the ground with her heel than an elephant does with one foot.
Many professional cooks sharpen their knives regularly on a wet whetstone.

teile.einleitung: A rain gauge, also called a precipitation gauge, is a device that measures how much rain or snow has fallen. The amount of rain is given in millimetres. Weather services need such measurements to observe the weather, spot floods and study the climate.
wichtigste: A rain gauge is also called a precipitation gauge.
The amount of rain is given in millimetres.
1 millimetre of rain equals 1 litre of water on one square metre.
If 3 millimetres fall on Monday and 5 millimetres on Tuesday, that makes 8 millimetres altogether.
After reading it, you have to empty the rain gauge.
You can make a simple rain gauge from a straight-sided glass with a scale.
In Switzerland, MeteoSwiss measures precipitation at many stations.

abschnitte.text: A rain gauge is a container with an opening of exactly known size that catches **precipitation**. This includes rain, snow, hail and soft hail. The best-known type in central Europe is the **Hellmann rain gauge**, a metal cylinder with a collecting opening of 200 square centimetres. It stands about a metre above the ground so that no splashes get in. Experts also call the device a **pluviometer**, after the Latin word for rain.

The amount of rain is given in **millimetres**. This means: this is how high the water would stand on a flat surface if it neither soaked away nor ran off. One millimetre of rain equals exactly one litre of water on one **square metre**. If 20 millimetres fall in one day, that is 20 litres per square metre, which is already heavy rain. The amounts for several days are simply added together.

In the past, an **observer** read the rain gauge every morning at the same time and then emptied it. Today many stations measure automatically, for example with a small **tipping bucket**, which tips over with each small amount of water and sends a signal. Other devices weigh the collected water continuously. Snow is melted in the device and measured as water. In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss** collects this data from all over the country.

In Switzerland, the amount of precipitation varies a lot from place to place. In the Swiss Plateau it is usually around 1000 millimetres a year, and in some areas of the Alps and on the southern side of the Alps clearly more. The inner **Valais** is particularly dry, because high mountains keep the rain off. In remote mountain areas there are large collecting containers, so-called **totalisers**, which are only read once or twice a year. Such series of measurements also show how the climate changes over decades.

You can make a simple rain gauge from a **straight-sided glass** or a container with vertical sides. It is important that the bottom is flat so that the height of the water is the same everywhere. With a ruler and a waterproof pen, you draw a scale in millimetres on the outside. You place the glass in the open, away from roofs and trees. After every reading you must **empty** it, or you will count the rain twice.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water that falls from the air to the ground, for example as rain, snow or hail.
Another word for rain gauge.
A small see-saw container that tips over at a certain amount of water and so counts it.
A large rain gauge in the mountains that collects the precipitation of a whole year.

gewusst: Rain was already being measured in India more than 2000 years ago to plan the harvest.
Wind can blow some of the raindrops over the opening, which is why rain gauges often measure a little too little in a storm.
A thunderstorm can bring more rain in an hour than usually falls in several weeks.

teile.einleitung: Relative velocity is the speed at which one object moves compared with another. It is crucial when overtaking, in collisions, when docking with a space station and even when cycling in the rain. It is calculated by subtracting the velocities as arrows, that is as vectors.
wichtigste: Relative velocity describes how fast one object moves compared with another.
For the same direction, you subtract the speeds.
For movements in different directions, you calculate with vectors and often with Pythagoras.
A car at 120 km/h gets closer to a lorry at 90 km/h at 30 km/h.
An aircraft at 800 km/h against a 100 km/h wind is going at 700 km/h over the ground.
Converting between frames of reference moving at constant speed is called the Galilean transformation.
At very high speeds, Albert Einstein's theory of relativity applies.

abschnitte.text: You get the **relative velocity** of object A compared with object B by subtracting B's velocity from A's velocity. If both are travelling in the same direction, the difference is small. So a car at 120 km/h only gets closer to a lorry at 90 km/h at 30 km/h. If they are travelling towards each other, the amounts add up, which is why head-on collisions are so violent.

Velocities have a direction and are therefore shown as arrows, as **vectors**. If a cyclist rides east at 6 m/s and a runner runs north at 3 m/s, the arrows are at right angles. Using **Pythagoras' theorem**, the relative velocity comes to around 6.7 m/s. In the same way, a swimmer who swims across a river at 1.2 m/s with a 0.5 m/s current moves at 1.3 m/s relative to the bank.

If rain is falling straight down at 6 m/s and a cyclist is riding at 8 m/s, from her point of view the drops hit her at an angle from the front. Their relative velocity is 10 m/s, again by Pythagoras. That is why you get much wetter at the front when cycling in the rain. Aircraft also calculate with relative velocities: relative to the air, a jet flies, for example, at 800 km/h, but with a 100 km/h **headwind** it is only going at 700 km/h over the ground.

With relative velocity, you can work out how long something will take. A car at 30 m/s overtaking a lorry at 25 m/s that has to gain 100 metres needs 100 divided by 5, that is 20 seconds. A boat moving at 5 m/s against a current of 2 m/s makes 3 m/s and needs exactly 200 seconds for 600 metres. What always matters is the **difference** in speeds.

The **International Space Station** orbits the Earth at around 28,000 km/h. A spacecraft that wants to dock flies almost exactly as fast. The relative velocity when docking is only a few centimetres per second. This means the two craft can be joined gently, even though both are travelling enormously fast.

The simple conversion between frames of reference moving at constant speed is called the **Galilean transformation**, after Galileo Galilei. For cars, trains and aircraft it works very well. But at speeds close to the speed of light it no longer applies. In 1905, in his special **theory of relativity**, Albert Einstein showed that light travels at the same speed for all observers, however fast they are moving.

begriffe.erklaerung: An arrow that represents a quantity with size and direction.
Converting positions and velocities between frames of reference moving at constant speed.
Speed relative to the Earth's surface, important for aircraft and ships.
The point of view from which movements are measured.

gewusst: Two fighter jets flying side by side can see each other almost standing still.
In a head-on collision between two cars each travelling at 50 km/h, they hit each other with a relative velocity of 100 km/h.
Light has the same speed for every observer, even if you fly after it.

teile.einleitung: The wheel and axle is one of the most important simple machines of humankind. A wheel turns around a rod, the axle, making movement and the transfer of force much easier. The principle is found in bicycles, cars, cranks, steering wheels and water mills.
wichtigste: The axle is the rod around which a wheel turns.
A wheel and axle works like a lever turning in a circle.
A large steering wheel is easier to turn than a small one.
The edge of a wheel moves faster than the places near the axle.
A normal car has two axles.
The middle part of a bicycle wheel, which holds the axle, is called the hub.
Oil on a squeaking axle reduces friction.

abschnitte.titel: What is a wheel and axle?
abschnitte.text: The **wheel and axle** is one of the classic **simple machines**, like the lever, the pulley and the inclined plane. The **axle** is the rod around which the wheel turns. Either the wheel turns loosely on the axle, or wheel and axle are firmly joined and turn together. With this invention, loads can be rolled instead of dragged, which needs much less force.

A wheel and axle works like a **lever** that moves in a circle. If you turn the large wheel, you need little force but have to cover a long distance. At the thin axle, on the other hand, a large force acts. That is why a bus's **steering wheel** is very large, so that the driver can turn it more easily. A **crank**, for example on an old coffee grinder, also uses this principle.

In one turn, the edge of the wheel covers a much longer distance than a point near the axle. Because both take the same time for one turn, the **edge** moves faster. With a bicycle wheel of about 2 metres in circumference, you get around 2 metres further with every turn. A large wheel also rolls more easily over stones and holes than a small one.

On a **bicycle**, the axle sits in the **hub**, the middle part of the wheel, and spokes connect the hub to the rim. A normal car has two axles; large lorries have three or more. Door handles, screwdrivers and taps also work on the principle of the wheel and axle. So that an axle turns easily, **ball bearings** are used, or oil is put on it when it squeaks.

In an old **mill**, flowing water drives a large **water wheel**. Through the axle, the turning is passed to gear wheels and millstones, which grind the grain. In the past, there were mills and sawmills like these on many Swiss streams. Modern hydroelectric power stations still use the same basic principle with their turbines.

The wheel was invented more than 5000 years ago. Very old finds come from Mesopotamia and from Europe; a wooden wheel from a marsh near Ljubljana in Slovenia is over 5000 years old. At first people probably used **potter's wheels**, later wheels on carts. In **lake dwelling settlements** in Switzerland, too, archaeologists have found parts of wooden wheels from the Neolithic period.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic device that helps to save or redirect force.
The rod around which a wheel turns.
The middle part of a wheel, which holds the axle.
A part with small balls that reduces friction at an axle.
A handle on an arm with which you turn an axle by hand.

gewusst: The Incas and Aztecs knew the wheel but did not use it for carts, probably because they had no large draught animals.
A Ferris wheel at the fair is basically an enormous wheel turning around a single axle.
Without the wheel and axle there would be no clocks with gear wheels, no bicycles and no trains.

teile.einleitung: Work done against friction is the work done against friction when something slides, rolls or is braked. This energy is not lost but is turned mainly into heat. That is why brakes get hot and hands get warm when you rub them together.
wichtigste: Work done against friction is the work done against a friction force.
It is turned mainly into internal energy, that is heat.
For sliding friction: work against friction equals coefficient of friction times weight times distance.
The work done against friction depends on the distance, because friction acts over the whole way.
Anyone pulling a cart at a constant speed does all their work against friction.
If a sledge glides to a stop, all its kinetic energy becomes work done against friction.

abschnitte.titel: What is work done against friction?
abschnitte.text: When two surfaces rub against each other, a braking **friction force** acts. If you still want to move something, you have to do **work** against this force. This work is called **work done against friction**. It is measured in joules, like any other work and energy.

For sliding friction, the friction force equals the **coefficient of friction** times the normal force. On level ground, the normal force is simply the weight, that is mass times g. The work done against friction is then friction force times distance. Example: a 50 kg box is pushed 10 m, and the coefficient of friction is 0.3. With g equal to 9.81 m/s², that gives about 1.47 kJ of work done against friction.

Work done against friction is turned mainly into **internal energy**, which means the objects get warmer. If you rub your hands together, you feel the **heat** immediately. A match lights through friction on the striking strip. In cars and trains, the **brake discs** can even glow after hard braking.

If a 40 kg sledge travelling at 5 m/s glides on level snow until it stops, all its **kinetic energy** becomes work done against friction, namely 500 J. If a 20 kg sledge goes down a slope 10 m high, it would have 1962 J of kinetic energy without friction. If it is only travelling at 10 m/s at the bottom, it has just 1000 J, so 962 J were lost through friction. A 70 kg skier gliding 500 m with a coefficient of friction of 0.05 does about 17.2 kJ of work against friction.

When a car **brakes**, kinetic energy is also turned into heat through work done against friction. If a car is travelling at 20 m/s, that is 72 km/h, and the coefficient of static friction of the tyres is 0.8, the braking distance is about 25.5 m. On a wet or icy road, the coefficient of friction is much smaller and the braking distance becomes much longer. That is why you should drive more slowly in winter and keep a bigger gap.

The work done against friction depends on the **distance** an object travels, because friction acts over the whole way. For work done in lifting, on the other hand, only the difference in height counts. That is why physicists say that friction is not a **conservative force**. If someone pulls a cart 50 m at a constant speed with 100 N, the work done against friction is 5000 J, because all the pulling work goes against friction.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that tells you how strongly two surfaces rub against each other.
The unit of work and energy.
The energy in the movement of an object's particles, which we feel as heat.
The force with which an object presses at right angles on a surface.

gewusst: Without friction we could neither walk nor tie a knot; we would constantly slip.
Ski wax reduces the friction between ski and snow so that you glide faster.
Stone Age people made fire by twirling a wooden stick quickly in a wooden hollow, producing heat from friction.

teile.einleitung: The proton is a tiny, positively charged particle in the nucleus of every atom. Its number decides which chemical element it is: an atom with 8 protons is always oxygen, one with 79 protons always gold. At CERN near Geneva, protons are made to collide at almost the speed of light in order to study the building blocks of the world.
wichtigste: Protons are positively charged particles in the atomic nucleus.
The number of protons decides which chemical element it is.
This number is called the atomic number.
Oxygen has 8 protons, gold 79.
A proton is about 1836 times heavier than an electron.
A proton consists of three quarks.
In the Large Hadron Collider at CERN near Geneva, protons collide with each other.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has a tiny **atomic nucleus** in the middle, around which electrons move. The nucleus contains positively charged **protons** and usually also uncharged neutrons. A proton is about 1836 times heavier than an electron, which is why almost the whole mass of an atom is in the nucleus. The positive charge of the proton is exactly as large as the negative charge of an electron. In a normal atom there are as many protons as electrons, so overall it is uncharged.

The number of protons in the nucleus is called the **atomic number**, and it decides the chemical element. Hydrogen has 1 proton, carbon 6, oxygen 8, iron 26 and gold 79. The elements are ordered by this number in the **periodic table**. If the number of protons changes, for example in a nuclear reaction, a different element is formed. The nucleus of the most common hydrogen atom even consists of just a single proton.

Around 1919, the physicist **Ernest Rutherford** showed that the nuclei of all atoms contain hydrogen nuclei, and soon called them protons. The name comes from the Greek word for “the first”. Later, researchers found out that a proton is not indivisible itself. It consists of three even smaller particles, the **quarks**, which are held together by a very strong force.

At **CERN**, the European laboratory for particle physics near Geneva, stands the **Large Hadron Collider**, LHC for short. In an underground ring around 27 kilometres long beneath Switzerland and France, protons are accelerated to almost the speed of light. When they collide, new particles are created, which huge detectors record. In 2012 the Higgs particle was detected there, one of the most important discoveries in physics.

abschnitte.titel: Protons in the Sun and in medicine
abschnitte.text: In the Sun, protons fuse into helium under enormous pressure and heat, releasing the energy that gives us light and warmth. This process is called **nuclear fusion**. In medicine, proton beams are used to treat tumours very precisely. The Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau has been treating cancer patients this way for many years, including children.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
The number of protons in an atom; it decides the element.
A table in which all the chemical elements are arranged.
A tiny particle that protons and neutrons are made of.
A large facility that makes tiny particles extremely fast.

gewusst: In the LHC, the protons go round the 27-kilometre ring more than 11,000 times a second.
If an atom were as big as a football stadium, the nucleus with its protons would only be about as big as a pea in the middle.
A proton is so stable that no one has ever seen a free proton decay.

teile.einleitung: Radon is a colourless, odourless and radioactive noble gas that forms naturally in the ground. It can enter houses unnoticed and collect in cellars and living spaces. In Switzerland, radon is the most important cause of lung cancer after smoking.
wichtigste: Radon is a noble gas with the chemical symbol Rn and the atomic number 86.
Radon-222 has a half-life of around 3.8 days.
It comes from the decay series of uranium-238 in rock.
The decay products of radon settle in the lungs and give off alpha radiation.
In Switzerland, a reference level of 300 becquerels per cubic metre has applied since 2018.
Sealing against the ground and good ventilation reduce exposure to radon.
Radon is measured with a dosimeter over several months.

abschnitte.text: In the periodic table, **radon** belongs to the **noble gases**, like helium, neon and argon. It hardly forms any chemical compounds and is heavier than air. You can neither see, smell nor taste it. It was discovered around 1900 by the German physicist Friedrich Ernst Dorn. All forms of radon are radioactive.

Many rocks and soils contain some **uranium**. Uranium-238 decays through many intermediate stages, including radium, and radon-222 is produced. Because radon is a gas, it can rise through cracks in the ground. Radon-222 has a **half-life** of about 3.8 days, so after this time half of it has decayed. In Switzerland, high levels occur mainly in the Alps and the Jura.

Radon itself is usually breathed out again. What is dangerous are its **decay products**, radioactive metals such as polonium. They stick to dust particles, get caught in the lungs and give off **alpha radiation** there. This radiation can damage the cells and cause lung cancer over many years. People who also smoke have an especially high risk.

Radon gets into the house mainly through leaky floors, cellar walls and openings for pipes and cables. In winter the exposure is often higher, because warm air rises in the house and creates a slight **low pressure** at the bottom. This sucks in soil air containing radon, rather like a chimney. That is why the concentration is usually highest on the ground floor and in the cellar.

Radon is measured in **becquerels** per cubic metre of air, where one becquerel means one decay per second. In Switzerland, a reference level of 300 becquerels per cubic metre has applied to living and working spaces since 2018. It is measured reliably with a small **dosimeter**, which is left in the room for several months, ideally during the heating season. The Federal Office of Public Health provides a radon map showing where higher levels are likely.

The most important measure is to **seal** the building against the ground, for example by closing cracks and openings for pipes. Regular airing dilutes the radon in the indoor air. For new buildings in radon areas, a tight floor slab or extraction under the house is often planned in. Cellar doors should be kept closed so that air containing radon does not get into the living spaces.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas that hardly reacts with other substances, for example helium or radon.
The time after which half of a radioactive substance has decayed.
The unit of radioactivity: one decay per second.
Radiation made of heavy particles that can do a lot of damage over a short distance.

gewusst: Radon is one of the heaviest gases, around seven times heavier than air.
Some spas in the alpine countries also have radon in their spring water.
A large part of the natural radiation that people in Switzerland are exposed to comes from radon.

teile.einleitung: A perpetual motion machine is an imagined machine that keeps running for ever without any energy being added, or even gives off energy. For many centuries inventors have tried to build such a machine, but all have failed. Physics also explains why it can never work.
wichtigste: A perpetual motion machine would be a machine that runs for ever without any energy being added.
Its Latin name, perpetuum mobile, means “the thing that is always moving”.
A perpetual motion machine breaks the law of conservation of energy.
Energy cannot come from nothing; it can only be converted.
Through friction, part of the kinetic energy is always turned into heat, which is why every wheel eventually stops.
In 1775, the Paris Academy of Sciences decided to stop examining proposals for perpetual motion machines.
Patent offices usually reject supposed perpetual motion inventions.

abschnitte.titel: What is a perpetual motion machine?
abschnitte.text: The term **perpetuum mobile** is Latin and means “the thing that is always moving”. It refers to a machine that, once set going, moves for ever without anyone putting energy into it. Even bolder are ideas for machines that also do work at the same time, for example producing electricity. Such a machine would solve all the world's energy problems, if it existed.

The most important reason is the **law of conservation of energy**: energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form into another. If someone claims that their device gives out 120 joules but takes in only 100 joules, that is impossible. On top of this there is **friction**, which turns part of the energy into heat in every movement. This heat can never be completely recovered, which is why even a wheel with very good bearings eventually stops.

As early as the 12th century, the Indian scholar Bhaskara described a wheel that was supposed to turn by itself. Around 1230, the French master builder Villard de Honnecourt drew a similar wheel. The classic model is a **wheel with movable weights** on its spokes: on one side the weights were supposed to hang further out and turn the wheel for ever. But on the other side there are more weights instead, and everything stays balanced and still.

Because so many false inventions were submitted, the **Paris Academy of Sciences** decided in 1775 to stop examining proposals for perpetual motion machines. Today's **patent offices** also usually reject such applications, because the invention cannot work. Even so, supposed miracle machines still appear on the internet today. Often there is a hidden drive, a battery or simply a mistake in thinking behind them.

The many failed attempts helped scientists understand the laws of energy. Physicists distinguish between a perpetual motion machine **of the first kind**, which would create energy from nothing, and one of the second kind, which would turn heat completely into work. According to the laws of **thermodynamics**, both are impossible. So anyone examining a machine always asks: where does the energy come from?

begriffe.erklaerung: A law of nature: energy is never lost and never comes from nothing.
A force that slows down movement and produces heat.
The unit of energy.
The part of physics that deals with heat and energy.
A right that secures an invention for its inventor.

gewusst: Even Leonardo da Vinci considered perpetual motion machines a deception.
Some toys that seem to bob for ever, such as the drinking bird, actually use heat from their surroundings.
Even the Earth's rotation is being very slowly slowed down by the tides.

teile.einleitung: A relay is a switch that is not operated by hand but by electricity. With a small current, it can switch a large circuit on and off, and it often makes a clear click as it does so.
wichtigste: A relay uses a small current to switch a large circuit.
In an electromechanical relay, an electromagnet pulls a movable armature.
The armature moves the switch contacts and makes a click as it does so.
A contact that closes when current flows through the coil is called a normally open contact.
In a relay, the control circuit and the load circuit are electrically separated from each other.
Relays first became important in 19th-century telegraphy.
Konrad Zuse's Z3 computer consisted mainly of relays.
A solid-state relay switches with no moving parts at all.

abschnitte.text: A classic relay consists of a **coil** of wire, an iron core and a movable piece of metal, the **armature**. When current flows through the coil, it becomes an electromagnet and pulls the armature towards it. The armature pushes contacts together or apart. When the current is switched off, a small spring pulls the armature back again.

A **normally open contact** connects the contacts as soon as current flows through the coil. A **normally closed contact** does the opposite: it breaks the circuit when the relay pulls in. A changeover contact can switch back and forth between two circuits. Many relays have several such contacts and so switch several things at the same time.

In the 1830s, the American Joseph Henry built one of the first relays. In **telegraphy**, the signals got weaker and weaker over long lines. Relays at intermediate stations picked up the weak signal and sent it on with fresh current. This meant messages could be sent over hundreds of kilometres.

In 1941 in Berlin, the German engineer **Konrad Zuse** completed the Z3, which is considered the first working program-controlled digital computer. It worked with around 2000 relays, each of which had only two states, on or off. This is exactly right for calculating with zeros and ones. Later, vacuum tubes and then transistors replaced the slow relays.

Relays are found in cars, washing machines, heating systems and lighting systems. With a small push button, for example, you can switch on a powerful motor without the large current flowing through the button. The **galvanic isolation** protects the sensitive control from the high current. Many railway signal boxes also worked with relays for a long time.

A **solid-state relay** switches with electronic components instead of an armature. It works silently and very fast and hardly wears out, because nothing moves. The circuits are often separated by light, using a so-called optocoupler. On the other hand, it gets warm when switching large currents and sometimes needs a heat sink.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wound-up wire that becomes a magnet when current flows through it.
The movable iron part in a relay that is pulled by the magnet.
A contact that closes when the relay is switched on.
Two circuits have no conducting connection with each other.

gewusst: The clicking you hear in older cars when indicating used to come from a flasher relay.
The word relay comes from French and originally meant a station where stagecoaches got fresh horses.
The term bug for a computer fault is often linked to a moth that was found in 1947 in a relay of an American computer.

teile.einleitung: A paper aeroplane is a small aircraft folded from a single sheet of paper. It has no engine but glides through the air after being thrown. By making and trying them out, you learn in a playful way how flying works.
wichtigste: A paper aeroplane is folded from a sheet of paper, without scissors or glue.
As it glides, the air under the wings carries it.
Smooth, symmetrical wings are important; crumpled paper flies badly.
If the nose is too heavy, the plane dives steeply.
Small flaps bent upwards at the back of the wings help it stay up longer.
It is best to throw it gently forwards.
The folding of figures out of paper is called origami.

abschnitte.text: A paper aeroplane is a **glider**, an aircraft without any drive. It gets its energy only from the throw. After that it sinks slowly and glides forwards as it does, much like a glider aircraft. Well-known models are the pointed dart, which flies fast and far, and wider gliders that float in the air for a long time.

Four things act on it in flight: gravity pulls it down, **lift** keeps it up, the throw gives it momentum forwards and **air resistance** slows it down. The wings are tilted slightly and push the oncoming air downwards. As a result, the air pushes the plane upwards. For it to fly smoothly, the centre of gravity and the shape of the wings must match well.

The point where the weight of the plane is concentrated is called the **centre of gravity**. If it is slightly in front of the middle, the plane flies steadily straight ahead, which is why the nose is usually folded several times. But if the nose is far too heavy, it tips forwards and dives steeply. If it is too light, it climbs, slows down and then stalls.

Fold neatly and press every crease sharp with your fingernail. Both wings must be exactly the same, or the plane will turn off to the side. If you bend small **flaps** slightly upwards at the back of the wings, the nose lifts and it glides for longer. Throw it gently and straight forwards, not steeply upwards. Indoors it flies straighter than outdoors, because there is no wind to disturb it.

Paper was invented in China, and folding has a long tradition in East Asia. The art of folding figures out of paper is called **origami** in Japanese. By the classic rules, a paper aeroplane needs no scissors, glue or sticky tape. Today there are competitions for the furthest and longest flights, and paper aeroplane competitions are held in many Swiss schools too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of the air that pushes a wing upwards.
The point at which you could balance an object.
An aircraft without an engine that flies forwards while slowly sinking.
The Japanese art of folding figures out of paper.

gewusst: The world record for the furthest paper aeroplane throw is over 70 metres, which is more than the width of a football pitch.
With a small paper clip on the nose, you can easily shift the centre of gravity of a paper aeroplane.
Large aircraft also have movable flaps at the back of their wings, much like a trimmed paper aeroplane.

teile.einleitung: The right-hand rule is a memory aid from physics for working out directions with current and magnetic fields. You shape your right hand in a particular way, and the fingers then show the directions you are looking for. This lets you find out without calculating how magnetic fields run around wires or in which direction a force acts.
wichtigste: The right-hand rule helps you work out directions for current, magnetic field and force.
If the thumb points in the direction of the current in a straight wire, the curled fingers show the direction of the field lines.
If the fingers point in the direction of the current through a coil, the thumb points to the north pole.
In the three-finger rule, the middle finger stands for the effect, that is the force.
Conventional current flows from plus to minus in the external circuit.
For electrons, you have to reverse the direction of the force or use the left hand.
Fleming's right-hand rule applies to the generator.

abschnitte.text: Current, magnetic field and force each have a **direction** in space. To remember these directions, you use your own right hand as a model. There are several versions of the rule, depending on what you want to find out. What they all have in common is that they refer to **conventional current**, that is from plus to minus.

In 1820, the Danish physicist **Hans Christian Ørsted** discovered that a wire carrying a current deflects a compass needle. A circular **magnetic field** forms around the wire. If you grip the wire with your right hand so that the thumb points in the direction of the current, the curled fingers show the direction of the **field lines**. So if the current flows away from you into the page, the field lines run clockwise.

A **coil** is a wound-up wire that acts like a bar magnet. If you place the fingers of your right hand around the coil so that they point in the direction of the current through the turns, the thumb points to the **north pole**. This lets you predict where the north pole of an electromagnet is. If you reverse the current, the north and south poles swap places.

When a charge moves through a magnetic field, the **Lorentz force** acts on it. In the German **UVW rule** (cause, mediation, effect), the thumb shows the cause, that is the movement of positive charge or the current. The index finger shows the mediation, that is the magnetic field, and the middle finger the effect, that is the force. An example: if a proton flies east and the magnetic field points straight up, the force acts towards the south. For negatively charged **electrons**, you have to reverse the direction of the force.

In English-speaking countries, people learn the rules of the engineer **John Ambrose Fleming**. His left-hand rule applies to the **electric motor**, in which current and magnetic field produce movement. His right-hand rule applies to the **generator**, in which movement in a magnetic field produces current. Because which finger stands for what can differ from one textbook to another, you should always remember exactly which finger means what.

The right-hand rule is also found in the **cross product** in mathematics, which uses two directions to work out a third one at right angles. Three-dimensional coordinate systems are usually drawn as a **right-handed system**, also following this rule. The corkscrew rule works in a similar way: if you turn a corkscrew clockwise, it moves away from you. Ordinary screws follow the same rule.

begriffe.erklaerung: The agreed direction of current from plus to minus.
Imaginary lines that show the direction and course of a magnetic field.
The force a magnetic field exerts on moving electric charges.
A wound-up wire that becomes a magnet when current flows through it.

gewusst: The rule can also explain which way an electric motor turns.
Anyone who uses their left hand by mistake gets exactly the opposite direction.
Ørsted is said to have discovered the link between electricity and magnetism during a lecture.

teile.einleitung: In a parallel circuit, several electrical devices are connected side by side to the same power source. Each device has its own branch through which current flows. This is also how all the lamps and sockets in a home are connected.
wichtigste: In a parallel circuit, each device has its own branch on the same source.
If one lamp fails, the others stay lit.
Each branch has the same voltage as the source.
Two identical lamps in parallel on a battery shine as brightly as a single lamp.
The total current is the sum of the currents in the branches.
If you connect another device in parallel, the total current increases.
The point where the circuit splits is called a junction.

abschnitte.text: In a parallel circuit, the circuit splits into several **branches** that lie side by side. Each branch contains a device, for example a lamp. The place where the wire branches is called a **junction**. The opposite is the series circuit, in which all the devices hang one after the other in a single loop.

Each branch has the full **voltage** of the source across it. That is why two identical lamps connected in parallel to a battery shine as brightly as a single lamp on the same battery. If one lamp burns out, only its branch is broken. The other lamp still gets current and stays lit.

The current from the source splits up between the branches at the junction. If 0.2 amperes flow through one lamp and 0.3 amperes through the other, 0.5 amperes flow in the main wire. You can also calculate the other way round: if 1.2 amperes flow in the main wire and 0.5 amperes in one branch, there are 0.7 amperes in the other. This rule is called the **junction rule** and was described by Gustav Robert Kirchhoff in 1845.

In Switzerland, all the sockets and lamps in a home are connected in parallel to the 230-volt mains. That way, every device gets the right voltage, and each one can be switched on and off separately. But every extra device increases the **total current** in the supply wire. If it gets too large, the **fuse** switches off so that the wires do not overheat.

Batteries can also be connected in parallel: the voltage stays the same, but together they last longer. For **resistance**, something surprising applies in a parallel circuit. The more branches there are, the smaller the total resistance becomes, because the current has more paths. Two identical resistors in parallel together give only half the resistance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the circuit that lies next to other parts.
A point where one wire splits into several wires.
What drives the current, measured in volts.
How much electricity flows, measured in amperes.
A circuit in which all the devices lie one after the other in a loop.

gewusst: Many modern fairy lights are wired in parallel so that the whole string does not go out when one bulb breaks.
If you plug too many powerful devices into a multi-socket adaptor, the wire can get dangerously hot.
The junction rule holds because no current is lost or added along the way.

teile.einleitung: The Schrödinger equation is the most important basic equation of quantum mechanics. It describes how tiny particles such as electrons behave, which do not work like little balls but more like waves. Erwin Schrödinger set it up in 1926, when he was a professor at the University of Zurich.
wichtigste: Erwin Schrödinger published his wave equation in 1926.
He worked on it around the turn of the year 1925/26 in the Graubünden health resort of Arosa.
The equation describes particles with a wave function, written with the Greek letter ψ.
According to Max Born, the squared magnitude |ψ|² tells you how likely you are to find a particle at a place.
The eigenvalues of the time-independent equation give the possible energy values of a bound system.
Because the equation is linear, solutions can be superposed to make new solutions.
In 1933, Schrödinger received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with Paul Dirac.

abschnitte.text: **Erwin Schrödinger** was born in Vienna in 1887 and was an Austrian physicist. From 1921 to 1927 he was professor of theoretical physics at the **University of Zurich**. Around the turn of the year 1925/26, during a stay in the health resort of **Arosa** in Graubünden, he worked on his famous equation. In 1926 he published it in several papers. In 1933 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with the British physicist Paul Dirac.

At the beginning of the 20th century, researchers noticed that tiny particles such as electrons sometimes behave like **waves**. The Frenchman Louis de Broglie had suggested this idea in 1924. Schrödinger looked for an equation to describe such matter waves. His equation says how the **wave function** ψ of a particle changes in space and over time. It plays a similarly important role in quantum physics as Newton's laws do in classical mechanics.

What the wave function actually means was explained by the physicist **Max Born** in 1926. The squared magnitude |ψ|² gives the **probability density**, in other words how likely you are to find the particle at a particular place. So an electron does not have a fixed path like a planet, but is found at different places with certain probabilities. Because the equation is linear, solutions can be superposed to make new solutions. This produces **superposition states**, in which a particle carries several possibilities within it at the same time.

For a bound particle, such as an electron in an atom, the time-independent Schrödinger equation gives only certain allowed energy values, the **eigenvalues**. So the energy cannot be anything at all but comes in steps; it is said to be quantised. A simple example is a particle in an infinitely deep **potential well**, a kind of box with impenetrable walls. There the energy grows with the square of the level number, so the third level has nine times as much energy as the ground state. The equation can also be used to calculate the energy levels of the hydrogen atom exactly.

In 1935, Schrödinger came up with the thought experiment **Schrödinger's cat**. It was meant to show how strange it would be to carry superposition states over from the world of atoms to large objects. It was never a real experiment but a puzzle for the mind that is still discussed today. The Schrödinger equation is now the basis of the chemistry of atoms and molecules. Without it there would be no computer chips, lasers or solar cells in their present form.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of physics that describes the behaviour of tiny particles such as atoms and electrons.
A mathematical description of a particle as a wave, written ψ.
Tells you how likely a particle is to be found at a particular place.
One of the allowed solutions, here a possible energy value.
A state made up of several possible states at the same time.

gewusst: Some of the ideas for the most famous equation of quantum physics came about during a holiday in the mountains of Graubünden.
At almost the same time, Werner Heisenberg developed a quantum theory that looked completely different, which later turned out to be equivalent.
In 1944, Schrödinger also wrote a book called “What Is Life?”, which inspired many later biologists.

teile.einleitung: A pedal is the part of a bike that you push with your feet to make it go. A normal bicycle has two pedals, which are attached to the cranks and turn in a circle. The force of our legs is cleverly turned into a turning movement.
wichtigste: A normal bicycle has two pedals.
The pedals sit on the cranks and turn in a circle as you ride.
It is best to push the pedal with the ball of your foot.
In Switzerland, pedals must have orange or yellow reflectors.
Uphill, riders sometimes stand up to push with their whole body weight.
With clipless pedals, the shoe clicks into the pedal.
The crank works like a lever.

abschnitte.text: The pedal is the surface you push with to drive a bike. It is attached so that it can turn on the **crank**, an arm connected to the bottom bracket axle. The two cranks are exactly opposite each other, so one foot is always up and one down. The turning movement is passed to the back wheel through the chainring and the **chain**.

The crank is a **lever**: the longer the crank, the less force you need to turn it. The turning effect of a force is called **torque**. It is greatest when the crank is horizontal and you push straight down. Uphill, cyclists often stand up so that they can push on the pedal with their whole body weight.

It is best to push the pedal with the **ball of your foot** and not with your heel. That way, your foot can pass on the force well and your ankle can act as a spring. Smooth, round pedalling protects your knees and saves energy. With the right gear, you can keep a comfortable pedalling speed even when it gets steep.

There are simple flat pedals, pedals with pins for mountain bikes and **clipless pedals**, where the shoe clicks in with a cleat. With these you can pull as well as push. In Switzerland, the law requires orange or yellow **reflectors** on the pedals. They move up and down as you ride and so are especially noticeable to drivers at night.

Karl Drais's first running machine from 1817 had no pedals at all; you pushed yourself along the ground with your feet. In the 1860s in France, cranks with pedals were fitted directly to the front wheel. Because each turn only took you one wheel's circumference forward, penny-farthings with huge front wheels were later built. Only with the chain, from about 1885, did the bicycle as we know it today come about.

begriffe.erklaerung: The arm the pedal is attached to, which turns in a circle.
A rod with which you can increase a force.
How strongly a force makes something turn.
A part that reflects light so that you can be seen in the dark.

gewusst: The left pedal has a left-hand thread so that it does not come loose by itself while riding.
The name pedelec for e-bikes comes from the English “pedal electric cycle”.
The word pedal comes from the Latin word for foot, “pes”.

teile.einleitung: Pascal's principle says that pressure in an enclosed liquid spreads out equally everywhere. With this simple law, you can lift a whole car with a small force. It is found in car brakes, vehicle lifts, excavators and hydraulic presses.
wichtigste: Pressure in an enclosed liquid spreads equally in all directions.
The principle is named after the 17th-century French scholar Blaise Pascal.
Pressure is calculated as force divided by area.
In a hydraulic press, a small piston produces a much larger force on the large piston.
What you gain in force, you pay for in distance; the work stays the same.
Hydraulic brakes in cars are based on Pascal's principle.
Liquids such as oil are used because they can hardly be compressed.

abschnitte.text: If you press on a liquid in a closed container, the **pressure** rises by the same amount everywhere in the liquid. It acts in all directions and equally strongly at every point on the wall. You can try this with a water bag with several small holes: if you squeeze the bag, water squirts out of all the holes at the same time. Blaise Pascal described this law in the 17th century.

A **hydraulic press** consists of two connected cylinders with pistons of different sizes. If you press with 50 newtons on a small piston with an area of 2 square centimetres, a certain pressure is produced. This pressure also acts on the large piston of 200 square centimetres, which is a hundred times larger. That is why the large piston pushes upwards with 5000 newtons, a hundred times as hard.

This increase in force is not completely free. The small piston has to travel a much longer **distance** than the large one, a hundred times longer in the example. The **work**, that is force times distance, is the same at both pistons if friction is ignored. It is like a lever or a pulley: you save force but need more distance.
