When you press the brake pedal in a car, a piston in the **master cylinder** presses on the brake fluid. The pressure, for example 40 bar, acts equally strongly in every wheel cylinder through thin pipes and presses the brake pads on. In garages, **vehicle lifts** raise cars with a weight of 12,000 newtons, and only 200 newtons are needed at the small piston if the areas are 0.0005 and 0.03 square metres. Excavators, cranes, snow groomers and office chairs also work with hydraulics.

Hydraulics needs a liquid that can hardly be **compressed**, usually a special oil. Air, on the other hand, is springy and can be squeezed together, so part of the force would be lost. That is why air in a brake pipe is dangerous: the brake pedal then feels spongy. For calculations: 300 newtons on 15 square centimetres give 200,000 pascals, that is 2 bar.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on an area, measured in pascals or bar.
A movable plug that slides back and forth in a cylinder.
Technology that transmits forces with the help of liquids.
A special liquid that carries the pressure from the pedal to the wheels in a car.

gewusst: In a famous experiment, Pascal is said to have burst a barrel with a long, thin pipe full of water.
A snow groomer in Swiss ski resorts moves its large blade with hydraulics.
Spiders also stretch their legs with fluid pressure instead of muscles.

teile.einleitung: A swing is a seat that hangs from ropes or chains and moves back and forth. In physics it is a pendulum, from which you can learn a lot about oscillations, energy and momentum. With the right movements you can even swing yourself high without anyone pushing you.
wichtigste: A swing moves back and forth like a pendulum.
Right at the bottom in the middle you are at your fastest.
At the highest point, the swing stops for a very short moment and turns back.
Air resistance and friction slow the swing down, which is why without a push it swings less and less high.
A swing with short ropes swings back and forth faster than one with long ropes.
A heavy child and a light child swing at about the same speed on the same swing.
Pushing or moving your legs in the right rhythm makes the swing go higher and higher.

abschnitte.text: A **pendulum** is an object that hangs from a point and swings back and forth. A swing works in exactly the same way: ropes or chains hold the seat on a beam. The time for one swing there and back is called the **period**. It depends almost only on the length of the ropes, not on the weight. That is why a swing with short ropes swings faster, and a heavy child swings at about the same speed as a light one.

Up at the turning point you are high and at rest for a very short moment; you have a lot of **potential energy**. As you swing down, it is turned into **kinetic energy**. Right at the bottom in the middle you are at your fastest. Then you go up again, and the kinetic energy turns back into potential energy. At the very top, as you turn, your body feels lighter than usual, almost as if you were floating.

You can build up momentum without help by stretching your **legs** forwards and pulling them back at the right moment. At the same time you lean back or forwards. This shifts your body and gives the swing a little extra energy with every swing. What matters is the right **rhythm**, staying in time with the swing.

If you want to push someone, you should push when the swing is just moving away from you. Small pushes in the right rhythm add up, and the swing flies higher and higher. This effect is called **resonance**. Without new momentum, the swing gets slower and slower because of air resistance and friction at the hanging point, until it stops. This weakening of the swinging is called **damping**.

Around 1600, the Italian scientist **Galileo Galilei** studied pendulums and realised that the period hardly depends on how wide the swing is. In 1656, the Dutchman Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, which was much more accurate than earlier clocks. Swings have existed for thousands of years and can be seen in old pictures from Greece. Today you find them on almost every playground in Switzerland, often also as a nest swing for several children.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hanging object that swings back and forth regularly.
The time for one complete swing there and back.
When small pushes in the right rhythm make a swinging movement stronger and stronger.
The gradual weakening of a swinging movement through friction.

gewusst: A swing with ropes four times as long takes twice as long for one swing there and back.
Galileo is said to have discovered the laws of the pendulum while watching a swinging lamp in Pisa Cathedral.
The same laws apply to the giant swings in theme parks as to the playground swing.

teile.einleitung: Rayleigh scattering explains why the sky is blue during the day. When sunlight hits the tiny particles of the air, blue light is scattered in all directions much more strongly than red. It is named after the British physicist Lord Rayleigh.
wichtigste: Rayleigh scattering is the scattering of light by particles much smaller than the wavelength of the light.
Blue light is scattered more strongly by the air than red light.
That is why the sky looks blue during the day.
At sunrise and sunset, the sky looks red or orange.
Lord Rayleigh described the phenomenon mathematically in the 19th century.
There is no air on the Moon and therefore no blue sky either.

abschnitte.text: Sunlight looks white but is made up of all the colours of the rainbow. Each colour has a different **wavelength**: blue a short one and red a long one. Air consists mainly of tiny nitrogen and oxygen molecules. When light hits these particles, part of it is sent off in other directions; this is called **scattering**.

The shorter the wavelength, the more strongly the light is scattered by the small air particles. Blue light is scattered several times more strongly than red light. The scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions of the sky. That is why the whole **sky** looks blue, wherever we look.

In the evening and morning, the Sun is low in the sky. Its light then has to travel a much longer way through the **atmosphere**. On the way, almost all the blue light is scattered to the side. What is left are mainly red and orange shades, which is why the **sunset glow** shines red.

The British physicist John William Strutt, known as **Lord Rayleigh**, explained the phenomenon with physical formulas from 1871 onwards. Before that, researchers such as John Tyndall had observed that light is scattered bluish by small particles. Lord Rayleigh received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1904, but for discovering the noble gas **argon**.

High up in the Alps, for example at the Jungfraujoch, the sky looks a deeper dark blue, because there is less air above us. Distant mountains often look slightly bluish; this too has to do with scattered light. In haze or fog, the particles are larger and scatter all colours by similar amounts, so the sky looks **whitish**. This also explains why clouds are white and not blue.

begriffe.erklaerung: Light being sent off in other directions by small particles.
The distance between two crests of a wave; it decides the colour of light.
The layer of air surrounding the Earth.

gewusst: Violet light is actually scattered even more strongly than blue, but our eyes are less sensitive to it.
On Mars, the sky is rather reddish during the day and the sunset is bluish.
Astronauts in space see a black sky, even though the Sun is shining.

teile.einleitung: A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two metal plates of the same size facing each other a short distance apart. It can store electric charge and energy and is the simplest model of a capacitor, as found in almost every electronic device.
wichtigste: A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two parallel metal plates.
The capacitance is calculated with C = ε0 · εr · A / d.
If you halve the distance between the plates, the capacitance doubles.
A dielectric with εr = 5 makes the capacitance five times as large.
Between the plates there is a uniform electric field.
At the edges, the field lines bulge outwards.
The field strength is voltage divided by the distance between the plates.

abschnitte.text: A **parallel-plate capacitor** has two metal plates that do not touch. If you connect a voltage source, electrons flow onto one plate while the other plate loses electrons. One plate becomes negatively charged, the other positively. The stored **charge** Q depends on the voltage U and the capacitance C: Q = C · U.

**Capacitance** tells you how much charge a capacitor can store per volt. For the parallel-plate capacitor, C = ε0 · εr · A / d. Here A is the area of the plates, d the distance and ε0 the electric constant of around 8.85 · 10 to the power of minus 12 farads per metre. Larger plates and a smaller distance give a larger capacitance. An air-filled capacitor with an area of 100 square centimetres and a gap of 1 millimetre has only about 89 picofarads.

If you fill the space between the plates with an insulating material, it is called a **dielectric**. The number εr, the relative permittivity, tells you by what factor this increases the capacitance. For air it is almost exactly 1, for water about 80. So with a dielectric of εr = 5, the capacitance becomes five times as large.

Between the plates of an ideal parallel-plate capacitor, the electric field is **uniform**. This means it is equally strong everywhere and the field lines run parallel. The field strength is calculated with E = U / d. At 200 volts and a gap of 4 millimetres, that gives 50,000 volts per metre. At the edge of a real capacitor, the field lines bulge outwards; this is called the **fringe field**.

If you disconnect a charged capacitor from the source and pull the plates apart, the charge stays the same. Because the capacitance falls, the **voltage** rises. If the capacitor stays connected to the source, on the other hand, the voltage stays the same and the charge on the plates decreases. These two cases are often compared at school.

Many devices work on the principle of the parallel-plate capacitor. A mobile phone **touchscreen** detects your finger because it changes the capacitance at one spot. In a condenser microphone, a thin plate vibrates and so changes the gap and with it the voltage. In a camera flash, a capacitor releases its stored energy in a flash.

begriffe.erklaerung: A capacitor's ability to store charge, measured in farads.
The unit of capacitance, named after Michael Faraday.
An insulating material between the plates that increases the capacitance.
A field that is equally strong and points the same way at every point.

gewusst: A 1-farad capacitor with air between the plates and a gap of 1 millimetre would need plates of more than 100 square kilometres.
One of the first capacitors was the Leyden jar from the 18th century.
A thundercloud and the ground together also form a kind of giant capacitor.

teile.einleitung: A sound wave is a wave that carries notes, voices and noises through the air and other materials. As it does so, the air is squeezed together and then thinned out again in turn. When the wave reaches your ear, it makes your eardrum vibrate, and you hear something.
wichtigste: Sound in air is a longitudinal wave: the particles vibrate back and forth in the direction the wave travels.
This produces alternating compressions and rarefactions of the air.
A sound wave carries energy, but no air from the source to the ear.
Sound needs a material to vibrate in, which is why there is no sound in empty space.
The distance between two neighbouring compressions is called the wavelength.
Sound waves are reflected by walls, which we hear as an echo.
Sound waves are diffracted around obstacles, which is why you can hear music round the corner of a house.

abschnitte.text: Sound is produced when something **vibrates**, for example a guitar string, the cone of a loudspeaker or your vocal cords. The vibrating surface pushes the air particles in front of it. These pass the push on to their neighbours, like a row of dominoes. In this way the vibration travels through the air as a **sound wave**. The air particles themselves only move a tiny bit back and forth; it is the energy that is carried.

In air and water, sound is a **longitudinal wave**. The particles vibrate in the same direction as the wave travels. This produces alternating **compressions**, where the air is squeezed together, and rarefactions. In solid bodies, sound can also travel as a **transverse wave**, in which the particles vibrate across the direction of travel. In empty space there is no material at all, so it stays completely silent there.

The **frequency** tells you how often per second the air vibrates and decides the pitch. People hear frequencies between about 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz. The **wavelength** is the distance between two compressions. You get it by dividing the speed of sound by the frequency: a note of 680 Hz at 340 m/s has a wavelength of 0.5 m. Low notes have long wavelengths, high notes short ones.

When a sound wave hits a rock face, it is thrown back; this is called **reflection**. If you shout loudly in the mountains, you hear your **echo** shortly afterwards. Sound waves can also travel around obstacles; this is called **diffraction**. That is why you can hear music round the corner of a house even though you cannot see the loudspeaker. Low notes with long waves are diffracted especially strongly, which is why from a distant party you mainly hear the bass.

Sound below 20 Hz is called **infrasound**, sound above 20,000 Hz is called **ultrasound**. People cannot hear either, but some animals can. Elephants communicate over long distances with infrasound. Bats and dolphins send out ultrasound and find their way by the echo. In medicine, ultrasound is used to make pictures of the inside of the body.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wave in which the particles vibrate back and forth in the direction of travel.
The distance between two matching points of a wave, such as two compressions.
The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
Reflected sound that you hear again a little later.
The spreading of a wave around an obstacle.

gewusst: As people get older, they hear the very high notes less and less well.
Dog whistles make sounds that dogs can hear but people hardly or not at all.
Divers can hear under water, but they find it hard to tell which direction the sound is coming from.

teile.einleitung: The Pauli principle is a basic rule of quantum physics: two electrons in an atom may never be in exactly the same state. The physicist Wolfgang Pauli formulated it in 1925. Without this principle there would be no periodic table, no chemistry and no solid objects as we know them.
wichtigste: The Pauli principle is also called the exclusion principle.
It applies to fermions, particles with half-integer spin such as electrons, protons and neutrons.
Wolfgang Pauli formulated it in 1925 and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1945.
An orbital can hold at most 2 electrons, and their spins are opposite.
The shell with n = 3 holds at most 18 electrons.
Electron degeneracy pressure stops white dwarfs from collapsing.
Pauli taught at ETH Zurich from 1928.

abschnitte.text: Every electron in an atom is described by four **quantum numbers**, a kind of address. The Pauli principle says that two electrons in the same atom may never match in all four quantum numbers. At least one must be different. You can picture it like a cinema, where only one person may sit in each seat.

Electrons have a property called **spin**, which, put simply, you can imagine as a tiny rotation. Spin can only have two values, “up” or “down”. That is why an **orbital**, a region where the electrons are found, can hold at most two electrons with opposite spins. In the ground state of a helium atom, the two electrons sit in the same orbital and have antiparallel spins.

Because the electrons cannot all fit into the lowest state, they spread out over **shells**. A shell with principal quantum number n holds at most 2 times n times n electrons: 2 in the first, 8 in the second, 18 in the third shell. This gives the structure of the **periodic table** of the elements. So the Pauli principle explains why sodium reacts quite differently from neon.

Because of the Pauli principle, electrons that are squeezed tightly together resist being squeezed any further. This **degeneracy pressure** keeps white dwarfs, the remains of Sun-like stars, stable. In metals, the electrons fill the states from the bottom up. The energy of the highest occupied state at absolute zero is called the **Fermi energy**.

Wolfgang Pauli was born in Vienna in 1900 and was already a child prodigy of physics as a student. From 1928 he was a professor at **ETH Zurich** and lived in Zurich until his death in 1958. He was known for his sharp criticism of unclear ideas. Physicists jokingly talked about the “Pauli effect”: experiments and equipment were said to fail often when he was nearby.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle with half-integer spin, for example an electron.
A quantum property of a particle; put simply, a kind of self-rotation.
A region around the atomic nucleus where electrons are found.
A number that describes a particular state of a particle.
A small, very dense remnant of a burnt-out star.

gewusst: The fact that you do not fall through the floor is closely linked to the Pauli principle.
A teaspoon of material from a white dwarf would weigh several tonnes on Earth.
Pauli predicted that there must be a tiny, barely detectable particle, which was later called the neutrino.

teile.einleitung: A circuit diagram is a drawing that shows how the parts of an electric circuit are connected. Instead of drawing the real components, it uses simple, standardised symbols. That way experts all over the world can read a diagram, even if they do not speak the same language.
wichtigste: A circuit diagram shows a circuit with standardised symbols, the circuit symbols.
Wires are drawn as straight lines with right angles.
A circuit diagram does not show exactly where the cables run or how long they are.
In a series circuit, all the components lie one after the other on a single line.
In a parallel circuit, the wire splits into several branches.
Two-way switching makes it possible to switch a lamp from two places.

abschnitte.text: A circuit diagram is a kind of map for electric current. It shows which components there are and which is connected to which. Each component is shown by a **circuit symbol**, for example a lamp as a circle with a cross. The connecting wires are drawn as **lines**, straight lines that usually turn at right angles.

A circuit diagram is not a photograph of the device. It does not tell you where the cables lie in the wall, how long they are or how big the components really are. All that matters is what is connected to what. For the exact position of the wires in a house, the electrician needs a different plan, the **wiring plan**.

If a battery, a switch and two lamps lie on a single line with no branches, that is a **series circuit**. If one lamp breaks there, they all go out, as with some old fairy lights. If the wire splits into several branches, however, it is called a **parallel circuit**. Then each lamp lights up on its own, and this is also how the sockets in a flat are connected.

If a switch is in the main wire before a branch, it switches all the lamps after it together. If it is in a single branch, it only switches the lamp in that branch. If you draw a wire straight past a lamp, you get a **short circuit**: the current takes the easy way, and the lamp stays dark. Filled-in dots show where wires are electrically connected.

Electricians work with circuit diagrams every day when they wire houses, machines or cars. You also often find a circuit diagram in the instructions for an electronics kit. A typical example from the home is **two-way switching** in a stairwell, where two switches control the same lamp. Today, circuit diagrams are usually drawn on a computer with special software.

begriffe.erklaerung: A standardised symbol for an electrical component.
All the components lie one after the other in a single circuit.
The current divides into several branches, and each device has its own path.
The current flows past a device along a path with almost no resistance.

gewusst: A circuit diagram for a modern computer chip would be so huge that it can only be looked at on a screen.
Because circuit symbols are standardised internationally, you can understand a circuit diagram from Japan in Switzerland too.

teile.einleitung: Quantum entanglement is one of the most puzzling phenomena in physics. Two entangled particles behave like a single whole, even when they are far apart. If you measure one, you immediately know something about the other.
wichtigste: Entangled particles form a shared state, even over large distances.
In 1935, Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen published a famous paradox about it.
Albert Einstein dismissively called entanglement “spooky action at a distance”.
In 1964, John Stewart Bell set up an inequality with which entanglement can be tested.
In 2022, Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger received the Nobel Prize in Physics for experiments with entangled photons.
Entanglement cannot be used to send information faster than light.
In the Geneva region, Nicolas Gisin's group demonstrated entanglement over more than 10 kilometres.

abschnitte.text: Normally you can describe each particle on its own. With **entangled** particles this is no longer possible; they only have a shared state. An example: two photons are entangled in such a way that their polarisation is always opposite. Before the measurement, it is not fixed for either of them how it is polarised, but after measuring one, you immediately know the result for the other. The term entanglement was coined in 1935 by the physicist **Erwin Schrödinger**.

In 1935, **Albert Einstein**, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen published a famous paper, the **EPR paradox**. They argued that quantum physics was incomplete and that there must be **hidden variables** that fix the result in advance. Einstein mocked entanglement as “spooky action at a distance”. For a long time the question was more philosophical, because it could not be tested.

In 1964, the Northern Irish physicist **John Stewart Bell** found a way to settle the question in the laboratory. He set up an **inequality** that would always have to hold if there were local hidden variables. From the 1970s onwards, experiments by John Clauser, Alain Aspect and later Anton Zeilinger showed that the inequality is violated. So quantum physics was right, and the three received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** for this in 2022.

Although entangled particles are linked instantly, they cannot be used to send a message faster than light. This is because the measurement result on each side is purely **random**. Only when both sides compare their results in the normal way can the connection be seen. That is why entanglement does not contradict Einstein's **theory of relativity**.

In **quantum teleportation**, entanglement is used to transfer the quantum state of one particle to another, but not the particle itself. **Quantum cryptography** uses entangled or single photons to distribute keys in a way that cannot be eavesdropped on. Any eavesdropping would change the state and be noticed. Quantum computers also need entanglement to unleash their computing power.

In the late 1990s, the group of the physicist **Nicolas Gisin** at the University of Geneva sent entangled photons through fibre-optic cables in the Geneva region. The particles were more than 10 kilometres apart and still showed the typical connections. A Geneva company for quantum cryptography also grew out of this research. Today, entanglement has even been demonstrated with satellites over more than 1000 kilometres.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shared quantum state of several particles that can no longer be described individually.
A particle of light.
An assumed, hidden property that would fix a measurement result in advance.
A mathematical rule that can be used in experiments to test whether there are hidden variables.
The transfer of a quantum state from one particle to another.

gewusst: Anton Zeilinger and his team teleported quantum states over 143 kilometres between two of the Canary Islands.
Einstein rejected entanglement, but today it is considered one of the best-confirmed phenomena in physics.
In teleportation, the original state is lost, so you do not get a copy.

teile.einleitung: Rain is water that falls in drops from the clouds to the Earth. Without rain there would be no streams, no meadows and no drinking water. But how does a raindrop actually form, and what shape does it really have?
wichtigste: Rain is liquid precipitation that falls from clouds.
The drops fall when they have become too heavy for the air to carry them.
Very fine rain is called drizzle, and sudden heavy rain a downpour.
Falling raindrops are not drop-shaped but almost round.
Rain is part of the water cycle between sea, air and land.
On the street, rainwater flows into the sewers.

abschnitte.text: The Sun warms seas, lakes and the ground, so water **evaporates** and rises as invisible water vapour. Higher up the air is colder, the vapour cools and forms tiny droplets. Many billions of such droplets make a **cloud**. The droplets bump into each other and grow until they are too heavy and fall as rain. In our latitudes, rain often comes from snowflakes that melt as they fall through warmer air.

A raindrop is usually between half a millimetre and about five millimetres across. Small drops are almost **perfectly round**, because surface tension holds them together. Large drops are squashed a little flat underneath by the air as they fall and look like a small bun. So a falling drop never has the familiar teardrop shape with a point. Large drops fall at about 30 kilometres per hour.

Very fine rain with tiny drops is called **drizzle**. A sudden, very heavy rain is called a **downpour** or cloudburst and often happens during thunderstorms. Steady rain lasts a long time and is even; it usually comes from a large, grey layer of cloud. If rain freezes at once on the cold ground, it is called black ice from freezing rain.

Rain is part of the **water cycle**. Water evaporates from the sea, forms clouds and falls back as rain or snow. Part of it soaks into the ground and becomes **groundwater**, and part flows back to the sea through streams and rivers. In this way, the same water has been used again and again for millions of years.

Because damp air has to rise over the Alps, it rains quite a lot in Switzerland. That is why it is also called the **water tower of Europe**, because the Rhine, the Rhône and the Inn rise here. Particularly heavy rain falls on the northern side of the Alps and in Ticino, where it often rains very hard. Valais, on the other hand, is comparatively dry. In towns, rainwater from streets and roofs flows into the **sewers**.

Plants need rain to grow, and so do animals and people. Rain fills lakes, rivers and the groundwater, which supplies much of the drinking water in Switzerland. But too much rain in a short time can cause floods and landslides. If there is no rain for a long time, there is **drought** and the harvest suffers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water that falls from the air to the ground, for example rain, snow or hail.
When liquid water turns into invisible water vapour.
When water vapour cools and turns back into tiny droplets.
Water that has soaked into the ground and collects deep down.
Underground pipes that carry away waste water and rainwater.

gewusst: The typical smell of rain on dry ground is called petrichor.
A rainbow forms when sunlight is refracted in raindrops and split into its colours.
Most raindrops here started out as snowflakes high up in the cloud.

t1te7m88.t: Nant de Drance pumped storage power station

teile.einleitung: Nant de Drance is a large pumped storage power station in the canton of Valais that lies deep inside the mountain between two reservoirs. It works like a huge water battery: when there is surplus electricity, it pumps water upwards; when electricity is needed, it lets the water flow back down through turbines. With a power of 900 megawatts, it is one of the most powerful plants of its kind in Europe.
wichtigste: Nant de Drance lies in Valais in the municipality of Finhaut near the border with France.
It works between the Lac d'Emosson and the higher Lac du Vieux Emosson.
Its power is 900 megawatts, spread over six machines of 150 megawatts each.
When there is too much electricity in the grid, it pumps water into the upper reservoir.
When demand for electricity is high, the water flows back and produces electricity.
To create more storage space, the dam wall of the Lac du Vieux Emosson was raised.
The power station balances out fluctuations especially in wind and solar power.

abschnitte.text: The power station lies in Lower Valais near **Finhaut**, not far from Martigny and the border with France. It uses two existing reservoirs: the large **Lac d'Emosson** below and the smaller Lac du Vieux Emosson above. The machine hall is in a huge rock cave, a **cavern**, deep inside the mountain between the two lakes. That is why you can hardly see anything of the plant from outside.

A **pumped storage power station** stores energy by pumping water uphill. When there is too much electricity in the grid, for example at sunny midday times, motors drive the pumps and move water into the upper lake. When a lot of electricity is needed, the water flows back down through penstocks and drives **turbines**, which produce electricity. At Nant de Drance, six **pump turbines** do both jobs; depending on which way they turn, they pump or produce electricity.

Together, the six machines produce **900 megawatts**, roughly as much as a large nuclear power station. Some energy is lost when pumping and recovering it; modern plants reach an overall efficiency of around 80 per cent. If the power station takes in, for example, 100 megawatt-hours of electricity for pumping, it later gives back about 80 megawatt-hours. The full upper lake can store around 20 gigawatt-hours of electricity.

Construction began in 2008 and took around 14 years. Hundreds of specialists drilled tunnels and a cavern several hundred metres deep into the rock. So that the upper lake could hold more water, the **dam wall** of the Lac du Vieux Emosson was raised by around 20 metres. The power station has been fully in operation since July 2022 and was officially opened in September 2022. It belongs to Alpiq, the SBB, Industrielle Werke Basel and Forces Motrices Valaisannes of Valais.

Sun and wind do not always deliver the same amount of electricity, and the power grid must be exactly in balance at every moment. Nant de Drance can switch from pumping to generating within a few minutes and so balance out **fluctuations**. This helps to keep the grid in Switzerland and Europe stable. That is why pumped storage power stations are an important part of the **Energy Strategy 2050**, with which Switzerland wants to use more renewable energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A power station that stores energy by pumping water into a higher lake.
A unit for a large amount of power, one million watts.
What percentage of the energy put in can be used again.
A large, artificially dug cave in the rock.
A machine that can pump water and also produce electricity.

gewusst: The machine hall lies so deep inside the mountain that the workers had around 600 metres of rock above them.
When the upper lake is full, Nant de Drance can supply electricity at full power for around 20 hours.

teile.einleitung: The melting point is the temperature at which a solid substance becomes liquid. Ice melts at 0 °C, iron only at around 1,540 °C. Every pure substance has its own melting point, which is why it can be used to identify substances.
wichtigste: At normal air pressure, ice melts at 0 °C.
For a pure substance, the freezing point is exactly the same as the melting point.
At about 3,420 °C, tungsten has the highest melting point of all metals.
Gallium melts at just under 30 °C, in other words in a warm hand.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Salt lowers the freezing point of water, which is why it is spread on the roads in winter.
If a substance melts at a lower temperature than expected, it is impure.

abschnitte.text: A solid substance consists of particles that sit firmly in place and only jiggle a little. If you heat it, the particles jiggle more and more. At the **melting point** they break free from their fixed places, and the substance becomes liquid. If you cool the liquid down again, it solidifies at the same temperature, the **freezing point**. For water, both are at 0 °C.

While a substance is melting, its temperature does not rise any further, even though heat is being added. All the energy is needed to break the firm bonds between the particles. This energy is called **heat of fusion**. A glass of water with ice cubes therefore stays at about 0 °C as long as there is still ice floating in it. Only when everything has melted does the water get warmer.

Melting points vary enormously. **Mercury** melts at about minus 39 °C and is therefore liquid at room temperature. Gallium melts at just under 30 °C, tin at about 232 °C and gold at around 1,064 °C. Iron needs around 1,540 °C, and **tungsten** as much as about 3,420 °C. Because tungsten is so heat resistant, it was used for the filaments of old light bulbs.

If you dissolve salt in water, the freezing point drops below 0 °C. That is why **road salt** is spread in winter, so that no ice forms on the roads or existing ice melts. Pressure also affects the melting point; for ice it falls a little under high pressure. This matters in glaciers, because the ice at the bottom lies under an enormous weight.

In chemistry, the melting point is measured to identify substances and check their **purity**. An impure substance melts at a lower temperature than expected and often not at one exact temperature. In technology, melting points are needed for casting metals and for **soldering**, in which metal parts are joined with solder that melts easily. Melting points matter in the kitchen too: good chocolate melts at about body temperature and therefore melts on your tongue.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which a solid substance becomes liquid.
The temperature at which a liquid becomes solid.
The energy needed to melt a substance without it getting warmer.
How few other substances are contained in a substance.
Joining metal parts with a metal that melts easily.

gewusst: A spoon made of gallium would simply melt in a cup of hot tea.
Not all substances have a melting point: wood burns or breaks down before it could melt.
Glass and butter gradually soften when heated, instead of melting at one exact temperature.

teile.einleitung: The law of reflection is one of the most important rules of optics. It says that a ray of light is thrown back from a mirror at the same angle at which it hits it. With this simple law, you can work out mirrors, periscopes and even billiard shots.
wichtigste: The law of reflection applies to smooth, reflecting surfaces.
The angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal.
Both angles are measured from the normal, which is at right angles to the surface.
The incoming ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in one plane.
The law was already known in ancient Greece.
It also applies to sound and other waves.

abschnitte.text: The **law of reflection** says that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. Both angles are measured not from the mirror surface but from the **normal**. The normal is an imaginary line at right angles to the mirror at the point where the ray hits.

First you draw the mirror as a straight line and the point where the ray hits. Then you draw the normal at right angles to the mirror at that point. With a **set square with protractor**, you measure the angle of incidence, for example 40 degrees. You now draw the reflected ray, also at 40 degrees, on the other side of the normal.

In **billiards**, the ball bounces off the cushion on roughly the same principle. A **periscope** consists of two mirrors set at an angle of 45 degrees and so sends the light round the corner. If a ray hits a mirror at right angles, the angle of incidence is zero degrees. Then it is thrown straight back along its own path.

The Greek mathematician **Euclid** already described the law around 300 BC in a work on optics. Later, Hero of Alexandria investigated why light takes this path. He realised that the reflected ray chooses the shortest possible path. In the 17th century, scientists such as Christiaan Huygens explained reflection by the **wave nature** of light.

The law of reflection is used to design rear-view mirrors, headlights and telescopes. A **concave mirror** uses it to collect light at a focal point, for example in solar furnaces. Radar devices and satellite dishes also work according to this rule. The law is part of physics lessons at every lower secondary school in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The angle between the incoming ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
A line at right angles to a surface.
A tube with mirrors that lets you look round corners or over walls.

gewusst: Cat's eyes and bicycle reflectors use three mirror surfaces in the corner of a cube, which always send light straight back.
The law of reflection even applies to radio waves that are reflected by a layer of air high above the Earth.

teile.einleitung: The RGB colour space describes colours as a mixture of the three colours of light red, green and blue. Almost every screen, whether mobile phone, television or computer, produces its millions of colours this way.
wichtigste: RGB stands for red, green and blue.
Each colour channel usually has 256 brightness levels, which needs 8 bits.
With 256 levels per channel, about 16.7 million colours can be shown.
The RGB value (255, 0, 0) gives pure red; (128, 128, 128) gives grey.
Red and green light together make yellow, that is (255, 255, 0).
In hex code, #0000FF stands for pure blue.
Every pixel on a colour screen is made up of a red, a green and a blue sub-pixel.

abschnitte.text: In the **RGB colour space**, every colour is described by three numbers: how much red, how much green and how much blue it contains. These three colours are called the **primary colours** of light. Our eyes have three kinds of colour-sensing cells, the cones, which react especially to red, green and blue light. That is why we can be tricked into seeing almost all colours with just three colours of light.

With light, colours are added: the more light is added, the brighter it gets. Red and green make yellow, green and blue make cyan, red and blue make magenta. All three together at full strength make **white**, and no light makes black. This is different from painting with a paintbox, where mixed colours get darker.

Each channel usually has values from 0 to 255, that is 256 levels, which fit exactly into **8 bits**. Together that gives 256 times 256 times 256, that is 16,777,216 colours. Equal values in all three channels give shades of grey; (128, 128, 128) is a medium grey. On websites, colours are often written as a **hex code** with digits from 0 to 9 and letters from A to F, so #FF0000 is red and #0000FF is blue.

If you look at a screen with a magnifying glass, you see tiny red, green and blue dots of light, the **sub-pixels**. Three of them make up one picture element, or **pixel**. From a normal distance they merge for our eyes into a single mixed colour. Digital cameras work the other way round: their sensor measures the light behind red, green and blue filters.

In 1861, the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell showed a colour picture made up of three photographs taken through red, green and blue filters. Later, colour televisions with picture tubes used red, green and blue phosphors. In 1996, the companies HP and Microsoft set the **sRGB** standard so that colours look as similar as possible on different devices. It is still the most common colour space on the internet today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest dot of a digital picture or screen.
Mixing colours of light, which always makes things brighter.
The smallest unit of information; it can be 0 or 1.
A way of writing colours with six characters made of digits and the letters A to F.

gewusst: Yellow on a screen contains no yellow light at all; it is just red and green light at the same time.
Printers do not use RGB but the colours cyan, magenta, yellow and black.

teile.einleitung: A sandpit is a box or pit filled with sand in which children play, dig and build. But it is also a small physics laboratory. In the sandpit you can see how grains trickle, stick together, soak up water and form cones.
wichtigste: Sand consists of many small grains, mostly of the mineral quartz.
Dry sand trickles and can be poured almost like water.
When dry sand trickles onto a heap, a cone forms.
Wet sand is better for building, because the water sticks the grains together.
Water soaks away quickly, because there are gaps between the grains.
With a sieve, you separate fine sand from little stones.

abschnitte.text: Sand is a mixture of small grains between about 0.06 and 2 millimetres in size. Most grains are made of **quartz**, a hard mineral. Sand forms when wind, water and frost break up rock over a very long time. Finer grains are called silt or clay, coarser ones **gravel**.

Dry grains of sand hardly stick to each other; they roll and slide past each other. That is why dry sand can be poured almost like a liquid. If you let it trickle onto a heap, a **cone** forms with sides that are always about equally steep. This slope is called the **angle of repose** and is roughly 30 to 35 degrees for dry sand. If the heap gets steeper, a small avalanche slides off.

If sand is slightly damp, tiny bridges of water form between the grains. The **surface tension** of the water pulls the grains towards each other, so the water sticks them together. This lets you build towers, walls and castles. If a sandcastle dries in the sun, the water bridges evaporate and it falls apart more easily. If the sand is soaked through, on the other hand, it becomes mushy again and flows.

Between the grains there are many small gaps, the **pores**. If you pour water onto sand, it flows quickly down through these gaps. That is why hardly any puddles are left in the sandpit after rain. Because sand lets water through so well and holds back dirt as it does so, it is also used in **sand filters** for cleaning drinking water.

If you walk barefoot through the sand, the loose grains move aside under your weight. That is why your feet sink in, whereas on solid tarmac they do not. With a **sieve** you can sort the sand: fine grains fall through the holes, and little stones and leaves stay behind. On building sites, too, sand and gravel are separated with large sieves.

Sandpits are found in playgrounds, gardens and nursery schools. By digging, shaping and shovelling, children practise using their fingers and learn in a playful way how materials behave. To keep the sand clean, private sandpits are often covered at night so that cats do not use them as a toilet. In many municipalities, the sand in playgrounds is replaced regularly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very hard, often transparent mineral that most grains of sand are made of.
The steepest slope a heap of loose material can have without sliding.
A force at the surface of water that acts like a thin skin.
A small space between grains.

gewusst: The world record for the tallest sandcastle is over 20 metres high.
Under the microscope you can see that some grains of sand are tiny shells of sea creatures.
After water, sand is one of the most used raw materials in the world, above all for concrete.

teile.einleitung: A shadow is a dark area that light cannot reach because an object is blocking the light's way. Shadows are with us everywhere, growing long and short depending on where the Sun is. In the past you could even tell the time with them.
wichtigste: For a shadow you need light and an object that blocks the light.
Light travels in straight lines and cannot go round objects.
At midday the Sun is high, which is why the shadow is shortest then.
A shadow always points away from the light source.
The closer an object is to the lamp, the bigger its shadow becomes.
Transparent objects such as clear glass cast almost no shadow.
A sundial shows the time with a shadow.

abschnitte.text: Light travels in **straight lines**. If an opaque object is in the way, no light arrives behind it. This dark area is the **shadow**, and it has the outline of the object. A clear pane of glass, on the other hand, lets almost all the light through and therefore casts hardly any shadow.

In the morning and evening the Sun is low, so shadows are very long. At **midday** it is at its highest, so your shadow is shortest then. In summer, midday shadows in Switzerland are shorter than in winter, because the Sun climbs higher. A shadow always points away from the Sun: if the Sun is in the east, the shadow points west.

If you move an object closer to a torch, its shadow on the wall gets bigger. If you move it further away, it gets smaller. This is used in **shadow theatre**, where figures perform behind a lit screen. With your hands you can make dogs, birds or rabbits appear on the wall like magic.

If the light source is large or there are several lamps, areas of different darkness form. The completely dark part is the **umbra**, where no light reaches at all. Next to it lies the lighter **penumbra**, where only part of the light arrives. On a cloudy day, light comes from everywhere, which is why you hardly see a shadow.

The **sundial** is an old device in which a rod casts a shadow onto a dial. On many churches and old houses in Switzerland you can still see painted sundials today. A **solar eclipse** is also a shadow event: the Moon casts its shadow onto the Earth. In a lunar eclipse, on the other hand, the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

begriffe.erklaerung: The completely dark part of a shadow, where no light falls.
A lighter shadow area that only part of the light reaches.
Something that gives out light itself, such as the Sun or a lamp.
A clock that shows the time with the shadow of a rod.

gewusst: A shadow never moves by itself; it always follows the object and the light.
More than 2,200 years ago, the Greek scholar Eratosthenes used shadows to work out the circumference of the Earth.
In the village of Viganella in Italy, a large mirror brings sunlight in winter onto the village square, which would otherwise lie in the shadow of the mountain for weeks.

teile.einleitung: In a series circuit, electrical components such as lamps or resistors are connected one after the other on a single path for the current. The current has to flow through all the components in turn. This has important consequences for current, voltage and brightness.
wichtigste: In a series circuit there is only one single path for the current.
The current is the same at every point.
The voltages across the individual components add up to the voltage of the source.
Two identical lamps on 12 volts get 6 volts each.
The resistances are added: 10 ohms and 20 ohms make 30 ohms.
If one lamp burns out, all the lamps go out.
A light switch is connected in series with its lamp.

abschnitte.text: In a **series circuit**, components are connected one after the other like beads on a string. The current flows from the source through the first component, then through the second and so on, until it returns to the source. There are no branches. The opposite is the **parallel circuit**, in which the current splits up into several paths.

Because there is only one path, exactly the same amount of current flows through all the components. If you measure the **current** before, between and after the lamps, the meter shows the same value everywhere. You can picture it like water in a single hose. What flows in at the front must come out again at the back.

The **voltage** of the source is shared out among the components. If there are 2, 3 and 4 volts across three components, the source has 9 volts. Two identical lamps on 12 volts get 6 volts each. That is why two lamps in series shine less brightly than one lamp on its own. Batteries, on the other hand, are connected in series, plus to minus, to add up their voltages: three 1.5-volt batteries make 4.5 volts.

Every component slows the current with its **resistance**, measured in ohms. In a series circuit, you simply add the resistances to get the total resistance. So 10 ohms and 20 ohms make 30 ohms. The more components you connect in series, the greater the total resistance and the smaller the current. These rules follow from **Kirchhoff's laws** and Ohm's law.

If one lamp burns out in a series circuit, the circuit is broken and all the lamps go out. You know this from old **fairy lights**, where you had to search laboriously for the faulty bulb. That is why lamps and sockets in the home are connected in parallel. A **switch**, on the other hand, must be in series with the lamp so that it can open and close the path for the current. A fuse is also connected in series and breaks the whole circuit if there is too much current.

begriffe.erklaerung: A closed path along which electric current can flow.
What drives the current, measured in volts.
How strongly a component slows down the current, measured in ohms.
A circuit in which the current splits up into several paths.

gewusst: In a torch, the batteries usually sit in series one behind the other in the tube.
Modern fairy lights are often built so that a faulty LED does not switch off the whole string.
The German physicist Gustav Kirchhoff formulated his rules for circuits in 1845 while still a student.

teile.einleitung: Every battery has two connections: the positive terminal and the negative terminal. Current can only flow if both are correctly connected to a device. That is why you find a plus sign (+) and a minus sign (−) in every battery compartment.
wichtigste: A battery has exactly two terminals, a positive and a negative terminal.
The positive terminal is marked with the sign +, the negative terminal with a minus sign.
On a round AA battery, the end with the small bump is the positive terminal.
The signs in the battery compartment show how to put the battery in.
If a battery is in the wrong way round, the device often does not work.
Leads for the positive terminal are often red, for the negative terminal usually black.
A normal car battery has a voltage of 12 volts.

abschnitte.text: The **terminals** are the two connections of a power source. At the **negative terminal** there is a surplus of electrons, at the **positive terminal** a shortage. Between the two terminals there is an electrical **voltage**, measured in volts. If you connect the terminals through a device, current flows and the device works.

On a round AA or AAA battery, the end with the small **bump** is the positive terminal and the flat end is the negative terminal. A normal AA battery has 1.5 volts. On a 9-volt block battery, both terminals are on the same side; the smaller round connector is the positive terminal. On button cells, the large flat side is usually marked with the +.

In the **battery compartment**, the plus and minus signs show which way round the battery must go in. There is often a small **spring** at the negative terminal. If a battery is in the torch the wrong way round, the torch usually does not light. Some devices can even be damaged by batteries put in the wrong way.

On leads for direct current, the positive terminal is often marked **red** and the negative terminal usually **black**. You can see this, for example, on jump leads for cars. A normal **car battery** has 12 volts. When connecting it, you must pay close attention to the colours, because mixing them up can cause sparks and damage.

If you connect the positive and negative terminals directly with a wire, you get a **short circuit**. Then a very large current flows, and the wire and battery get hot. This can be dangerous and, at worst, start a fire. That is why you should never carry loose batteries in your trouser pocket together with keys or coins.

abschnitte.titel: Which way does the current flow?
abschnitte.text: In the wire, the electrons move from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. In the past this was not yet known, and it was decided that current flows from plus to minus. This convention is called **conventional current** and is still used in circuit diagrams today. But for everyday use it makes no difference.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the two connections of a battery or power source.
The electrical pressure between the positive and negative terminals, measured in volts.
A direct connection between the terminals through which a dangerously large current flows.
A tiny, negatively charged particle that carries the current in a wire.

gewusst: A socket also has connections, but there the direction of the current changes 50 times a second.
With a lemon, a piece of copper and a piece of zinc, you can build a simple battery with positive and negative terminals.
If you connect two 1.5-volt batteries one after the other, plus to minus, you get 3 volts.

teile.einleitung: The Paul Scherrer Institute, PSI for short, is the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. It lies on the River Aare in the canton of Aargau and runs huge research facilities that exist nowhere else in Switzerland. Researchers from all over the world come here to look into tiny structures with particle beams and especially bright light.
wichtigste: PSI is located mainly in the Aargau municipality of Villigen.
It belongs to the ETH Domain, like ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne.
It is named after Paul Scherrer, a physicist at ETH Zurich.
PSI was created in 1988 from two predecessor institutes, EIR and SIN.
The Swiss Light Source is a synchrotron light source that produces extremely bright X-ray light.
SwissFEL produces very short and intense X-ray laser pulses.
Cancer patients are treated with proton therapy at PSI.

abschnitte.text: PSI lies on both sides of the **River Aare**, in the municipalities of Villigen and Würenlingen. It was founded in 1988 by merging the Federal Institute for Reactor Research (**EIR**) and the Swiss Institute for Nuclear Research (**SIN**). Today more than 2000 people work there. The institute belongs to the ETH Domain and is funded mainly by the federal government.

**Paul Scherrer** lived from 1890 to 1969 and was a professor of physics at ETH Zurich. Among other things, he studied crystals with X-rays and built up nuclear physics in Switzerland. He was considered an inspiring teacher and encouraged many young researchers. In his honour, the new institute was given his name in 1988.

The **Swiss Light Source** is a ring-shaped particle accelerator in which electrons circle at almost the speed of light. As they do, they give off extremely bright X-ray light, which is used, for example, to study the structure of proteins or new materials. **SwissFEL** is an X-ray laser that has been in operation since 2016. Its flashes of light are so short that they can be used to watch chemical reactions almost in slow motion.

The heart of the proton facility is a large **ring cyclotron**, which brings protons to very high speeds. These protons are used to produce other particles. The SINQ neutron source supplies neutrons that let you look inside materials. The SμS source supplies **muons**, short-lived elementary particles used to study the magnetic properties of materials.

PSI has a centre for **proton therapy**. In it, tumours are treated very precisely with a beam of protons. The advantage is that the healthy tissue around the tumour is better protected. This is especially important for children and for tumours close to sensitive organs such as the eyes or the brain.

PSI does not only research the basics but also practical questions. These include batteries, fuel cells, renewable energy and the safety of nuclear power stations. Air pollutants and the climate are also studied. In the school laboratory **iLab**, school classes can do physics experiments themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ring-shaped particle accelerator in which particles fly in a circle and give off light.
An accelerator in which particles get faster and faster on a spiral path.
Cancer treatment with a beam of protons instead of X-rays.
An elementary particle similar to the electron but much heavier, which decays quickly.
The group made up of the two federal institutes of technology and four federal research institutes.

gewusst: SwissFEL is housed in a building around 740 metres long in the forest.
At PSI, the masses and properties of particles have been measured that appear in textbooks all over the world.
Every year, several thousand guest researchers from abroad come to PSI.

teile.einleitung: Relative motion is movement seen from another moving object. Whether something is at rest or moving depends on where you are looking from. In a moving train you sit still, but seen from the platform you whizz past at 100 km/h.
wichtigste: Every movement is described in relation to a frame of reference.
If two cars travel in the same direction, you subtract their speeds.
If two cars travel towards each other, you add their speeds.
If a child walks forwards at 5 km/h in a train going at 100 km/h, it is moving at 105 km/h relative to the ground.
A boat going against the current makes slower progress than in still water.
Raindrops run diagonally across train windows because the train is moving relative to the rain.
The Earth is also constantly moving, even though we do not feel it.

abschnitte.text: If you sit in a moving train, you are at rest relative to your seat. But relative to the trees outside, you are moving fast. The object or place from which a movement is described is called the **frame of reference**. Movement relative to another moving object is called **relative motion**. Galileo Galilei already realised that in a ship moving steadily you cannot feel whether it is moving.

If a car at 100 km/h is following one at 80 km/h, it only gets closer at 20 km/h. So you subtract the speeds. If the two cars are travelling towards each other, they get closer at 180 km/h, because you add the speeds. Two trains 150 kilometres apart travelling towards each other at 70 and 80 km/h therefore meet after one **hour**.

abschnitte.titel: On the train and on the escalator
abschnitte.text: A child walks forwards at 5 km/h in a train going at 100 km/h. Relative to the ground, it is then moving at 105 km/h; if it walks backwards, only 95 km/h. On an **escalator**, the speeds add up in the same way. If a 30-metre escalator moves at 0.5 m/s and a man walks up it at 1 m/s, he moves at 1.5 m/s and takes 20 seconds.

A boat that moves through the water at 5 m/s only makes 3 m/s relative to the bank against a **current** of 2 m/s. Downstream, on the other hand, it would be going at 7 m/s. Aircraft know this too: a headwind makes them slower relative to the ground, a tailwind faster. That is why a flight from Europe to America often takes longer than the return flight.

When **overtaking**, only the difference in speed counts. A car at 30 m/s overtaking a lorry at 25 m/s is only 5 m/s faster. If it has to gain 50 metres, overtaking takes 10 seconds. But in this time the car travels 300 metres. That is why overtaking on country roads is so dangerous.

Even when we stand still, we are moving very fast relative to the Sun. At the equator, the Earth's rotation carries us round at about 1670 km/h. At the same time, the Earth orbits the Sun at around 30 kilometres per second. We do not feel this, because everything around us is moving with us. So whether something is at rest is always a question of your **point of view**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place or object from which a movement is described.
The speed of an object relative to another moving object.
The movement of water or air in a particular direction.

gewusst: When an aircraft is refuelled in the air, both aircraft fly so that they are almost at a standstill relative to each other.
If you sit in a stationary train and the train next to you pulls away, you often think your own train is moving.
A geostationary satellite seems to stand still when seen from the ground, even though it is flying round the Earth at over 10,000 km/h.

teile.einleitung: A rear-view mirror is a mirror on a vehicle that lets you look behind and to the side without turning round. It uses the physics of the reflection of light and is essential for safety on the road.
wichtigste: A rear-view mirror is used to see behind you in the car.
The interior mirror hangs at the top in the middle of the windscreen.
A normal car usually has two door mirrors.
Some door mirrors are slightly curved so that you can see more.
The area next to a vehicle that you cannot see in the mirrors is called the blind spot.
At night you can dip the interior mirror so that headlights behind you do not dazzle you.
On a bike, a rear-view mirror is fixed to the handlebars.

abschnitte.text: A mirror throws light back; this is called **reflection**. The rule is that light bounces off at the same angle at which it hits the mirror. That is why you can see in the mirror what is behind you without turning your head. Rear-view mirrors are usually made of glass with a thin layer of metal on the back.

The **interior mirror** hangs at the top in the middle of the windscreen and shows the view backwards through the rear window. The two **door mirrors** on the left and right show the road beside and behind the car. Before changing lanes, turning and reversing, you look in the mirrors. Lorries and buses also have several large mirrors, including one above the passenger door.

A flat mirror shows everything at the right size but only a small part of the view. An outward-curving, **convex** mirror shows a larger area, but things look smaller and further away in it. That is why many door mirrors are slightly curved, often only at the outer edge. Curved mirrors also hang at blind exits and bends.

Despite all the mirrors, there are areas next to a vehicle that the driver cannot see: the **blind spot**. On lorries it is especially large, and a bike or a child next to it can be completely invisible. That is why, as a cyclist, you should never wait on the right next to a lorry that is turning. A good rule is: if you cannot see the driver in the mirror, the driver cannot see you either.

At night, the headlights of the cars behind can dazzle you in the interior mirror. Many interior mirrors can be tilted with a small lever, and then you only see a faint reflection from the front of the glass. Modern mirrors darken themselves electronically. Some new cars even replace the door mirrors with small **cameras** and screens inside the car.

One of the first rear-view mirrors was used in 1911 in the car race at Indianapolis. The driver Ray Harroun drove alone, without the passenger who usually looked backwards, and so fitted a mirror. Later, rear-view mirrors became usual in all cars. Today they are required by law in Switzerland and many other countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: The throwing back of light from a smooth surface.
An outward-curving mirror that shows a larger area.
The area next to a vehicle that the driver cannot see.
Adjusting the mirror so that bright light no longer dazzles you.

gewusst: Many door mirrors carry a note saying that objects are closer than they appear in the mirror.
With his mirror, Ray Harroun won the first Indianapolis 500 race in 1911.

teile.einleitung: A parabolic flight is a special flight manoeuvre in which people on board an aircraft float weightless for a short time. To do this, the aircraft flies a path in the shape of an arch, a parabola. Researchers and astronauts use these flights to carry out experiments and to train for space.
wichtigste: On a parabolic flight, an aircraft flies an arch-shaped path, a parabola.
One parabola gives about 22 seconds of weightlessness.
Before and after the weightless phase, you are pressed into your seat with about 1.8 times normal gravity.
A European research flight typically includes about 30 parabolas.
In Europe, the Airbus A310 Zero G is used for this (as of 2026).
The lower gravity on the Moon or Mars can also be recreated.
Many people on board feel sick because their sense of balance gets confused.

abschnitte.text: On a parabolic flight, a large aircraft takes turns flying steeply upwards and back down again. At the top of the arch, the aircraft and the people inside are all in **free fall** together. Because everything falls at the same speed, the people float in the cabin. This state is called **weightlessness**, even though the Earth of course keeps pulling.

First the aircraft flies level and then pulls steeply upwards, pressing the people into their seats with about 1.8 times normal gravity. Then the pilot reduces the thrust so far that the aircraft flies a **ballistic parabola**, like a thrown ball. The engines keep running, but only to make up for air resistance. After about 22 seconds of floating, the pilot pulls the aircraft out again, and once more about 1.8 times normal gravity acts.

Parabolic flights are used mainly for **experiments** and for astronaut training. Researchers study, for example, how flames, liquids or plants react without gravity. Astronauts practise moving and working while floating. If the aircraft flies flatter arches, gravity is only reduced, so the conditions on the **Moon** or Mars can be recreated.

In Europe, the French company **Novespace** organises the flights, usually from Bordeaux, on behalf of space agencies such as ESA. It uses the converted Airbus A310 Zero G, which used to serve as a government aircraft. In the cabin, most of the seats have been removed and the walls and floor are padded. Swiss research groups, for example from the University of Zurich, have also carried out experiments on parabolic flights.

abschnitte.titel: The body on a roller coaster
abschnitte.text: The constant switching between heavy and weightless confuses the **organ of balance** in the inner ear. The eyes and the ear tell the brain contradictory things, and many people feel sick. That is why participants are often given a medicine against travel sickness beforehand. Because of this effect, NASA's aircraft got the nickname “Vomit Comet”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which you feel nothing of your weight and float.
An arch-shaped curve, like the path of a thrown ball.
Movement in which only gravity acts on an object.
The part of the inner ear that senses how we move and which way is up.

gewusst: A flight with about 30 parabolas adds up to around ten minutes of weightlessness altogether.
Film scenes set in space have been shot in parabolic flight aircraft so that the actors really float.
The International Space Station is constantly in free fall around the Earth, like an endless parabolic flight.

teile.einleitung: The resultant force is the single force that can replace all the forces acting on an object at the same time. It decides whether an object starts moving, speeds up or slows down, or stays at rest.
wichtigste: The resultant force replaces all the forces acting on an object together.
If two forces act in the same direction, you add them, for example 20 N and 30 N to make 50 N.
If two forces act in opposite directions, you subtract them: 50 N and 30 N give 20 N in the direction of the larger force.
If the resultant force is zero, an object at rest stays at rest.
A sledge pulled with 80 N against 30 N of friction experiences a resultant force of 50 N.
From the resultant force and the mass, you calculate the acceleration.
Two forces of 5 N and 7 N can give at most 12 N together; 13 N is impossible.

abschnitte.text: Several **forces** often act on an object at the same time, for example pulling, pushing, friction and weight. The **resultant force** is their sum; it is also called the net force or the resultant. It acts as if only this one force were pulling on the object. Forces are measured in **newtons**, abbreviated N.

If forces point in the same direction, they are added. If they point in opposite directions, they are subtracted, and the resultant points in the direction of the stronger side. If two children pull to the right with 40 N and 35 N and one pulls to the left with 60 N, that gives 75 N minus 60 N, so 15 N to the right. This is exactly how a **tug of war** decides which team wins.

Forces have a size and a direction; they are **vectors**. If they are at an angle to each other, you draw them as arrows and complete them into a **parallelogram of forces**. The diagonal is then the resultant. That is why two forces of 5 N and 7 N give a value between 2 N and 12 N, depending on the angle.

According to Newton's second law: force equals mass times acceleration. If a 10 kg trolley is pulled with 50 N and friction slows it with 20 N, 30 N are left. Divided by 10 kg, that gives an acceleration of 3 m/s². If the resultant force is zero, the motion does not change: an object stays at rest or keeps moving steadily.

A book on the table stays where it is because its weight and the supporting force of the table cancel each other out exactly. The forces are said to be in **equilibrium**. Bridges, buildings and cranes are calculated so that all the forces on them cancel out. A cyclist riding at a steady speed is also pedalling exactly as hard as the air and friction are slowing them down.

begriffe.erklaerung: The cause of an object changing its shape or its motion.
The unit of force, named after Isaac Newton.
A quantity with size and direction, often drawn as an arrow.
A state in which all the forces cancel each other out.

gewusst: A force of 1 newton is roughly the weight of a small 100-gram bar of chocolate.
An aircraft in calm cruising flight is also in equilibrium: lift and weight, and thrust and air resistance, cancel each other out.

teile.einleitung: The puck is the flat, black disc used to play ice hockey. It is made of hard rubber, weighs about 160 grams and can travel faster than 150 km/h from hard shots. A lot of physics about friction, momentum and cold can be discovered with it.
wichtigste: An ice hockey puck is a flat, round disc of hard rubber.
A puck is black and weighs about 160 grams.
The players shoot the puck with their sticks.
On ice the puck slides much further than on tarmac, because ice is very smooth.
Before a game, pucks are cooled in a freezer so that they bounce less.
Very hard shots make the puck go faster than 150 km/h.

abschnitte.text: An official ice hockey puck is a **disc** about 7.6 centimetres across and 2.5 centimetres thick. That is exactly 3 inches and 1 inch. It is made of **hard rubber**, that is vulcanised rubber, and is black. Its mass is about 160 grams, about as much as a medium-sized apple.

Rubber gets softer and bouncier when warm. So a warm puck bounces up easily on the ice and is harder to control. That is why pucks are stored in a **freezer** before a game. When cold, they are harder and **bounce** less, and during a game they are regularly swapped for freshly cooled ones.

On ice, **friction** is very low, which is why the puck glides a long way across the whole rink after a shot. On tarmac, the rough surface slows it down quickly. That is why there are special plastic pucks or balls for street hockey. Because the puck lies flat, it can hardly roll away as it glides, which makes it easier to control than a ball.

Players shoot and pass the puck with their **sticks**. For a **slapshot**, they swing back a long way and bend the stick like a spring as it hits the ice. This energy passes to the puck, so that it can travel faster than 150 km/h. In hardest-shot competitions, speeds of over 170 km/h have even been measured, which is why goalkeepers wear thick protective gear.

Ice hockey is one of the most popular sports in Switzerland. The top league is called the **National League**, and its clubs include SC Bern, HC Davos and the ZSC Lions. Every year around Christmas, HC Davos hosts the long-standing **Spengler Cup**. The Swiss national team has won silver several times at world championships, for example in 2013 and 2018.

begriffe.erklaerung: The flat hard rubber disc used to play ice hockey.
Rubber that has been hardened by heating it with sulphur.
A force that slows things down when two surfaces slide against each other.
An especially hard shot for which the player swings back a long way.

gewusst: In a professional game, dozens of pucks are often needed, because they have to stay cold or fly into the crowd.
In air hockey, the puck floats on a thin cushion of air and so glides with almost no friction.
At the Olympic Games and world championships, the pucks are printed with the tournament logo and are popular collectors' items.

teile.einleitung: A quartz clock is a clock whose rhythm is set by a tiny vibrating quartz crystal. It is much more accurate than a simple mechanical clock and is now built into almost every wristwatch, kitchen clock and computer. For the Swiss watch industry, its invention was both an opportunity and a shock.
wichtigste: The quartz in most wristwatches vibrates 32,768 times a second.
This number is 2 to the power of 15 and can easily be divided down electronically to one second.
The quartz is made to vibrate through the piezoelectric effect.
Jacques and Pierre Curie discovered the direct piezoelectric effect in 1880.
In Neuchâtel, the quartz movement “Beta 21” was developed in the 1960s.
The collapse of the Swiss watch industry in the 1970s and 1980s is called the quartz crisis.
A watch quartz is usually shaped like a tiny tuning fork.

abschnitte.text: **Quartz** is a common mineral made of silicon and oxygen, known for example as rock crystal. A quartz clock contains a tiny, precisely cut quartz plate in the shape of a **tuning fork**. It vibrates at a very stable frequency, much as a struck bell always gives the same note. Because the quartz is damped very little, it vibrates extremely evenly. A typical watch quartz is most accurate at about 25 °C, close to the temperature at the wrist.

If you press on a quartz crystal, an electrical voltage appears on its surface. The brothers **Jacques and Pierre Curie** discovered this in 1880. The other way round, the crystal changes shape when a voltage is applied. The clock uses this **piezoelectric effect**: a small electronic circuit makes the quartz vibrate and at the same time measures its vibrations.

The watch quartz vibrates 32,768 times a second, that is at 32,768 **hertz**. This number is exactly 2 to the power of 15. An electronic counter can therefore halve the frequency fifteen times and so get exactly one pulse per second. This pulse drives a small stepper motor for the hands or moves the digital display on. A good quartz clock is only a few seconds out per month.

The first quartz clock was built in the USA in 1927 and still filled a whole cupboard. In Switzerland, the **Centre Electronique Horloger** in Neuchâtel developed the Beta 21 quartz wristwatch movement in the 1960s, which was sold by several brands from 1970. At the end of 1969, the Japanese company Seiko brought out the Astron, the first quartz wristwatch you could buy. Thanks to cheap electronics, quartz watches quickly became affordable for everyone in the 1970s.

Many Swiss watch companies kept relying on mechanical watches for a long time. Cheap quartz watches from Japan and Hong Kong conquered the world market, and the **quartz crisis** hit the Swiss watch industry hard in the 1970s and 1980s. Tens of thousands of jobs were lost. An important fresh start was the **Swatch**, a cheap plastic watch with a quartz movement, which came onto the market in 1983 and became popular worldwide.

Quartz oscillators are not only found in clocks. Computers, mobile phones, televisions and cars need them as **timekeepers** so that their electronics work in the right rhythm. Atomic clocks are even more accurate than quartz clocks. Radio-controlled clocks receive their time signal by radio and regularly correct their quartz movement.

begriffe.erklaerung: A voltage appearing when certain crystals are squeezed, and the other way round.
The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
A precisely cut piece of quartz that vibrates at a fixed frequency.
A severe crisis of the Swiss watch industry caused by cheap quartz watches from Asia.

gewusst: The Swatch was deliberately designed with few parts so that it could be made cheaply in Switzerland.
A watch quartz is often only a few millimetres long and sits in a tiny metal tube.
The word piezo comes from the Greek word for press.

teile.einleitung: Rolling is a movement in which a round object turns and moves forwards at the same time. Balls, wheels and spheres roll, and because rolling needs much less force than pushing, the wheel is one of the most important inventions of humankind.
wichtigste: When rolling, an object turns and moves forwards at the same time.
A ball rolls most easily because it is round in every direction.
A heavy box is much easier to move on rollers than by dragging it.
The wheel lets carts and bikes roll; it has to be perfectly round for this.
A tin can only rolls if you lay it on its round side.
A snowball gets bigger and bigger if you roll it through wet snow.
The dung beetle rolls a ball of dung along in front of it.

abschnitte.text: When **rolling**, two movements happen at the same time: the object turns around its axis and moves forwards. If it rolls without slipping, the point that is just touching the ground is still for a moment. That is why nothing has to drag over the ground. Rolling is therefore much easier than **sliding**.

For something to roll evenly, it must be round: a **sphere**, a cylinder or a wheel. A ball rolls in all directions, a can or a tree trunk in only one direction, namely on its round side. A wheel must be **perfectly round**, or the cart will bounce up and down as it moves. A cube can tip over, but it cannot roll.

The **wheel** was invented more than 5000 years ago. Very old wooden wheels have been found in Mesopotamia and in Europe, and wooden wheels from the Neolithic period were also found in lake dwelling settlements on Lake Zurich. Even before that, people pushed heavy stones on round tree trunks used as rollers. Today cars, trains, bikes, skateboards with four wheels and suitcases roll.

The **dung beetle** shapes a ball out of dung and rolls it away backwards with its hind legs. Some animals roll themselves up into a ball to defend themselves, such as hedgehogs or armadillos. Stones in streams are also ground round over a long time because they roll and knock against each other. And when you build a snowman, the snowball grows because new snow keeps sticking to it as it rolls.

In machines, **ball bearings** make sure that axles turn easily. In them, small steel balls roll between two rings instead of the parts rubbing against each other.
