Ball bearings are found in bikes, inline skates, washing machines and wind turbines. Conveyor belts in parcel centres and at airports also run over many rollers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A turning movement around an axis.
An imaginary or real line around which something turns.
A part with small balls that makes turning easy.
A movement in which one surface slips over another.

gewusst: A wheel rolling without slipping is completely still for a moment at the point where it touches the ground.
Dung beetles even find their way by the light of the Sun or the Milky Way when rolling their balls.

teile.einleitung: A polarising filter, or polariser for short, only lets through light that vibrates in a particular direction. This means it can greatly reduce reflections and glare. Polarising filters are found in sunglasses, cameras, screens and 3D glasses.
wichtigste: A polarising filter only lets through light with a particular direction of vibration.
Two ideal polarising filters crossed at 90 degrees let no light through.
Most polarising filters made of plastic film are based on dichroism.
Photographers use polarising filters to reduce reflections on water or glass.
Polarising sunglasses mainly let through vertically vibrating light.
In the late 1920s, Edwin Land developed an inexpensive polarising film.
In photoelasticity, crossed polarising filters make stresses in plastic visible.

abschnitte.text: Light is a wave that vibrates across its direction of travel. In normal sunlight or lamplight it vibrates in all directions mixed up; it is **unpolarised**. If the light vibrates in only one direction, it is called **polarised**. A polarising filter has a **transmission axis** and lets through only the matching part of the light.

Unpolarised light loses half its brightness in an ideal polarising filter. When polarised light hits a turned filter, **Malus's law** applies: the intensity falls with the square of the cosine of the angle of rotation. At 60 degrees, only a quarter, that is 25 per cent, gets through. At 90 degrees, with crossed filters, no light gets through at all. Amazingly, if you slide a third filter at 45 degrees between crossed filters, 12.5 per cent of the original light gets through again.

Light reflected by horizontal surfaces such as water, a wet road or snow is mostly horizontally polarised. **Polarising sunglasses** mainly let through vertically vibrating light and so absorb the glare. Anglers can see into the water better with them. Photographers screw a polarising filter onto the **lens** to reduce reflections and get a bluer sky.

Most polarising filters are made of a **plastic film** with long, stretched molecules lined up in parallel. Light that vibrates parallel to these chains of molecules is absorbed; the rest gets through. This property is called **dichroism**. In the late 1920s, the American **Edwin Land** developed an inexpensive polarising film, and his work later led to the company Polaroid.

If you put a transparent plastic object, such as a ruler or a CD case, between two crossed polarising filters, colourful stripes appear. They show where there are **mechanical stresses** in the material. This method is called **photoelasticity**. Engineers use it to test models of components and find weak spots.

**LCD screens** in mobile phones, watches and calculators contain polarising filters; without them you would see no picture. Many cinema **3D glasses** have lenses that polarise differently for each eye. If you hold polarising glasses in front of a mobile phone screen and turn them, the picture goes dark at a certain angle. This is a simple experiment for discovering polarised light.

begriffe.erklaerung: The direction of vibration of a light wave.
The direction in which light may vibrate to pass through a polarising filter.
The property of a substance of absorbing or letting through light depending on its direction of vibration.
A method that uses polarising filters to make forces in transparent material visible.

gewusst: Bees and other insects can see polarised skylight and use it to find their way.
The blue of the sky is also partly polarised, which is why it gets darker with a polarising filter.
The Vikings probably used a special crystal, the sunstone, to find the Sun when the sky was cloudy.

teile.einleitung: Photovoltaics means turning sunlight directly into electric current. This happens in solar cells, which you can see on roofs, on building fronts and even on dam walls in the Alps. Without any noise, exhaust fumes or moving parts, electricity is made from light.
wichtigste: Photovoltaics turns sunlight directly into electric current.
The scientist Alexandre Edmond Becquerel discovered the photovoltaic effect in 1839.
Most solar cells are made of the semiconductor silicon.
Today's commercial solar panels have an efficiency of about 20 per cent.
The peak power of a solar installation is given in kilowatt-peak (kWp).
An inverter turns the direct current from the panels into alternating current for the household supply.
In winter, solar installations in the Alps produce more electricity than in the foggy, grey Swiss Plateau.

abschnitte.text: The word is made from the Greek “phos” for light and the name of the physicist Alessandro Volta. In a **solar cell**, particles of light hit a semiconductor material, usually **silicon**. This sets electrons moving and creates an electrical voltage. Many solar cells together make a **solar panel**, and many panels make a solar installation.

abschnitte.titel: From the roof to the socket
abschnitte.text: Solar cells produce **direct current**, but in the house you need alternating current. That is why an **inverter** converts the current. If a household uses the solar power directly itself, this is called **self-consumption**. Whatever is left over is fed into the grid or stored in a battery.

The peak power of an installation is measured in **kilowatt-peak**, abbreviated kWp. In Switzerland, one kilowatt-peak produces around 1000 kilowatt-hours of electricity a year. So an installation of 10 kWp produces about 10,000 kWh a year, which is more than a typical detached house uses. The **efficiency** of today's panels is about 20 per cent, so a fifth of the light energy becomes electricity.

In winter, the Swiss Plateau often lies under a thick blanket of fog. Installations in the mountains, on the other hand, are often above the **fog** and get more sun. In addition, the white **snow** reflects a lot of light. **Bifacial panels**, which also take in light through their back, benefit especially from this. A large alpine solar installation stands on the Muttsee dam wall in the canton of Glarus.

In 1839, the French physicist **Alexandre Edmond Becquerel** discovered that light produces a voltage in certain materials. In 1954, researchers in the USA presented the first usable silicon solar cell. At first, solar cells were used mainly in **satellites**, because there are no sockets in space. Since about 2010, solar panels have become much cheaper and are now on countless rooftops.

Solar power is produced without exhaust fumes and helps to slow down **climate change**. In Switzerland, photovoltaics is an important pillar of the **Energy Strategy 2050**. One drawback is that solar installations produce no electricity at night and less in winter. That is why storage and other power stations are also needed, for example hydroelectric power stations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flat component that turns light directly into electricity.
A device that turns direct current into alternating current.
The highest power of a solar installation in full sunshine under standard conditions.
Using the solar power you produce yourself straight away.
A solar panel that can catch light from the front and the back.

gewusst: The solar aircraft Solar Impulse of the Swiss Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg flew around the world in 2015 and 2016 using only solar energy.
Solar cells also work well in the cold; in great heat their efficiency actually drops a little.
Silicon, the most important material for solar cells, is obtained from quartz sand.

teile.einleitung: A bathroom scale is a measuring device for finding out a person's body weight. Many families have one in the bathroom, and doctors' surgeries often use one too. What is interesting in physics is that it actually measures a force and works out the mass in kilograms from it.
wichtigste: At home, a bathroom scale often stands in the bathroom.
In Switzerland it shows weight in kilograms.
You stand still on the scale with both feet.
On a thick carpet, a bathroom scale measures inaccurately; it belongs on a hard, level floor.
If two people stand on the scale together, it adds their weights.
You can weigh a pet by weighing yourself with and without it and subtracting the values.
At check-ups at the children's doctor, weight and height are often measured.

abschnitte.text: The Earth pulls us downwards with the force of our **weight**. A bathroom scale measures how hard we press on it. From this it works out our **mass** and shows it in kilograms. In everyday life we just call this “weight”, although physicists distinguish between mass and the force of weight.

Older bathroom scales are **spring scales**: our weight squashes a spring, and levers turn a dial with numbers. Modern digital scales have small **load cells** in their feet. In them, a piece of metal bends very slightly, and sensors measure this tiny bending electrically. A small computer works out the weight from it and shows it on a display.

The scale must stand on a hard, level floor, such as tiles. On a thick **carpet** it sinks in, and the springs or sensors measure inaccurately. You stand still with both feet in the middle and do not move. If you bounce or jump, you briefly press harder or less hard, and the display jumps back and forth.

If two children weighing 25 and 27 kilograms stand on the scale together, it shows 52 kilograms. A cat that will not sit still can be weighed with a trick: you first weigh yourself holding the cat and then on your own, and work out the **difference**. If the scale shows 40 kilograms with the dog and 32 without, the dog weighs 8 kilograms. Vets and parents also weigh small animals or babies this way.

abschnitte.titel: Scales at the doctor's and in everyday life
abschnitte.text: At the **children's doctor**, weight and height are often measured at check-ups to see whether a child is growing well. Especially accurate, officially calibrated scales are usually used there. A person's weight varies a little over the day, depending on what they have eaten and drunk. So a single measurement does not say much; what matters more is whether you feel healthy and fit.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter there is in an object, measured in kilograms.
The force with which the Earth pulls an object downwards.
A scale that uses a spring to measure how hard something pulls or presses.
A sensor in digital scales that measures a tiny amount of bending.
To have a measuring device officially checked so that it measures accurately.

gewusst: On the Moon, a normal bathroom scale would show only about a sixth of your weight on Earth.
If you stand on a scale in a lift, it briefly shows more when the lift starts going up.
Some digital scales switch on automatically as soon as you tap them lightly.

teile.einleitung: An ice skate is a boot with a narrow metal blade underneath that lets you glide over ice. Because the friction between blade and ice is very small, you can move forwards fast with little effort. Ice skating is a popular winter pastime in Switzerland and the basis for sports such as ice hockey and figure skating.
wichtigste: The blades of ice skates are usually made of steel.
Ice skates glide well because the friction between blade and ice is very small.
Sharp edges stop you slipping sideways on a bend.
You cannot glide on tarmac with ice skates, because the friction there is far too great.
Ice hockey and figure skating are sports on ice skates.
Many Swiss towns and villages have ice rinks in winter.
On frozen lakes you may only go onto thick ice that has been declared safe.

abschnitte.titel: How an ice skate is built
abschnitte.text: An ice skate consists of a firm boot that supports the ankle and the **blade** underneath. The blade is a narrow rail of hardened **steel**, often only a few millimetres wide. Its underside is usually ground slightly hollow, so that two sharp edges are formed. With these edges the skate grips the ice like a knife.

The **friction** between blade and ice is surprisingly small. Today, researchers explain this mainly by a wafer-thin, almost liquid layer on the surface of the ice that acts like a lubricant. People used to believe that the pressure of the blade alone melted the ice, but this effect is much too weak for that. On tarmac there is no such layer, and the friction is so great that you cannot glide.

To push off, you tilt the blade and press the edge against the ice. On a bend you lean inwards, and the edge keeps the skate on its track. If the edges are blunt, you slip away sideways. That is why skates are regularly **sharpened** in a sports shop.

**Ice hockey** is one of the most popular sports in Switzerland, and the Spengler Cup in Davos has been held since 1923. In **figure skating**, skaters perform jumps, spins and step sequences to music. The Swiss skater Denise Biellmann invented a famous spin that is named after her, and Stéphane Lambiel became world champion twice. In speed skating, especially long blades are used, while in curling no skates are worn.

The safest place to skate is an **ice rink**, which many Swiss communes have in winter, some of them artificial. On frozen lakes and ponds you may only go out if the commune has officially declared the ice safe. In some places, for example near inflowing streams or reeds, ice can be much thinner than it looks. For beginners, a helmet and gloves make sense, because you often fall at first.

begriffe.erklaerung: The narrow metal rail under the ice skate on which you glide.
A force that slows two surfaces sliding against each other.
A fast turn on one leg, as in figure skating.
An ice rink whose ice is made with cooling machines.

gewusst: The oldest ice skates were made of animal bones tied under the shoes, and they are several thousand years old.
Professional speed skaters reach speeds of over 50 kilometres per hour on the ice.

teile.einleitung: Radioactivity is the property of certain atomic nuclei of changing by themselves into other nuclei and giving off invisible radiation as they do so. You can neither see, smell nor feel it, but it can be detected with measuring devices such as the Geiger counter. It is dangerous but also very useful, for example in medicine or for dating things.
wichtigste: Radioactive atomic nuclei are unstable and decay by themselves.
Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 in uranium salts.
There are three main kinds of radiation: alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
Alpha radiation consists of helium nuclei and is stopped even by a sheet of paper.
The half-life tells you after what time half of the nuclei have decayed.
The biological effect of radiation is given in sieverts.
With the C-14 method, the age of wood, bones and other remains can be determined.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has a tiny **atomic nucleus** made of protons and neutrons. In some nuclei this mixture is not stable. Such nuclei eventually change by themselves and give off energy as **ionising radiation**. Exactly when a single nucleus decays is pure chance, but with very many nuclei it can be predicted well.

In 1896, the French physicist **Henri Becquerel** noticed that uranium salts blackened a wrapped photographic plate, even though no light reached it. Shortly afterwards, **Marie Curie** and Pierre Curie studied this radiation more closely. Marie Curie coined the name radioactivity and discovered the elements polonium and radium. She received two Nobel Prizes for her work, in physics and in chemistry.

The three kinds of radiation consist of different particles and go different distances into materials. **Alpha radiation** consists of helium nuclei, each with two protons and two neutrons, and is stopped even by paper or the skin. **Beta radiation** consists of fast electrons; in beta-minus decay, the atomic number of the nucleus increases by 1, because a neutron becomes a proton. **Gamma radiation** is high-energy electromagnetic radiation, similar to light, and is only strongly weakened by thick walls of lead or concrete.

The **half-life** is the time after which half of a radioactive substance has decayed. After two half-lives a quarter is left, after three half-lives 12.5 per cent. Carbon-14 has a half-life of around 5730 years. So if a wood sample still contains 25 per cent of its original C-14, it is around 11,460 years old. Archaeologists use this **radiocarbon method** very often.

Strong radiation can damage cells and genetic material and cause cancer. That is why its effect on the body is measured as the **equivalent dose**, in the unit sievert. But in medicine, radiation also helps, for example in the treatment of tumours or in examinations in nuclear medicine. Nuclear power stations use the energy from splitting uranium nuclei to produce electricity.

There is a little radiation everywhere in nature too, for example from rocks, from space or from the gas **radon**. In some areas of Switzerland, for example in the Jura and the Alps, radon can occur more strongly in cellars. The Federal Office of Public Health monitors radiation throughout the country. In 2026, the Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt nuclear power stations were still operating in Switzerland; Mühleberg was shut down in 2019.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of atom of an element with a particular number of neutrons in the nucleus.
The time after which half of the radioactive nuclei have decayed.
A measuring device that shows radioactive radiation with audible clicks.
The unit that tells you how strongly radiation affects the body.

gewusst: Bananas contain tiny amounts of radioactive potassium, but this is completely harmless.
Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive today and are kept in lead boxes.
Uranium-238 has a half-life of around 4.5 billion years, about as old as the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Melting is the change of a substance from a solid to a liquid state. It happens when a substance takes in enough heat, for example when an ice cube turns into water in your warm hand. Every substance has its own melting temperature.
wichtigste: When something melts, a solid substance becomes liquid.
For this, the substance needs heat.
Ice melts at 0 °C when the air pressure is normal.
The temperature at which a substance melts is called its melting point.
The opposite process is called solidifying or freezing.
While melting, the temperature stays the same until everything has melted.
In Switzerland, the glaciers are melting fast because of global warming.

abschnitte.text: Substances can be **solid**, **liquid** or gas; these are called states of matter. When melting, a substance changes from solid to liquid. An ice cube in your hand melts because your body heat warms it. The ice turns into water, but the substance itself stays the same.

In a solid substance, the tiny particles are held firmly in place and only jiggle a little. When they take in heat, they jiggle more and more. At the **melting point** they break free from their fixed places and can slide past each other. The heat added is used for this, which is why the temperature does not rise during melting; this is called **heat of fusion**.

Every pure substance has its own melting point. Ice melts at 0 °C, chocolate at only about 30 to 35 °C, which is why it melts in your mouth. Lead melts at around 327 °C and iron only at around 1,538 °C. At over 3,400 °C, **tungsten** has the highest melting point of all metals.

When a liquid cools down, it becomes solid again; this is called **solidifying**, or freezing in the case of water. The melting point and freezing point are at the same temperature. Foundries make use of this back and forth by pouring liquid metal into moulds. Candles are also made from melted wax that solidifies in the mould.

In spring, the snow in the Alps melts, and the **snowmelt** fills streams, rivers and reservoirs. Switzerland's glaciers have been melting fast for decades because of **global warming**. The Great Aletsch Glacier, the largest glacier in the Alps, has become several kilometres shorter since the middle of the 19th century. Experts fear that a large part of the Swiss glaciers will disappear by the end of the 21st century.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form in which a substance exists: solid, liquid or gas.
The temperature at which a substance melts.
The change from liquid to solid.
The heat a substance needs in order to melt.

gewusst: Salt on the road lowers the melting point of ice, which is why it thaws even below 0 °C.
The metal gallium melts at only around 30 °C and can turn liquid in your hand.
Dirty snow melts faster in the sun, because dark surfaces take in more heat.

teile.einleitung: Potential energy is stored energy that an object has because of its position or its state. The best-known example is gravitational potential energy: an object that you lift up can give this energy back when it falls.
wichtigste: Potential energy is stored energy of position or shape.
Gravitational potential energy depends on the mass and height of an object.
It is calculated with the formula E = m · g · h.
If you lift an object twice as high, its potential energy doubles.
For the height, you always have to choose a zero level.
On the Moon, potential energy at the same height is smaller than on Earth.
Pumped storage power stations such as Nant de Drance store energy as the potential energy of water.

abschnitte.text: When you lift an object, you have to do **work** against gravity. This work is not lost; it is then stored in the object as **gravitational potential energy**. If you let go, the potential energy is turned into kinetic energy as it falls. So an apple on a tree, the water in a reservoir or a cyclist at the top of a pass all have potential energy.

Gravitational potential energy is calculated with **E = m · g · h**. Here m is the mass in kilograms, h the height in metres and g the acceleration due to gravity, on Earth around 9.81 or, simplified, 10 newtons per kilogram. So a 2-kilogram stone at a height of 5 metres has 2 · 10 · 5 = 100 joules. A hiker of 60 kilograms who climbs 1000 metres gains 600,000 joules.

Potential energy is always relative to a chosen **reference point**, the zero level. Whether you measure from the floor, the table or sea level is up to you. What matters in the end are the differences. If you move a 1-kilogram book from a 0.8-metre-high table to a 2-metre-high shelf, it gains 1 · 10 · 1.2 = 12 joules, whatever zero level you choose.

On the Moon, gravity is only about a sixth as strong as on Earth. So a stone at the same height has much less potential energy there. As well as gravitational potential energy, there are other forms of potential energy. A stretched spring or a drawn bow stores **elastic energy**. Electric fields and chemical bonds also contain potential energy.

According to the **law of conservation of energy**, energy is never lost; it is only converted. A roller coaster is first pulled up and gains potential energy. On the way down, this turns into kinetic energy, and on the next hill back into potential energy. In the pendulum of a clock or on a swing, too, the two forms of energy keep taking turns.

Switzerland makes great use of the potential energy of water in the Alps. Water from high reservoirs flows down through pipes and drives turbines. A **pumped storage power station** pumps water uphill with surplus electricity and lets it flow back down when it is needed. The large **Nant de Drance** pumped storage power station in Valais started operating in 2022 and works between the Emosson and Vieux Emosson reservoirs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of energy, named after the physicist James Prescott Joule.
The value g, which tells you how strongly gravity acts; on Earth around 9.81 N/kg.
The chosen height from which potential energy is measured.
The basic law that energy does not disappear but is only converted.

gewusst: The potential energy of 1 litre of water falling 100 metres would light a 5-watt LED lamp for around three minutes.
The caverns of Nant de Drance lie deep inside the mountain, in a huge rock cave.
Pendulum clocks and cuckoo clocks are often driven by weights that slowly sink downwards, giving off potential energy.

teile.einleitung: A screw is a component with a spiral thread that is moved into a material by turning. It holds things together, but the principle of the screw is also found in car jacks, vices and even water pumps. In physics, the screw counts as one of the simple machines, because it saves force.
wichtigste: A screw has a spiral thread that grips into the material.
Normal screws are turned in clockwise.
A nut can be turned onto a screw with a thread.
The pitch is the distance a screw moves forwards in one complete turn.
A small pitch needs less force but more turns.
Friction in the thread stops a screw from coming loose by itself.
An Archimedes screw can lift water upwards.

abschnitte.text: A screw consists of a **shank** with a thread and usually a head. The **thread** is a slanting groove that winds round the shank like a spiral staircase. The head has a slot, a cross or a recess for the tool. A screw with a cross in its head is called a cross-head screw, and there are also hexagon socket and star shapes.

The thread is basically an **inclined plane** wrapped around a cylinder. When you turn it, you cover a long distance in a circle, but the screw only moves forwards a little way. That is why you need little force and can still tighten it very firmly. If a screw has a **pitch** of 1.5 mm, it goes 30 mm deep after 20 turns.

In wood, a screw usually holds more firmly than a nail, because its turns grip into the wood. In metal parts, a screw is often combined with a **nut** that is turned onto the thread. In concrete or brick walls, a plastic wall plug goes in first, and the screw is turned into it. Friction in the thread makes sure that a tightened screw does not turn itself out under load.

A **corkscrew** turns into the cork of a bottle like a screw. A scissor jack lifts a car with a threaded spindle. With the vice on a workbench, you clamp workpieces with great force. On many piano stools, you adjust the height by turning the seat.

Most threads are right-hand threads and are tightened clockwise. But some parts deliberately have a **left-hand thread**. A well-known example is the left pedal on a bicycle, which would otherwise come loose as you pedal. Some gas bottles also have left-hand threads, so that they cannot be mixed up.

The idea of the screw is very old and is often credited to the Greek scientist Archimedes. With the **Archimedes screw**, a rotating spiral inside a tube, water was lifted upwards. In ancient times, screws were also used in presses for wine and olive oil. Only since the 19th century have screws with standardised threads been made in large numbers by machines.

begriffe.erklaerung: The spiral groove around the shank of a screw.
The distance a screw moves forwards in one turn.
A ring with an inner thread that is turned onto a screw.
A thread that is tightened anticlockwise.
A simple aid such as a lever or screw that saves force.

gewusst: A German memory aid for screws is “Rechts rein, links raus” (right to go in, left to come out); in English people say “righty tighty, lefty loosey”.
Archimedes screws are still used today in sewage treatment plants to lift waste water.
A mincer also pushes the meat forwards with a large screw.

teile.einleitung: Polarisation describes the direction in which a wave vibrates across its direction of travel. With light, special filters can pick out particular directions of vibration. Sunglasses, cameras, screens and even bees make use of this.
wichtigste: Only transverse waves can be polarised.
Sunlight is practically unpolarised.
Light is partly polarised when it is reflected by glass or water.
In 1808, Étienne-Louis Malus discovered polarisation by reflection.
At Brewster's angle, the reflected light is completely polarised.
Calcite shows such strong double refraction that you see writing twice.
LCD screens and 3D cinema glasses work with polarised light.

abschnitte.text: Light is a **transverse wave**, which means it vibrates across the direction in which it travels. You can picture a rope that you shake up and down or from side to side. If a wave vibrates in only one plane, it is **linearly polarised**. Sound waves in air are longitudinal waves and so cannot be polarised. Natural light from the Sun or a light bulb vibrates in all directions mixed up and is practically unpolarised.

A **polarising filter** only lets through light with a particular direction of vibration. If you put two such filters on top of each other and turn one by 90 degrees, it becomes almost completely dark. Polarising sunglasses absorb the reflected light from water or snow. That is why you can see into the water better with them when fishing, and glare when skiing is reduced.

In 1808, the Frenchman **Étienne-Louis Malus** discovered that light is polarised when it is reflected. At a particular angle of incidence, the reflected light is even completely polarised. This angle is called **Brewster's angle**, after the Scot David Brewster. For glass with a refractive index of 1.5, it is about 56 degrees. Then the reflected and the refracted rays are exactly at right angles to each other.

Some crystals split a ray of light into two rays that are polarised differently. This is called **double refraction**. Calcite shows this especially strongly. If you put a clear calcite crystal on a newspaper, you see the letters twice. This property was already described in the 17th century.

The light of the blue sky is partly polarised, depending on where the Sun is. People cannot see this, but **honeybees** can detect this pattern. They use it as a compass, even when the Sun is hidden behind clouds. Other insects and some birds probably find their way like this too.

A **liquid crystal display** (LCD) contains two polarising filters with liquid crystals between them. These turn the direction of vibration of the light more or less depending on the voltage and so control the brightness of each pixel. Many **3D cinema glasses** have a differently polarised lens for each eye, so each eye sees its own picture. Photographers use polarising filters to remove reflections and make the sky look deep blue.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wave that vibrates across its direction of travel.
A filter that only lets through light with a particular direction of vibration.
The angle of incidence at which reflected light is completely polarised.
The splitting of a ray of light into two rays in some crystals.

gewusst: If you hold polarising sunglasses in front of a mobile phone screen and turn them, the screen can suddenly look black.
Some researchers think that the Vikings used crystals to navigate by the polarised light of the sky.
Radio waves are polarised too, which is why it matters which way an aerial is pointing.

teile.einleitung: Scissors are a cutting tool made of two blades joined in the middle by a screw. In physics terms, they are a double lever. That is why a little force on the handles can produce a lot of force at the blades.
wichtigste: Scissors consist of two levers that move about a shared pivot.
The pivot is at the screw in the middle.
Scissors cut most powerfully close to the pivot.
Long handles, as on garden shears, give more force.
The blades cut by sliding past each other and shearing the material.
On real left-handed scissors, the blades are swapped round.
You pass scissors on closed and handle first.

abschnitte.text: Scissors have two metal **blades** joined at the screw in the middle so that they can turn. Behind the pivot are the handles, usually with holes for thumb and fingers. The screw must be tightened just right: if it is too loose, the paper gets stuck between the blades instead of being cut. If it is too tight, the scissors are hard to move.

Each half of a pair of scissors is a **lever** that turns about the **pivot** at the screw. The longer the handle is compared with the distance to the cutting point, the greater the force at the blade. That is why thick card is best cut close to the pivot and not with the tip. For the same reason, garden shears for thick branches and tin snips have long handles.

The two blades slide past each other very closely. The material between them is pushed upwards from one side and downwards from the other until it tears apart. This kind of load is called **shear**, and in German it gives scissors their name (“Schere”). The blades are slightly curved towards each other so that they always touch at the cutting point.

There are paper scissors, fabric scissors, hair scissors, nail scissors and kitchen scissors. Gardeners use secateurs and large hedge trimmers, and craftspeople use tin snips. For small children there are craft scissors with **rounded tips**, so that you cannot stab yourself. On real left-handed scissors the blades are swapped round, so that left-handers can see the cutting line and the blades are pressed together properly.

Always pass scissors on closed and handle first. When walking, hold them with the tips pointing down. After use, put them back in their place closed. The ancient Romans were already using scissors with a pivot in the middle around 2,000 years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rigid body that moves about a pivot and can increase force.
The point about which a lever turns; on scissors, the screw.
The sharp part of a cutting tool.
A load in which two forces act in opposite directions very close to each other.

gewusst: The oldest scissors were made from a single bent piece of metal that sprang open again like a spring, similar to today's sheep shears.
Tin snips can cut thin metal because their long handles multiply the force.

teile.einleitung: Reaction time is the time that passes between noticing a signal or a danger and taking action. It is usually only a fraction of a second, but on the road it can be a matter of life and death. In physics it is used to calculate stopping distances.
wichtigste: Reaction time is the time from noticing a danger to taking action.
On the road, about one second is often used for calculations.
During the reaction time, a car keeps going at the same speed.
At 50 km/h, a car covers about 14 metres in one second.
If you drive twice as fast, the reaction distance becomes twice as long.
Being distracted by a mobile phone clearly lengthens reaction time.
In sprinting, a start less than 0.1 seconds after the gun counts as a false start.

abschnitte.text: If a ball suddenly rolls onto the road, you first have to **see** it, then recognise it in your brain and decide, and finally move your muscles. The time for this whole chain is called **reaction time**. People react to a simple light signal in about 0.2 seconds. In a real traffic situation, where you first have to work out what is going on, it usually takes longer.

During the reaction time, the driver has not yet braked, so the car keeps going at the same speed. The distance it covers is called the **reaction distance**. At 50 km/h, just under 14 metres per second, with one second of reaction time it is about 14 metres. At 100 km/h it is already about 28 metres. So the reaction distance grows in the same proportion as the speed.

The **stopping distance** is the reaction distance plus the braking distance. The braking distance grows much more strongly than the speed: at twice the speed it becomes about four times as long. That is why an accident at 50 km/h is much more dangerous than at 30 km/h. On a wet or icy road, the braking distance gets even longer.

You can measure your own reaction time with a **ruler**. One person holds the ruler at the top, and the other holds their thumb and forefinger open at the zero mark. Without warning, the ruler is let go and must be caught as quickly as possible. If it falls 20 centimetres, for example, the reaction time according to the laws of falling is about 0.2 seconds.

**Distraction** from a mobile phone, loud music or conversations clearly lengthens reaction time. Tiredness, alcohol and some medicines also make you slower. Anyone who looks at their phone while cycling or walking often sees dangers far too late. Concentrating in traffic is therefore the best protection.

In sport, a quick reaction is especially important. In sprint races, sensors in the **starting block** measure when a runner sets off after the starting gun. If it is faster than 0.1 seconds, it counts as a **false start**, because a person cannot react to the gun that quickly. Goalkeepers in football or ice hockey also train their reactions specifically.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance a vehicle covers during the reaction time.
The distance from starting to brake until coming to a stop.
Reaction distance and braking distance together.
A start that happens too early; in sprinting, less than 0.1 seconds after the gun.

gewusst: People usually react a little faster to sounds than to light.
Anyone who looks at their phone for two seconds while driving at 50 km/h travels almost 28 metres blind.
Flies react so fast that they can often dodge a hand with ease.

teile.einleitung: Tyre pressure tells you how hard the air in a tyre presses against its walls. Whether bike, car or aeroplane: with the right pressure, you travel more safely and faster and save effort.
wichtigste: You pump air into a bicycle tyre, usually with a bicycle pump.
The air gets into the inner tube through the valve and cannot get back out.
Tyre pressure is often measured in the unit bar.
With too little air, a bike is hard work and slow to ride.
If the inner tube has a hole, the air escapes and the tyre goes flat.
John Boyd Dunlop made the pneumatic tyre well known when he built one for his son's tricycle.
You can find a small hole in an inner tube by holding it in water.

abschnitte.text: Air is made of tiny particles that constantly dart about and bump against the inside wall of the tyre. The more air you pump in, the more particles hit the wall and the **pressure** rises. This makes the tyre firm, so it can carry the weight of the bike and rider. The pressure is measured with a **pressure gauge**, which is often fitted directly on the pump.

The most common unit for tyre pressure is the **bar**. One bar is roughly the air pressure around us at sea level. A racing bike often needs 6 to 8 bar, a mountain bike with wide tyres only about 1.5 to 2.5 bar. For cars the pressure is usually about 2 to 3 bar; in America, on the other hand, people often use **psi**.

The **valve** is a kind of one-way street for air: it can get in, but not out again by itself. On bikes there are three common types: the car valve, the Dunlop valve and the slim French valve. To pump up a tyre you need a **bicycle pump** with the right attachment. A track pump with a pressure gauge shows straight away how high the pressure already is as you pump.

If there is too little air in the tyre, it gets squashed a lot as you ride, which slows you down and costs effort. The inner tube can also get pinched against the rim and get a hole; this is called a **pinch flat**. If the pressure is too high, on the other hand, the ride is bumpy and the tyre has less grip. The right range is usually printed as a number on the side of the tyre.

abschnitte.titel: The invention of the pneumatic tyre
abschnitte.text: In the past, bikes and carriages ran on wheels made of wood, iron or solid rubber, which was very bumpy. The Scot Robert William Thomson patented an air-filled tyre as early as 1845, but the idea was forgotten again. In 1888 in Belfast, the vet **John Boyd Dunlop** built a pneumatic tyre for his son's tricycle and applied for a patent. After that, the pneumatic tyre spread quickly on bikes and later on cars.

If you have a puncture, you take the inner tube out of the tyre and pump it up a little. If you then hold it in water, small **air bubbles** rise from the leaky spot. The spot is roughened and sealed with a patch and rubber solution. Before refitting it, you look inside the tyre for thorns or bits of glass, or the inner tube will soon go flat again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit of pressure; one bar is roughly normal air pressure at sea level.
A small part on the inner tube that lets air in but not out again.
A measuring device that shows pressure.
A tyre from which the air has escaped; also called a flat.

gewusst: Aircraft tyres are often filled with nitrogen instead of normal air and have a much higher pressure than car tyres.
A tyre slowly loses air even without a hole, because the air particles move through the rubber.
New cars in Europe today often have a system that shows a warning if the tyre pressure is too low.

teile.einleitung: A paper bridge is a simple experiment that lets you learn in a playful way how bridges and building parts become stable. A flat sheet of paper carries almost nothing, but a folded sheet carries a surprising amount. The secret is not in the material but in the shape.
wichtigste: A flat sheet between two cups bends under a single coin.
If you fold the paper in a zigzag, the bridge carries much more.
The folds make the paper stiffer, because it can no longer bend so easily.
A sheet rolled into a tube and stood upright carries a surprising amount.
To test it, it is best to put coins on the bridge as weights.
Corrugated cardboard, corrugated iron and steel girders use the same principle.
Engineers call building with clever shapes lightweight construction.

abschnitte.text: You place two cups or piles of books of the same height about 15 centimetres apart. You lay a flat sheet of paper across them as a **bridge**. Even a single coin in the middle makes the sheet sag and fall down. Then you fold a sheet of the same size in a **zigzag** like an accordion and lay it across the gap again. Now you can stack coin after coin on it, often many dozens.

A flat sheet is very thin, so it bends easily. With the folds, the paper sticks out above and below the middle. If the folded bridge wants to bend, the top side has to be squashed and the bottom side stretched, and that takes much more force. This makes the paper **stiffer**, even though it is still the same sheet. Experts say that the shape increases the **bending stiffness**.

If you roll a sheet into a **tube** and stand it upright, it becomes a column. You can put surprisingly heavy things on it, sometimes even a book. The weight is spread evenly over the whole round wall. Only when the wall buckles somewhere does the column collapse. Several tubes side by side carry even more.

**Corrugated cardboard** consists of two flat layers of paper with a wavy layer in between, which is why cardboard boxes are so stable. The roofs of barns and halls are often made of corrugated iron. Steel girders on building sites are shaped like an I or H so that they carry a lot with little material. Bridges, too, often have frameworks of triangles or hollow boxes instead of thick, solid beams. Nature uses the principle as well, for example in hollow blades of grass and birds' bones.

Paper bridges are a popular experiment in lessons and competitions. Often the rule is to build the strongest possible bridge with just one sheet and no glue. You can test different shapes: zigzags, tubes, arches or U-shapes. It is worth counting the coins carefully and noting the results in a table. That way you work like real **researchers**.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly something resists bending or changing shape.
Cardboard with a wavy paper layer in the middle, which is light yet stable.
An upright building part that carries weight from above.
Building with as little material as possible but with clever, stable shapes.

gewusst: A sheet folded in a zigzag can carry many times its own weight.
Hollow tubes are almost as stable as solid rods but much lighter.
Blades of grass are hollow and bend in the wind without breaking.

teile.einleitung: Plastic deformation is a change of shape that stays even when no force is acting any more. When you squeeze modelling clay or bend a wire, the material does not go back to its old shape. Without this property, metals could neither be forged nor rolled into sheets.
wichtigste: A plastic deformation remains after the load is removed.
In an elastic deformation, by contrast, an object returns to its old shape.
In metals, crystal defects called dislocations make plastic deformation possible.
Bending metal several times makes it harder; this is called work hardening.
Recrystallisation annealing makes work-hardened metal easy to shape again.
At room temperature, glass breaks with practically no plastic deformation.
The crumple zone of a car absorbs impact energy through plastic deformation.

abschnitte.text: If you pull a spring and let go, it springs back; that is an **elastic deformation**. If you pull too hard, the spring stays stretched out; that is a **plastic deformation**. The boundary between the two is called the **yield point** or yield strength. For many metals, the proof stress R_p0.2 is given instead: the stress at which a permanent stretch of 0.2 per cent occurs.

Metals are made of tiny crystals in which the atoms are arranged in regular rows. There are faults in these crystals, which are called **dislocations**. Under force, these dislocations move through the crystal, and layers of atoms slide past each other. This changes the shape without the metal breaking.

If you bend a copper wire back and forth several times, it becomes stiffer and harder. The reason is **work hardening**: so many dislocations are created that they get in each other's way. If you keep bending, the wire eventually breaks. In **recrystallisation annealing**, the metal is heated, new crystals form and it becomes soft and easy to shape again.

In a **tensile test**, a sample is clamped into a machine and slowly pulled apart until it breaks. You measure how much force is needed and how much the sample stretches. The permanent lengthening after breaking, compared with the original length, is called **elongation at break**. Brittle materials such as **glass** or ceramics have almost no elongation at break; they break without warning.

In **forging**, rolling and deep drawing, metal is deliberately shaped plastically; this is how aluminium drinks cans are made, for example. The **crumple zone** of a car deforms in an accident and absorbs impact energy. This protects the people inside. Clay, modelling clay and plasticine can also be shaped plastically, which is why you can model with them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A change of shape that stays when the force is gone.
A change of shape that disappears when the force is gone.
A fault in the arrangement of atoms in a crystal that can move.
A metal getting harder by being shaped without heating.
How much a sample has permanently lengthened by the time it breaks.

gewusst: The word “plastic” comes from the Greek “plassein”, which means to shape or knead.
Glass can only be shaped when it is strongly heated, as glassblowers do.
Gold can be shaped plastically so well that it can be beaten into wafer-thin gold leaf.

teile.einleitung: A periscope, called a Sehrohr (seeing tube) in German, is an optical device that lets you look over obstacles without being seen yourself. It is best known from submarines, which use it to look above the surface of the water. You can make a simple periscope yourself with two mirrors and some cardboard.
wichtigste: In German, a periscope is called a Sehrohr.
The word comes from Greek and means roughly “look around”.
A simple periscope needs 2 mirrors.
The two mirrors are tilted at an angle and parallel to each other.
The image in a simple periscope with two mirrors is upright.
Submarines use periscopes to look over the water.
On land you can use one, for example, to look over a wall.

abschnitte.text: A periscope is a tube that sends light round two corners. At the top, an opening looks in one direction; at the bottom, you look in facing the same direction. This lets you see what is happening above or behind an **obstacle**. The name comes from the Greek words “peri” for around and “skopein” for look.

In the simplest periscope there is a **mirror** at the top and one at the bottom, both tilted at an angle of 45 degrees. Light falls on the first mirror at the top and is sent downwards. The second mirror sends it horizontally into the eye again. Here the **law of reflection** applies: light is reflected at the same angle at which it hits the mirror. Because there are two reflections, the image ends up upright and not reversed left to right.

A **submarine** can stay just below the surface of the water and poke out only the slim periscope. This lets the crew see ships and coasts while staying almost invisible themselves. Such periscopes are several metres long and contain prisms and lenses instead of simple mirrors, so that you can zoom in. Modern submarines also use cameras that send the image to screens.

In the First World War, soldiers used periscopes to look out of the trenches without raising their heads. Tanks also have angled mirrors with which the crew can look out while staying protected. In large crowds, for example at parades, spectators sometimes hold small **cardboard periscopes** above other people's heads. In medicine and engineering, there are similar devices for looking into narrow spaces.

You can build a simple periscope from a long **cardboard tube**, for example a milk carton, and two small mirrors. You cut a window at the top and one at the bottom on opposite sides. You stick the mirrors in at an angle of 45 degrees so that they are parallel to each other. Now you can look over the edge of the table or round a corner.

begriffe.erklaerung: A smooth surface that reflects light.
The bouncing back of light from a surface.
A transparent, cut piece of glass that can redirect light.
A ship that can travel under water.

gewusst: By turning the periscope in a submarine, you can search the whole horizon all the way round.
A single mirror shows the world reversed left to right, but a periscope with two mirrors shows it the right way round.
When a submarine travels with its periscope up, it makes a small wave by which the periscope can be spotted from far away.

teile.einleitung: Static electricity, or triboelectricity, arises when two different materials are rubbed together and electric charge is passed from one to the other. You know it from the balloon that sticks to the wall after being rubbed on a jumper. The little shock when you touch a door handle is also static electricity.
wichtigste: Static electricity is electricity produced by rubbing.
If you rub a balloon on a woollen jumper, it becomes electrically charged.
If the balloon takes electrons from the wool, it becomes negatively charged.
A rubbed balloon attracts hair and can move an empty can without touching it.
A rubbed balloon stays stuck to the wall for a while and then falls down.
Anyone who slides across a woollen sofa and then touches someone sometimes feels a small shock.

abschnitte.text: All materials are made of atoms with positively charged nuclei and negatively charged **electrons**. If you rub two different materials together, some electrons move from one material to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes **negatively** charged. The material that loses electrons becomes **positively** charged.

If you rub a balloon on **wool**, the balloon takes electrons from the wool and becomes negatively charged. If you hold it above your head, your hair is attracted and stands on end. If you put an empty drinks can on the table, it rolls after the balloon without the balloon touching it. If you stick the balloon to the wall, it stays there for a while until the charge slowly leaks away and it falls down.

If you slide across a woollen sofa or walk across a carpet in rubber soles, your body becomes charged. If you then touch a door handle, a car or another person, the charge evens out with a small **spark**. You feel a shock that is startling but harmless. It happens especially often in winter, when the air in heated rooms is very **dry**.

The Greek scholar **Thales of Miletus** is said to have noticed around 600 BC that rubbed **amber** attracts light particles such as feathers. The Greek word for amber is “elektron”. That is where our word **electricity** comes from. In the 18th century, researchers built friction machines with which they produced large sparks.

Which material becomes positively and which negatively charged is shown by the **triboelectric series**. Materials such as hair, wool and glass tend to give away electrons and become positive. Materials such as rubber, plastic and Teflon tend to take electrons and become negative. The further apart two materials are in the series, the more strongly they become charged.

Photocopiers and laser printers use electric charges to put the toner powder exactly onto the paper. A **Van de Graaff generator** uses a moving belt to produce so much charge that your hair stands on end. Static electricity can be dangerous where there are flammable vapours, for example when filling up with fuel. That is why charges are deliberately conducted away in factories and at petrol stations, and electronic components are protected from sparks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, negatively charged particle in the outer part of atoms.
A property of particles that can be positive or negative.
A list of materials showing which becomes positive or negative when rubbed.
The evening out of charge, often visible as a small spark.

gewusst: Lightning is also a huge electrical discharge; the charges in thunderclouds are separated partly by collisions between ice particles.
The small shock from a door handle can be several thousand volts, but it is harmless because the charge is tiny.
The word “electricity” comes from the Greek word for amber.

teile.einleitung: René Descartes was a French philosopher, mathematician and natural scientist who lived from 1596 to 1650. He wanted to put all knowledge on firm foundations, so he first doubted everything. You still come across him at school today, for example with the coordinate system or the Cartesian diver.
wichtigste: René Descartes was born in 1596 in La Haye in France and died in 1650 in Stockholm.
He is considered one of the founders of modern philosophy.
His most famous sentence in Latin is “Cogito, ergo sum”, in English “I think, therefore I am”.
The Cartesian coordinate system, which is used in maths for graphs, is named after him.
The bottle diver is also called the “Cartesian diver” after him.
Descartes also worked on physics, for example on light and the rainbow.
He lived for many years in the Netherlands, where he wrote his most important books.

abschnitte.text: René Descartes was born on 31 March 1596 in La Haye, a small place in France that is now called “Descartes” in his honour. He attended a Jesuit school in La Flèche and then studied law. As a young man he travelled a lot and served as a soldier for a while. Later he moved to the **Netherlands**, because there he could research and write in peace.

Descartes wanted to find out what can be known with complete certainty. So he doubted everything, even his senses, because eyes can deceive us too. In doing so he realised: even someone who doubts must think, and someone who thinks must exist. This led him to his famous sentence **“Cogito, ergo sum”**. He described this method of **systematic doubt** in 1637 in his book “Discourse on the Method”.

Descartes had the idea of describing points with numbers: one value for right and left and one for up and down. This gave rise to the **Cartesian coordinate system** with an x-axis and a y-axis. It lets you draw formulas as lines and curves and study shapes with calculations. This branch of maths is called **analytic geometry**. Without this idea there would be no graphs, no maps with grids and no computer graphics as we know them today.

The **Cartesian diver**, also called the bottle diver, is a popular experiment. A small tube with an air bubble floats in a closed bottle full of water. If you squeeze the bottle, the air bubble gets smaller, the diver becomes heavier compared with its volume and sinks. If you let go, the air expands again and it rises. The experiment shows **buoyancy** and is named after Descartes, although it is not certain whether he invented it himself.

Descartes also researched light and seeing. He explained how light is refracted and reflected in water drops and so was able to calculate the angle at which you see a **rainbow**. He also described the law of **refraction**, which Snell knew too. He imagined the world as a great machine that works according to fixed rules.

In 1649, Queen **Christina** of Sweden invited Descartes to Stockholm to teach her philosophy. The lessons took place very early in the morning, and the winter was cold. Descartes caught pneumonia and died on 11 February 1650. But his ideas lived on and shaped philosophy and science in the following centuries.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study that thinks about big questions, such as what knowledge, truth or the good are.
A grid of two axes with which any point can be given exactly by two numbers.
The force with which water or air pushes an object upwards.
Named after Descartes, whose Latin name was Cartesius.

gewusst: The word “Cartesian” comes from Cartesius, the Latin form of Descartes' name.
His birthplace, La Haye, was later renamed and is now simply called Descartes.
As a child, Descartes liked to stay in bed for a long time and said that he did his best thinking there.

teile.einleitung: The heat of fusion is the energy needed to melt a solid substance without its temperature rising. When ice melts, a mixture of ice and water stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted. All the heat added is used to break the bonds holding the particles together.
wichtigste: As long as ice is melting, the temperature of the ice and water mixture stays at 0 °C.
The heat of fusion breaks the bonds holding the particles together in the solid.
To melt 1 kg of ice you need around 334 kilojoules.
With that you could warm 1 kg of water from 0 °C to about 80 °C.
When it solidifies, exactly the same amount of heat is released again, the heat of solidification.
In the 18th century, Joseph Black discovered hidden, latent heat.
An ice cube cools well because it takes in a lot of heat as it melts.

abschnitte.text: In a solid substance such as ice, the particles hold firmly together and sit in fixed places. Energy is needed to free them from this lattice. This energy is called **heat of fusion**. It does not make the substance warmer but only changes its **state of matter** from solid to liquid.

If you put a glass of ice and water in a warm room, the thermometer shows 0 °C. Although heat is constantly flowing into the glass, the temperature does not rise until the last piece of ice has melted. Only then does the water get warmer. The Scottish scientist **Joseph Black** recognised this in the 18th century and called the heat that seemed to have disappeared “latent”, meaning hidden, heat.

For ice, the **specific heat of fusion** is around 334 kilojoules per kilogram. So for 3 kg of ice you need 3 times 334, which is 1,002 kilojoules. With the same amount of energy as for 1 kg of ice, you could warm 1 kg of water from 0 °C to about 80 °C. Other substances have other values, but water is one of the substances with an especially large heat of fusion.

An **ice cube** cools a drink much better than water at the same temperature, because it takes a lot of heat from the drink as it melts. Ice packs in a cool bag work on the same principle. In the Alps, patches of snow often lie for weeks in spring, even though the air is already warmer than 0 °C. Melting the huge amounts of ice and snow simply takes a great deal of energy.

When water freezes, it gives off exactly as much heat as it needed to melt. Fruit growers make use of this **heat of solidification**: when there is a risk of frost in spring, they spray the blossoms with water. As it freezes, heat is released, and the blossoms under the layer of ice stay at about 0 °C and do not freeze. Some hand warmers, which you start by clicking a small disc, also give off heat as their liquid solidifies.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy needed to melt a solid substance at the same temperature.
The form in which a substance exists: solid, liquid or gas.
Hidden heat that is taken in during melting or evaporating without changing the temperature.
A unit of energy; 1 kilojoule is 1,000 joules.

gewusst: If ice needed no heat of fusion, glaciers and snow would melt almost all at once in spring and cause great floods.
Melting 1 kg of ice takes about as much energy as a 100 watt lamp uses in just under an hour.

teile.einleitung: A string vibration happens when a stretched string is plucked, bowed or struck and vibrates back and forth. This is how guitars, violins, harps and pianos make their notes. How high the note sounds depends on the length, the tension and the weight of the string.
wichtigste: There are always nodes at the two fixed ends of a string.
The fundamental frequency of a string is the wave speed divided by twice the length of the string.
A shorter string sounds higher than a longer one.
If you tighten a string more, the note gets higher; at four times the tension, the frequency doubles.
A thicker, heavier string sounds lower at the same length and tension.
Overtones always vibrate along with the fundamental and shape the sound of an instrument.
In the 17th century, the Frenchman Marin Mersenne formulated the laws of vibrating strings.

abschnitte.text: If you pluck a stretched string, it vibrates back and forth between its two fixings. **Waves** travel back and forth along the string and are reflected at the ends. This creates a **standing wave**, which seems not to move along. The string cannot move at the ends; that is where the **nodes** are. In the fundamental vibration, it vibrates most strongly in the middle, where the antinode is.

In the fundamental vibration, exactly half a wavelength fits on the string. So a guitar string with a vibrating length of 65 cm has a wavelength of 1.3 m. You get the **frequency** by dividing the wave speed by this wavelength. If the wave travels at 440 m/s on a string 0.5 m long, it vibrates at 440 Hz, which is concert pitch A. When a guitarist presses a string onto a fret, he shortens it and the note gets higher.

The wave speed on the string depends on its tension and its mass per metre. You take the square root of the tension divided by the mass per metre. So a string with a tension of 100 N and 1 g per metre has a wave speed of about 316 m/s. When **tuning**, you turn the pegs and so change the tension. The low strings of a guitar or piano are thicker and often wound with wire so that they are heavier and sound low.

A string does not only vibrate as a whole but at the same time also in two, three or more sections. These extra vibrations are called **overtones** or harmonics, and their frequencies are whole-number multiples of the fundamental. If a string has a fundamental of 200 Hz, the first overtone is at 400 Hz and the second at 600 Hz. If you touch a string very lightly exactly in the middle, you get a **harmonic**: the fundamental is missing and the second harmonic sounds bright and delicate. The mix of overtones decides whether a note sounds like a violin, a guitar or a harp.

The Greek scholar Pythagoras is said to have studied note ratios with a **monochord**, a box with a single string. He realised that half the string length gives the octave. In the 17th century, the French monk and scholar **Marin Mersenne** summed up how length, tension and thickness decide the pitch. Later, mathematicians such as Daniel Bernoulli from Basel and Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert calculated string vibration precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
A point on the string that does not move as it vibrates.
A higher note that vibrates along with the fundamental.
A wave that travels back and forth and forms nodes and antinodes at fixed points.
The hollow body of an instrument that amplifies the sound of the string.

gewusst: A string on its own is very quiet; only the wooden sound box of a guitar or violin makes the note properly audible.
A concert grand piano has over 200 strings stretched in it, which together pull on the frame with enormous force.
Concert pitch A at 440 Hz is used as the tuning note by orchestras all over the world.

teile.einleitung: Frictional heat is the heat produced when two things rub against each other. You can feel it when you rub your hands together in winter or slide quickly down a rope. People were already making fire with frictional heat in the Stone Age.
wichtigste: When two surfaces rub against each other, heat is produced.
In the process, kinetic energy is turned into heat.
Many people rub their hands together when they are cold.
A match lights through frictional heat on the striking surface.
Stone Age people made fire by twirling a wooden stick quickly in a wooden board.
Brakes get very hot on long descents from mountain passes.
Skis glide well because frictional heat creates a thin film of water.

abschnitte.text: When two surfaces rub against each other, tiny bumps catch on each other and are shaken back and forth. In the process, **kinetic energy** is turned into heat; this is called **frictional heat**. The faster and harder you rub, the hotter it gets. That is why a drill bit gets hot when drilling a hole and a saw blade gets warm when sawing.

When you are cold, you rub your hands together and they get noticeably warmer. If you slide quickly across a carpet on bare knees, the skin can get hot and sore. Anyone who slides quickly down a rope gets hot hands, which is why climbers often wear gloves when abseiling. Even a rubber gets warm if you rub out for a long time and hard.

Before there were matches, people made fire by rubbing wood quickly. In **fire drilling**, a wooden stick is twirled quickly in a hollow in a wooden board until fine wood dust begins to glow. With dry grass or tinder, a flame is then coaxed from it. Today a **match** lights through frictional heat on the striking surface of the box.

When steel is ground on a fast-spinning grinding wheel, sparks fly. These are tiny metal particles that become red-hot through frictional heat. In engines and machines, frictional heat is usually unwanted, which is why **lubricants** such as oil are used. In friction welding, on the other hand, it is used deliberately to join metal parts together.

When braking, the brakes turn the car's kinetic energy into heat. On a long descent from a pass, such as the Gotthard or the Susten, the **brake discs** can get very hot. If they get too hot, they brake less well. That is why in Switzerland you should drive downhill in a low gear, so that the engine helps to brake and the brakes do not overheat.

Skis glide well on snow because frictional heat creates a wafer-thin **film of water** between the base and the snow. The skis slide on this film almost as if on a lubricant. At very low temperatures, less water forms, which is why the snow then feels dull and slow. Ski wax also helps to keep friction low.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that slows things down when two surfaces slide past each other.
When energy changes from one form into another, for example from movement into heat.
A substance such as oil or grease that reduces friction.
Very easily burnt material used to turn embers into a flame.

gewusst: Around 1798, the scientist Benjamin Thompson noticed while boring cannon barrels that friction produces almost endless heat, and concluded that heat has to do with movement.
Formula 1 racing cars have brake discs that glow red under hard braking.

teile.einleitung: A quantum computer is a computer that uses the strange laws of quantum physics to calculate. Instead of ordinary bits, it works with qubits, which can be 0 and 1 at the same time in a superposition. For certain tasks, quantum computers could one day be much faster than any of today's supercomputers.
wichtigste: A qubit can be in a superposition of 0 and 1; a classical bit can only be either 0 or 1.
A register of 10 qubits can superpose 1024 basis states at the same time.
Shor's algorithm could factorise large numbers efficiently and endanger RSA encryption.
The main problem in building large quantum computers is decoherence caused by disturbances.
Superconducting qubits are operated at a few millikelvin, that is at extremely low temperatures.
In 2019, Google reported that it had achieved quantum supremacy with the “Sycamore” processor.
The no-cloning theorem forbids making an exact copy of an unknown quantum state.

abschnitte.text: A normal computer calculates with **bits**, which are either 0 or 1. A quantum computer uses **qubits**. A qubit can be in a **superposition** of 0 and 1, rather like a coin that is still spinning. Only when it is measured is it decided whether 0 or 1 comes out. Several qubits together can superpose a great many states at the same time: 10 qubits already 2 to the power of 10, that is 1024.

A quantum computer changes the qubits with so-called **quantum gates**. The **Hadamard gate**, for example, turns the state 0 into an equally weighted superposition of 0 and 1. Qubits can also be **entangled** with each other, so that they are no longer independent of each other. A good quantum algorithm makes sure that wrong results cancel each other out and the right one is strengthened.

In 1994, Peter Shor developed **Shor's algorithm**, with which a large quantum computer could quickly break huge numbers down into prime factors. The security of the widely used **RSA encryption** depends on this, which is why new, quantum-safe methods are already being developed. Quantum computers could also help to simulate molecules for new medicines and materials. But for everyday tasks such as games or texts, normal computers remain better suited.

Qubits are extremely sensitive. Even the slightest heat, vibration or electromagnetic disturbance destroys the superposition; this is called **decoherence**. That is why superconducting qubits are operated in large cooling machines at a few **millikelvin**, which is colder than outer space. To make up for errors, a complex **quantum error correction** is needed, in which many qubits work together.

In the early 1980s, the physicist Richard Feynman suggested simulating quantum systems with quantum computers. In 1994 and 1996, the algorithms of Peter Shor and Lov Grover followed as the first important applications. In 2019, **Google** reported that its **Sycamore** processor had solved a task that a classical supercomputer would take much longer to do. This milestone is called **quantum supremacy**.

In Switzerland, there is intensive research into quantum technology, for example at **ETH Zurich**, the University of Basel and EPFL in Lausanne. IBM's research laboratory in Rüschlikon is also working on quantum computers. Around the world, companies and universities are building quantum computers with different technologies, such as superconducting circuits or single trapped **ions**. But it will probably be some years before large, error-free quantum computers are available.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest unit of information of a quantum computer, which can superpose 0 and 1.
A state in which a quantum particle has several possibilities at once.
The loss of quantum properties through disturbances from the surroundings.
A calculating step that deliberately changes the state of qubits.
The rule that an unknown quantum state cannot be copied exactly.

gewusst: With 300 qubits, you could superpose more states than there are atoms in the visible universe.
Many quantum computers look like upside-down golden chandeliers; these are their cooling systems.
Because of the no-cloning theorem, a quantum state cannot simply be copied like a file.

teile.einleitung: Auroras, or polar lights, are glowing displays in the night sky that usually shimmer green, sometimes also red or violet. They appear when particles from the Sun hit the Earth's atmosphere. They are most often seen near the North and South Poles.
wichtigste: Auroras are caused by particles from the solar wind hitting the Earth's air.
The aurora in the north is also called the northern lights, the one in the south the southern lights.
Most often it glows green, but there are also red and violet auroras.
Auroras often look like glowing curtains that move.
From the space station, you can even see auroras from above.
In Switzerland, auroras are only seen rarely, for example in May 2024.
Good places to watch them are northern Norway, Iceland, Finland and Canada.

abschnitte.text: An **aurora** is a natural glow in the night sky. It appears as bands, arcs, rays or waving **curtains** of light. In the northern hemisphere it is called the **northern lights**, or in Latin aurora borealis; in the southern hemisphere the southern lights, or aurora australis. The lights glow at a height of about 100 to several hundred kilometres, far above the clouds. They can be visible for a few minutes or for several hours.

The Sun constantly hurls electrically charged particles into space: the **solar wind**. The Earth's **magnetic field** deflects most of these particles, like a protective shield. But near the poles they can enter the upper atmosphere along the magnetic field lines. There they collide with oxygen and nitrogen particles and make them glow. This is similar to a fluorescent tube, in which gas is made to glow by electricity.

The colour depends on which gas is glowing and at what height this happens. The most common is **green** light, which comes from oxygen at about 100 to 250 kilometres. Oxygen even higher up glows **red**. Nitrogen produces bluish and violet shades, often at the bottom edge of the curtains. Cameras often show the colours more strongly than the human eye sees them at night.

Auroras mainly occur in a ring around the magnetic poles, the **auroral oval**. Good places in the north are northern Norway with the town of Tromsø, Lapland in Finland and Sweden, Iceland, Alaska and Canada. They are best seen on dark, clear nights between autumn and spring. Astronauts on the International **Space Station** can admire auroras from above. Other planets such as Jupiter and Saturn also have auroras.

When the Sun is especially active, the auroral oval gets bigger and reaches further south. Then auroras can sometimes appear in Switzerland too, usually as a reddish glow on the northern horizon. A well-known example was the strong **solar storm** of 10 to 11 May 2024, when people all over Switzerland photographed coloured lights. The Sun's activity goes up and down in a cycle of about 11 years. Around 2024 and 2025 it was at a maximum, which is why there were especially many auroras at that time.

Very strong solar storms can not only trigger auroras but also disrupt technology. They can damage satellites, make GPS less accurate and disrupt radio communications. In 1859, a solar storm was so strong that auroras could be seen as far as the tropics and telegraph lines gave off sparks. This event is called the **Carrington Event**, after the British astronomer Richard Carrington. That is why researchers watch the Sun closely today, so that they can give warnings in time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stream of electrically charged particles that the Sun sends out into space.
An invisible force field around the Earth that acts like a protective shield.
The scientific name for the northern lights.
An especially strong outburst of particles and energy from the Sun.

gewusst: The word Aurora is the name of the Roman goddess of the dawn.
The northern and southern lights often appear at the same time and sometimes look almost like mirror images of each other.
Auroras are usually completely silent, although some people report faint crackling sounds.

teile.einleitung: A lifebuoy is a floating ring that you throw to a person in the water so that they can hold on to it. It hangs on many lakeshores, in harbours and on ships, and it can save lives.
wichtigste: You throw a lifebuoy to people in the water so that they can hold on.
It is shaped like a doughnut and is usually red and white or orange.
A lifebuoy floats because it is made of very light material.
A rope is often attached to the ring so that you can pull the person to the shore.
In Switzerland, lifebuoys are often found on lakeshores and on boats.
If you see someone in difficulty in the water, you should first call loudly for help.
The emergency number for an ambulance in Switzerland is 144.

abschnitte.text: A **lifebuoy** is a ring-shaped float with a hole in the middle. A person in the water can put their arms around it or slip into it and is kept above water. On the outside there is usually a **grab line** in loops, which is easy to hold on to. It often hangs ready in a box or on a post on the shore.

Today a lifebuoy is usually made of hard **foam** with a tough plastic cover. The foam contains countless tiny air bubbles, which is why it is much lighter than the same amount of water. So the water pushes it upwards; this is called **buoyancy**. In the past, lifebuoys were made of cork, which is also very light.

The bright colours red and white or orange can be seen on the water from far away. Many rings also have stripes that reflect in the light of searchlights. The ring shape is easy to throw and can be grabbed from all sides. On ships, the ship's name is often written on the ring.

At many Swiss lakes and rivers, lifebuoys hang on jetties, in harbours and at bathing places. The **Swiss Lifesaving Society** SLRG trains lifeguards and spreads the water safety rules. The passenger boats on Lake Lucerne, Lake Zurich and Lake Geneva also have lifebuoys on board. Lifebuoys may only be used in an emergency; anyone who damages or removes them puts human lives at risk.

Anyone who sees someone in difficulty in the water first shouts loudly for help and calls the emergency number, **144** for the ambulance or 112. Then you throw a lifebuoy or another floating object near the person, not straight at their head. You can pull them to the shore with the rope. You should only jump into the water yourself if you are well trained, otherwise you put yourself in danger.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water pushes an object upwards.
The rope on the outside of the lifebuoy that you hold on to.
The Swiss Lifesaving Society, which trains lifeguards.
A telephone number on which you get help immediately in an emergency.

gewusst: The emergency number 112 works all over Europe, including in Switzerland.
People who are drowning often cannot shout or wave, which is why an emergency in the water can sometimes look surprisingly calm.

teile.einleitung: A planet is a large celestial body that orbits a star and does not shine by itself. There are eight planets in our solar system, and the Earth is one of them. The word comes from Greek and means “wanderer”, because planets wander between the stars in the night sky.
