wichtigste: Our solar system has eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Mercury orbits closest to the Sun.
Mars is called “the Red Planet” because of its reddish colour.
Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.
Since 2006, Pluto has no longer counted as a planet but as a dwarf planet.
Planets do not shine by themselves but reflect the light of the Sun.
Planets also orbit other stars; they are called exoplanets.

abschnitte.text: A **planet** is a celestial body that orbits a star. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union set three conditions. A planet must orbit the Sun, be heavy enough to be almost round, and have cleared other chunks out of its path. Pluto does not meet the third condition, which is why it is now called a **dwarf planet**. Unlike stars, planets do not produce their own light.

The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are **rocky planets** with a solid surface. **Mercury** is the smallest planet and orbits closest to the Sun. Venus is the hottest planet, because its thick layer of gas holds in the heat. The Earth is the only known planet with liquid water on its surface and with life. **Mars** is reddish because its soil contains a lot of rusty iron, which is why it is called “the Red Planet”.

Further out, the four **giant planets** orbit. Jupiter and Saturn consist mainly of gas and are called gas giants. **Jupiter** is so big that more than a thousand Earths would fit inside it. Saturn is famous for its magnificent rings of ice and rock. Uranus and Neptune are colder and are called ice giants; Neptune takes about 165 years to go once around the Sun.

Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn can be seen with the naked eye and have been known since ancient times. Uranus was only discovered in 1781 by William Herschel with a telescope. Neptune was found in 1846, after researchers had first calculated where it should be. For a long time people believed the Earth was at the centre, until Copernicus and others showed that all the planets orbit the Sun. The days of the week still recall the old planets; Monday, for example, is named after the Moon.

Planets that orbit stars other than the Sun are called **exoplanets**. The first exoplanet around a Sun-like star was discovered in 1995 by the Geneva astronomers **Michel Mayor** and Didier Queloz. They received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 2019. Today several thousand exoplanets are known. Researchers are especially looking for planets where there could be liquid water.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Sun and all the celestial bodies that orbit it.
A round celestial body that has not cleared its path, for example Pluto.
The path along which a planet circles the Sun.
A planet that orbits a star other than our Sun.

gewusst: On Venus, a day lasts longer than a whole Venus year.
Saturn has such a low density that it would float in a giant bathtub.

With a German memory sentence such as “Mein Vater erklärt mir jeden Sonntag unseren Nachthimmel” (“My father explains our night sky to me every Sunday”), you can remember the order of the planets from the first letters.

teile.einleitung: Positron emission tomography, PET for short, is a medical technique that lets doctors look inside the living body. It shows not only what organs look like but also where the metabolism is especially active. It uses tiny amounts of radioactive substances and particles of antimatter.
wichtigste: PET makes metabolic processes in the body visible.
The most commonly used substance is fluorodeoxyglucose, a sugar labelled with fluorine-18.
Fluorine-18 has a half-life of around 110 minutes.
When a positron meets an electron, two photons of 511 keV each are produced.
The two photons fly apart at almost exactly 180 degrees.
The scanner recognises photons that belong together by coincidence detection.
PET is often combined with computed tomography in one machine.

abschnitte.text: PET is an **imaging technique** in nuclear medicine. The patient is given an injection of a small amount of a radioactively labelled substance, a so-called **tracer**. The tracer spreads through the body and collects where it is used up. A ring-shaped scanner measures the radiation, and a computer uses it to calculate cross-sectional images of the body.

The tracer contains a **positron emitter** such as fluorine-18. Its atomic nuclei decay and send out a **positron**, the antiparticle of the electron. After less than a millimetre, the positron meets an electron and the two annihilate each other. This produces two **photons**, particles of light, each with an energy of 511 keV.

The two photons fly off in opposite directions at almost exactly 180 degrees. All around the scanner there are many **detectors**. If two photons hit opposite detectors almost at the same time, the machine knows that they come from the same annihilation. This method is called **coincidence detection**. The origin must lie somewhere on the line between the two detectors, and the image is built up from millions of such lines.

The most common tracer is **fluorodeoxyglucose**, FDG for short, a sugar with a fluorine-18 atom. Cells that use a lot of energy take up especially large amounts of it. Many **tumour cells** grow fast and need a great deal of sugar, which is why they light up brightly in the PET image. The metabolism in the brain and the heart muscle can also be studied this way.

Fluorine-18 has a half-life of only around 110 minutes. So after just under two hours, half of it has already decayed. That is why the substance has to be made shortly before the scan, usually in a **cyclotron**, a circular particle accelerator. Many large hospitals therefore work closely with a cyclotron nearby.

A PET image mainly shows the metabolism, but hardly the exact shape of the organs. That is why PET is often combined with **computed tomography** in a single machine, called **PET/CT**. The two images are laid on top of each other, so you can see metabolism and anatomy at the same time. Doctors use PET especially in cancer medicine, heart medicine and brain research.

begriffe.erklaerung: The antiparticle of the electron, with the same mass but a positive charge.
A labelled substance whose path through the body can be followed.
The time after which half of a radioactive substance has decayed.
Two signals arriving at almost exactly the same time.
A particle accelerator in which particles are speeded up on circular paths.

gewusst: In PET, antimatter really is produced in the body, though only in the tiniest amounts.
The energy of 511 keV corresponds exactly to the mass of an electron, converted with Einstein's formula E = mc².
Because fluorine-18 decays so quickly, the tracer has practically disappeared completely after a day.

teile.einleitung: Lubricating substance is the technical term for all substances that reduce friction and wear between moving parts. They include oils, greases and solids such as graphite. Without lubricating substances, almost no machine would run for long, from the bicycle to the jet engine.
wichtigste: Lubricating substances reduce friction and wear between machine parts.
Oil separates two metal surfaces with a thin lubricating film.
Graphite is a solid lubricating substance.
Engine oil does not just lubricate but also carries heat away.
How thick and runny an oil is is called its viscosity.
Grease is used where the lubricant should not flow away.
In the body, the joint fluid lubricates the joints.

abschnitte.text: A **lubricating substance** is put between two surfaces that move against each other. It forms a thin **lubricating film** that keeps the surfaces apart. Instead of metal rubbing on metal, the parts slide on the film. This lowers friction, prevents wear and makes machines quieter and longer lasting.

There are liquid, paste-like and solid lubricating substances. **Lubricating oils** are liquid and are made from crude oil, from vegetable oil or artificially. Greases consist of oil that has been made into a thick mass with a thickener, and they stay in place. Solid lubricants are, for example, **graphite**, molybdenum disulphide or the plastic Teflon, which split into thin, sliding layers.

In a car, engine oil has several jobs at once. It lubricates, carries heat away from hot parts, seals and carries tiny dirt particles to the oil filter. It also protects the metal from rust. That is why engine oil has to be changed regularly, because over time it ages and gets dirty.

How thick an oil is is called its **viscosity**. Honey has a high viscosity, water a low one. When oil gets cold it becomes thicker, and when it gets hot it becomes thinner. That is why engine oils have names such as 5W-30, which show how they behave in cold and in heat. In winter, an oil that still flows well below zero is important.

A bicycle chain should be oiled regularly so that it runs easily and does not rust. The ball bearings in roller skates and skateboards are filled with grease. Mechanical watches need tiny amounts of a special oil. Because waste oil seriously pollutes the environment, in Switzerland it is taken back to collection points or shops and never poured down the drain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin layer of a lubricating substance between two surfaces.
A measure of how thick or runny a liquid is.
A soft form of carbon, also found in pencil leads, that lubricates well.
Used oil that has to be collected and properly disposed of or recycled.

gewusst: Graphite lubricates because it consists of many thin layers of carbon that slide easily over each other.
A single litre of waste oil can contaminate a great deal of drinking water, which is why it must never go down the drain.

teile.einleitung: The hull is the body of a ship, the large, watertight shell that floats in the water. It carries everything on the ship and makes sure it does not sink. Even huge ships made of steel float because of the shape of their hollow hull.
wichtigste: The hull is the watertight shell of a ship.
A steel ship floats because its hollow hull pushes aside a great deal of water.
The keel runs like a backbone along the bottom of the whole hull.
The front part is called the bow, the back part the stern.
The draught tells you how deep the hull reaches below the waterline.
Bulkheads divide the hull into compartments, so that not everything floods if there is a leak.
A catamaran has two hulls.

abschnitte.text: Steel is almost eight times as dense as water, and a block of steel sinks at once. But a ship's hull is hollow and full of air. As it goes into the water it pushes a lot of water aside, and this displaced water produces **buoyancy**. The ship sinks in exactly until the displaced water weighs as much as the whole ship. The Greek scholar Archimedes already described this principle.

The front part of a ship is called the **bow**, the back part the **stern**. Right at the bottom runs the **keel**, the most important lengthwise beam, like a backbone from bow to stern. The frames are fixed across it and give the shape like ribs. Over them lies the outer skin of steel plates, wood or plastic.

The **waterline** is the line up to which the water reaches on the hull. How deep the hull reaches into the water below it is called the **draught**. The more heavily a ship is loaded, the greater the draught. On the side of many cargo ships you can see markings that show the deepest the ship may sink in. On the Rhine at Basel, the water level decides how much cargo a ship can take.

Walls across the ship, the **bulkheads**, divide the hull into separate watertight compartments. If the ship springs a leak, only one compartment fills up and the ship stays afloat. Modern oil tankers also have a **double hull**: if the outer hull is damaged, the inner hull holds the oil back. This design was made compulsory after serious tanker accidents such as that of the Exxon Valdez in 1989.

Many large ships have a rounded nose below the waterline, the **bulbous bow**. It creates its own wave, which partly cancels out the bow wave, and so reduces water resistance, which saves fuel. A catamaran has two slim hulls, and a trimaran even three, which makes them very stable. Fast motorboats have flat hulls that skim over the water at high speed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of water that pushes a body in it upwards.
The lowest lengthwise beam of the hull, the backbone of the ship.
The distance from the waterline to the lowest point of the hull.
A watertight dividing wall inside a ship.

gewusst: Switzerland has no sea coast, but it still has ocean-going ships that sail under the Swiss flag with Basel as their home port.
On large cargo ships, a bulbous bow can save several per cent of fuel.

teile.einleitung: A whisk is a kitchen tool made of bent wires, used to whip and stir cream, egg whites or sauces. When you whisk fast, it puts lots of air bubbles into the liquid. Behind this lies exciting physics, because it turns runny cream into firm whipped cream.
wichtigste: With a whisk you turn cream into whipped cream.
When whisking, you put air into the liquid.
Egg white that is whisked for a long time becomes stiffly beaten egg white.
In German, the whisk is called “Schneebesen” (snow broom), after beaten egg white, which looks like snow.
The wires of a whisk are usually made of metal.
Cream whips best when it is well chilled.
If you whip cream for far too long, it turns into butter.

abschnitte.text: A whisk has a handle and several bent **wires**, which together form a kind of teardrop or balloon. The wires are usually made of stainless metal, some of plastic or silicone, so that they do not scratch coated pans. The more wires it has, the more air you can whisk in at once. An electric **mixer** with beaters does the same job much faster.

When you move the whisk quickly in a circle or from bottom to top, it drags air into the liquid. The air is broken up into tiny bubbles. Certain substances in the liquid, such as **proteins** and fat, settle around these bubbles and hold them in place. This creates a **foam**, which takes up much more space than the liquid did before.

Cream contains small globules of fat. When whipping, these globules are partly broken open and stick together, so that they trap the air bubbles like a scaffold. For this to work, the cream must be well **chilled**, because warm fat is too soft. In Switzerland, full cream with around 35 per cent fat is used for this. If you whip for far too long, the fat clumps together completely, the liquid separates and **butter** is formed.

If you whisk egg white for a long time, it becomes a white, stiff foam called **beaten egg white**, in German “Eischnee” (egg snow). It looks like freshly fallen snow, which is where the German name for the whisk comes from. The proteins unfold as you whisk and form a net around the air bubbles. Even a small trace of yolk or fat in the bowl can stop the egg white from going stiff.

Beaten egg white is needed for sponge cakes, mousse and meringues. A well-known legend says that the meringue was invented in the Bernese Oberland village of **Meiringen**, but this is not reliably proven. Meringues with double cream are a popular Swiss dessert, especially in the Gruyère region. Sauces, pancake batter and scrambled eggs are also often stirred with a whisk, because it gets rid of lumps well.

begriffe.erklaerung: Lots of air bubbles trapped in a liquid.
Egg white whisked until stiff.
Cream whipped up with air.
Tiny droplets of fat floating in milk and cream.

gewusst: A carton of cream gives about twice as much whipped cream when whipped, because so much air goes in.
You can even whisk the cooking water from chickpeas into a foam similar to beaten egg white.

teile.einleitung: A satellite is an object that orbits a planet or another celestial body. The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth, and today there are also thousands of artificial satellites circling our planet. They help us with the weather forecast, with finding our way and with making phone calls.
wichtigste: A satellite is an object that orbits a planet.
The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite.
The first artificial satellite was Sputnik 1; it was launched in 1957.
A satellite does not fall down because it flies around the Earth very fast.
Weather satellites watch clouds, and navigation devices use satellite signals.
Old satellites and bits in space are called space debris.
The first Swiss satellite was called SwissCube and went into space in 2009.

abschnitte.text: The word satellite comes from Latin and means companion. A satellite is any object that circles a larger celestial body in an **orbit**. The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth, and Jupiter and Saturn even have many dozens of moons. But by satellite we usually mean a device built by people and taken into space by a **rocket**.

abschnitte.titel: Why it does not fall down
abschnitte.text: A satellite is also pulled by the Earth and is actually falling down all the time. But because it is flying sideways very fast, the Earth curves away beneath it just as fast as it falls. So it keeps falling around the Earth. The ISS space station flies at a height of about 400 kilometres at around 28,000 kilometres per hour and goes round the Earth in about 90 minutes. This speed is called the **orbital speed**.

On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union sent the first artificial satellite into space: **Sputnik 1**. It was a metal ball with aerials and sent beeping sounds to Earth. This was the start of the space race between the Soviet Union and the USA. Today more than 10,000 active satellites orbit the Earth (as of 2025), many of them belonging to large internet networks.

**Weather satellites** photograph clouds and storms from above and help with weather forecasting. Navigation satellites such as GPS or the European Galileo send signals from which a navigation device works out its position. Communications satellites carry television, telephone and internet. Other satellites observe the Earth, measure the ice at the poles or, as **space telescopes**, look into the depths of space.

The first satellite from Switzerland was **SwissCube**, a tiny cube only ten centimetres along each side. It was built mainly by students at EPFL in Lausanne and launched into space in 2009. The University of Bern led the building of the **CHEOPS** space telescope, which has been studying planets around other stars since 2019. Swiss companies also supply parts for many rockets and satellites.

Worn-out satellites, rocket parts and fragments often stay in space for a long time; they are called **space debris**. They fly very fast and can destroy other satellites in a collision. That is why the larger pieces are constantly watched from Earth. The Lausanne company ClearSpace is working on a satellite that is meant to catch debris and get rid of it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path along which a celestial body or satellite circles another.
A satellite at a height of around 36,000 kilometres that always stays above the same point on Earth.
A satellite system with which devices find their exact position.
Old satellites, rocket parts and wreckage circling uselessly in space.

gewusst: At night you can see the ISS space station without a telescope as a bright, moving dot of light.
Satellite dishes on rooftops all point in the same direction, because the television satellites seem to stand still in the sky.
For navigation devices, the satellites' clocks have to be very accurate, otherwise the position would be kilometres out.

teile.einleitung: Snow is precipitation made of fine ice crystals that form in the clouds and fall to the ground as flakes. It turns landscapes into white winter worlds and is especially important for Switzerland, with its mountains, ski resorts and glaciers. At the same time, snow can become dangerous as an avalanche.
wichtigste: Snow consists of ice crystals that form in the clouds.
Snowflakes usually have six arms.
Snow settles well when it is around zero degrees or colder.
When rain and snow fall together, it is called sleet.
Loose, dry snow that cannot be shaped is called powder snow.
On high mountains in Switzerland there is snow even in summer.
On steep slopes with a lot of snow, an avalanche can slide down.

abschnitte.text: In the clouds there are tiny water droplets and water vapour. If it is colder than zero degrees there, the water vapour settles on small dust particles and forms **ice crystals**. Because water molecules in ice arrange themselves in a hexagonal pattern, the crystals usually grow with **six arms**. Several crystals often stick together and fall to the ground as a snowflake.

Whether it snows or rains depends on the temperature in the air below the cloud. If it is a little warmer than zero degrees there, the flakes partly melt and **sleet** falls. Snow settles mainly at temperatures around zero degrees or below. In great cold, snow crunches under your shoes, because the small ice crystals break.

Loose, dry **powder snow** falls at low temperatures and is very popular with skiers, but it cannot be shaped into snowballs. Wet snow at temperatures around zero degrees is heavy and sticks well, ideal for snowmen. When thawing and freezing alternate, grainy slush or a hard crust forms. Fresh snow contains a great deal of air and therefore acts like a warm blanket for plants and animals.

If there is a lot of snow on a steep slope, an **avalanche** can slide down. It is especially dangerous after heavy fresh snowfall, in wind or when there is a weak layer in the snowpack. In Switzerland, the **WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF** in Davos studies snow and publishes the avalanche bulletin every day in winter. Anyone going off the pistes needs good training and emergency equipment.

On the high mountains of the Alps there is snow all year round, and over many years it turns into **glaciers**. In spring the snow slowly melts and fills streams, rivers and reservoirs, which is important for drinking water and hydroelectric power. Winter tourism with skiing, sledging and cross-country skiing is an important source of income for many mountain villages. Because of global warming, snow at lower altitudes now lies for a shorter time on average than in the past.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, regularly shaped piece of frozen water.
Loose, dry snow that falls in great cold.
A large amount of snow that suddenly slides down a slope.
A daily report from the SLF describing the avalanche danger in the mountains.

gewusst: Freshly fallen snow is mostly air, which is why it swallows sounds and it becomes very quiet outside after a snowfall.
Fresh snow reflects most of the sunlight, which is why you need sunglasses in the mountains.

teile.einleitung: The scanning tunnelling microscope is a microscope with which you can see single atoms and even move them. It was developed in 1981 at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich. Instead of using light, it feels its way over a surface with a tiny metal tip.
wichtigste: The scanning tunnelling microscope was developed in 1981 at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon.
Its inventors were Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1986.
It is based on the quantum mechanical tunnelling effect.
The tunnelling current falls exponentially with the distance between tip and sample.
For the classic scanning tunnelling microscope, the sample must conduct electricity.
Piezo elements move the tip with atomic precision.
In 1989, Don Eigler wrote the letters “IBM” with 35 xenon atoms.

abschnitte.titel: What is a scanning tunnelling microscope?
abschnitte.text: A **scanning tunnelling microscope**, STM for short, is a device that makes surfaces visible down to single atoms. It does not work with light, because atoms are far too small to be seen with light microscopes. Instead, an extremely fine metal tip moves over the sample line by line, much as you would scan a field. From the measurements, a computer puts together a picture of the surface.

The tip does not touch the sample; it stays about a nanometre away. If a small voltage is applied, electrons still jump across the gap, even though classical physics says they should not. This phenomenon is called the **tunnelling effect** and belongs to quantum mechanics. The **tunnelling current** falls exponentially with the distance, so even a tiny difference changes it a lot. That is why the device is so sensitive.

The tip is controlled by **piezo elements**, crystals that expand by tiny amounts when a voltage is applied. This lets it be moved with atomic precision. Ideally, the tip ends in a **single atom**. The device must be very well protected against vibrations, or the picture will be blurred.

The German **Gerd Binnig** and the Swiss **Heinrich Rohrer** developed the scanning tunnelling microscope in 1981 at the IBM research laboratory in **Rüschlikon** near Zurich. As early as 1986 they received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it. In the same year, Gerd Binnig, Calvin Quate and Christoph Gerber presented the **atomic force microscope**. It can also scan non-conducting samples such as plastic or cells with atomic precision.

With the scanning tunnelling microscope, atoms can not only be seen but also moved. In 1989, the physicist **Don Eigler** at IBM in California wrote the letters “IBM” with 35 xenon atoms. At the time, this was the smallest writing in the world. Later, IBM researchers even made a short animated film with single atoms.

The scanning tunnelling microscope was a starting signal for **nanotechnology**. Researchers use it to study metals, semiconductors and new materials such as graphene. For developing smaller computer chips, it is important to know how atoms are arranged on surfaces. However, the classic device only works with electrically **conducting** samples.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantum effect in which particles cross a barrier that they should not actually be able to cross.
A crystal that expands or contracts very slightly under an electrical voltage.
A billionth of a metre, about the size of a few atoms side by side.
Technology that works with things on the scale of atoms and molecules.

gewusst: The tip of a scanning tunnelling microscope can be made from a simple wire cut off at an angle.
IBM's animated film made of single atoms is called “A Boy and His Atom” and is considered the smallest film in the world.
Only five years after its invention, the scanning tunnelling microscope already won the Nobel Prize.

teile.einleitung: In the photoelectric effect, light knocks electrons out of a metal. For a long time this phenomenon could not be explained, until Albert Einstein had a new idea in 1905: light consists of small packets of energy. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this explanation.
wichtigste: In the photoelectric effect, light can knock electrons out of a metal.
The effect was discovered at the end of the 19th century, among others by Heinrich Hertz.
Albert Einstein explained it in 1905 with particles of light, the photons.
Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for this explanation.
Whether electrons come out depends on the colour, that is the frequency of the light, not on its brightness.
The photoelectric effect was an important step towards quantum physics.
Solar cells and light sensors are based on similar effects.

abschnitte.text: If you shine light on a metal plate, electrons can fly out of the metal. This process is called the **photoelectric effect**. The electrons that are knocked out are called **photoelectrons**. They can be measured as an electric current.

In 1887, Heinrich Hertz noticed that ultraviolet light makes it easier for electric sparks to jump. Shortly afterwards, **Wilhelm Hallwachs** studied the effect more closely on metal plates. The researchers found something puzzling. Red light did not knock out any electrons, no matter how bright it was, but even weak **ultraviolet light** managed it.

In 1905, Albert Einstein suggested that light consists of small packets of energy, the **photons**. The energy of a photon depends on its **frequency**, that is on the colour of the light. A photon gives its energy to a single electron. If this energy is enough to free the electron from the metal, it flies out.

Einstein received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics for 1921 for explaining the photoelectric effect. Many people think he got it for the theory of relativity, but that is not true. Robert Millikan later confirmed Einstein's formula with precise measurements. The photoelectric effect showed that light is both a wave and a particle and became a cornerstone of **quantum physics**.

In **solar cells**, light sets electrons moving and so produces electricity. Camera sensors in mobile phones and light barriers at doors use similar effects. With photomultipliers, you can even detect single photons. Motion detectors and automatic street lamps also work with light-sensitive components.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest packet of energy of light.
A tiny, negatively charged particle found in every atom.
How often a wave oscillates per second; for light it decides the colour.
The energy needed to free an electron from a metal.

gewusst: Einstein published his explanation of the photoelectric effect in 1905, while he was working at the patent office in Bern.
Einstein was only handed the 1921 Nobel Prize a year later, in 1922.
The word photon comes from the Greek word for light.

teile.einleitung: Quantum physics describes the world of the very smallest particles, such as atoms, electrons and particles of light. Astonishing rules apply there, which often contradict our everyday experience. Even so, it is the most accurate theory in physics and is found in every mobile phone and laser.
wichtigste: Quantum physics describes atoms, electrons and photons.
Energy is passed on in small packets whose size depends on Planck's constant h.
Planck's constant h is about 6.626 · 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
Einstein received the Nobel Prize for explaining the photoelectric effect.
In 1924, Louis de Broglie put forward the idea that electrons also have wave properties.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says that position and momentum cannot both be known to any accuracy you like at the same time.
Wolfgang Pauli, a professor at ETH Zurich from 1928, formulated the exclusion principle.

abschnitte.text: **Quantum physics** studies processes at the scale of atoms and even smaller particles. Its name comes from **quanta**, the smallest packets of energy. It came about between 1900 and about 1930. In this world, particles sometimes behave like waves and waves like particles.

In 1900, Max Planck introduced **Planck's constant** h, about 6.626 · 10⁻³⁴ J·s. In 1905, Albert Einstein used it to explain the photoelectric effect, in which light frees electrons from metal, and received the Nobel Prize for it. A particle of light, a **photon**, has the energy E = h · f. Green light with a wavelength of 500 nanometres, for example, has photons of around 2.5 electronvolts.

In 1924, the Frenchman **Louis de Broglie** put forward the idea that particles of matter such as electrons also have wave properties. Soon afterwards this was confirmed by experiment. In 1926, at the University of Zurich, Erwin Schrödinger developed an equation that describes such matter waves. Today, electron waves are used in **electron microscopes**.

In 1927, Werner Heisenberg discovered the **uncertainty principle**. It says that the position and momentum of a particle cannot both be known to any accuracy you like at the same time. In addition, often only probabilities can be predicted for where a particle will be found. Einstein disliked this element of chance, but many experiments have confirmed quantum physics.

In 1925, **Wolfgang Pauli** formulated the **exclusion principle**: two electrons in an atom can never be in exactly the same state. From 1928 he was a professor at ETH Zurich, and in 1945 he received the Nobel Prize. Thanks to his principle, we understand the structure of the periodic table. Today, too, a lot of research goes on in Switzerland, for example at CERN near Geneva and on quantum computers.

Without quantum physics there would be no computer chips, no **lasers** and no LED lamps. Solar cells and MRI scanners in hospitals are also based on it. Researchers are working on **quantum computers**, which are meant to solve some tasks much faster. So the theory is not only strange but also very useful.

begriffe.erklaerung: A smallest, indivisible packet, for example of energy.
A particle of light.
The rule that you cannot know position and momentum both exactly at the same time.
Two electrons in an atom can never be in exactly the same state.

gewusst: Einstein is said to have said that God does not play dice, because the chance in quantum physics bothered him.
With Schrödinger's cat, which is supposed to be alive and dead at the same time, Schrödinger wanted to show how strange quantum physics is.
The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for experiments with entangled particles of light.

teile.einleitung: A switch is a component that can open or close an electric circuit. With one click the light goes on or off, the blender starts or a big machine stops. Switches come in many forms, from the small light switch to the red emergency stop button.
wichtigste: A switch opens or closes an electric circuit.
Current only flows and the lamp only lights up when the circuit is closed.
A push button only lets current flow while you press it, for example on a doorbell.
With a dimmer you make the light brighter or darker.
The symbol “0” on a switch means “off”, the symbol “I” means “on”.
The red emergency stop switch stops a machine immediately in an emergency.
If two switches are connected one after the other and one is open, the lamp stays off.

abschnitte.text: An electric circuit only works if it is closed all the way round. A switch is like a drawbridge in this circuit: when the bridge is down, the **electrons** can flow. When it is up, the path is broken and the current stops. Inside, two metal parts called **contacts** touch each other or are separated.

An ordinary light switch stays in its position until you press it again. A **push button**, on the other hand, springs back as soon as you let go. That is why the doorbell only rings while someone is pressing the button. The keys on a computer keyboard and the buttons in a lift are also push buttons. The small **cord switch** in the middle of a standard lamp's cable, however, is a proper switch.

Some switches do not need a hand. A **timer switch** in a stairwell switches the light off again by itself after a few minutes, saving electricity. A **motion sensor** detects the warmth of a person walking past and switches on an outdoor light. A thermostat switches the heating depending on the temperature, and a dusk switch turns on the street lamp as darkness falls.

A **dimmer** does not simply switch on or off but controls how much energy reaches the lamp. That way you can turn the light down to make it cosy. In long corridors or stairwells you often need two switches for the same lamp. For this there is **two-way switching**, which lets you switch the light on and off at both ends.

Machines, escalators and conveyor belts have a large red **emergency stop switch** on a yellow background. Pressing it stops the machine immediately, and it only runs again once someone deliberately releases it. Switches in the home are built so that you cannot touch the parts carrying current. Even so, never use a switch with wet hands or unscrew it yourself; that is a job for electricians.

begriffe.erklaerung: A closed path along which electric current flows from the source to the device and back.
A switch that only works for as long as you press it.
A switch with which you can smoothly set the brightness of a lamp.
A metal part in a switch that touches other metal parts so that current can flow.

gewusst: When you press a light switch you often hear a click, because a small spring inside quickly pushes the contacts together.
The symbols “I” and “0” on device switches come from the digits 1 and 0, meaning on and off, as in the binary system of computers.

teile.einleitung: Friction is a force that arises when two surfaces rub against each other or slide over each other. It slows movements down and produces heat as it does so. Without friction we could neither walk nor brake on a bike.
wichtigste: Friction is a force that slows movements down.
It always acts against the direction of movement.
A rolling bike slows down because of friction if you do not pedal.
There is static friction, sliding friction and rolling friction.
Under the same conditions, rolling friction is usually the smallest.
Friction produces heat, for example when you rub your hands together.
Oil reduces friction; grit on ice increases it.

abschnitte.text: Even smooth surfaces are full of tiny bumps under the microscope. When two surfaces slide over each other, these bumps catch on each other. This creates the **friction force**, which acts against the movement. The harder the surfaces are pressed together and the rougher they are, the greater the friction.

**Static friction** holds an object at rest in place, such as a heavy wardrobe that only moves after a strong push. **Sliding friction** acts when something slides, for example a sledge on snow. **Rolling friction** occurs with wheels and balls and is usually the smallest. That is why a box on wheels is much easier to push than one without.

If you rub your hands together hard, they get warm. This is because friction turns kinetic energy into **heat**. In the past, people made fire this way by twirling a wooden stick quickly on a board. The brake discs of a car or train also get very hot when braking.

Without friction, we would slip when walking, as if on black ice. When you **brake** on a bike, the brake pads press on the rim or disc and so slow the wheel down. In winter, municipalities spread **grit** on icy pavements to increase friction. Treaded soles on walking boots and winter tyres also give good grip.

Sometimes friction is a nuisance, because it wastes energy and wears parts out. **Lubricating oil** on a bike chain reduces friction, so the chain runs more easily and rusts less. In machines, engineers use **ball bearings** so that axles turn with almost no resistance. Skiers wax their skis to glide faster over the snow.

begriffe.erklaerung: Friction that stops an object at rest from sliding away.
Friction between two surfaces sliding past each other.
Friction when wheels or balls roll.
A part with small balls that allows turning with almost no friction.

gewusst: A match lights because of the heat from friction on the striking surface.
In curling, players sweep the ice so that the stone is slowed down less and glides further.
Without friction, knots in shoelaces would come undone at once.

teile.einleitung: A snowflake is a small structure made of one or more ice crystals that falls from the sky. Many flakes show beautiful six-armed stars, and no two look exactly alike. Billions of snowflakes make snow cover, snowdrifts and overhanging cornices.
wichtigste: A snowflake consists of one or more ice crystals.
Snowflakes fall more slowly than raindrops.
There is a lot of air trapped between the flakes of fresh snow cover.
Freshly fallen snow is called fresh snow.
Snow blown into heaps by the wind is called a snowdrift.
A rim of snow shaped by the wind that sticks out over a ridge is called a cornice.
You can look at snowflakes well on a cold, dark glove.

abschnitte.text: In a cold cloud, water vapour grows on a tiny grain of dust into an **ice crystal**. Because water molecules arrange themselves in hexagons, stars, plates or little columns with six sides are formed. Which shape forms depends on the temperature and humidity in the cloud. Often many crystals hook together as they fall, and that is how a larger **snowflake** is made.

Snowflakes are very light and have a large surface compared with their weight. That is why the air slows them down strongly, and they fall much **more slowly** than raindrops, often only about as fast as someone out for a leisurely walk. That is why snowfall looks so calm and floating. In wind the flakes also fly sideways, and skiers wear **ski goggles** so that no flakes fly into their eyes.

If you catch snowflakes on a cold, dark glove or piece of fabric, you can see their shape well with a magnifying glass. On warm skin they melt at once. From 1885, the American **Wilson Bentley** was one of the first people to photograph snow crystals through a microscope, and he took thousands of pictures. In the 1930s, the Japanese scientist Ukichiro Nakaya was the first to make artificial snow crystals in a laboratory.

Freshly fallen snow is called **fresh snow** and consists mostly of air trapped between the flakes. That is why it is so loose and insulates well. The wind can blow snow together into high heaps; these are **snowdrifts**. On mountain ridges the wind sometimes forms an overhanging rim of snow, the **cornice**, which can break off and set off avalanches and is therefore dangerous.

People with a house clear the pavement with a **snow shovel** after snowfall, so that nobody slips. Communes use snowploughs and salt spreaders so that roads stay passable. Children build snowmen and igloos out of wet snow. When it is snowing so hard that you can no longer tell the flakes apart, it is called a thick flurry.

begriffe.erklaerung: A regularly shaped piece of frozen water, usually hexagonal.
Freshly fallen snow.
A heap of snow blown together by the wind.
An overhanging rim of snow on a mountain ridge, shaped by the wind.

gewusst: Large, wet snowflakes form mainly at temperatures around zero degrees, when many crystals stick together.
Because there are countless ways a crystal can grow, two exactly identical snowflakes are considered extremely unlikely.

teile.einleitung: Popcorn is burst grains of maize that turn into a white, crunchy flake with a loud pop when heated. A special kind of maize, popping corn, is used for popcorn. The bursting is an exciting example of what steam and pressure can do.
wichtigste: Popcorn is made from grains of a special kind of maize, popping corn.
There is a little water in the grain, which turns into steam when heated.
The steam pushes the hard shell open, and the grain bursts.
The inside of finished popcorn is white to yellowish.
When making popcorn, you often put a little oil in the pan first.
You put a lid on the pan, because the grains jump up.
A grain that does not burst stays hard.

abschnitte.text: Popcorn is made from **popping corn**, a kind of maize with a particularly hard and dense shell. Inside, the grain contains starch and a small amount of water, about a seventh of its weight. The shell is so dense that this water cannot escape when heated. Normal sweetcorn, as eaten on the cob, does not burst open properly. That is why you buy special grains for popcorn.

When you heat the grain, the water inside turns into **steam**. The steam needs much more space than the water, so the **pressure** inside the grain rises sharply. At about 180 degrees Celsius, the shell can no longer hold the pressure and tears open with a pop. The hot, soft starch swells out and puffs up into a foam. In the air, the foam cools immediately and becomes the crunchy, white to yellowish flake.

First you put some **oil** in a pan and heat it. Then you pour in the grains so that the bottom is covered. A **lid** is important, because the grains jump up when they burst and can fly out of the pan. You shake the pan now and then so that nothing burns. When there is hardly any popping left, the popcorn is ready and can be flavoured with sugar or salt.

abschnitte.titel: When a grain does not burst
abschnitte.text: At the end, a few **hard grains** are often left at the bottom of the pan. Usually they had too little water inside or a small crack in the shell. The steam could escape through the crack before enough pressure built up. That is why popping corn should be stored well sealed and not too dry. You should not bite on the hard grains, as they can damage your teeth.

Maize originally comes from **Mexico** and Central America, where people were already roasting popping corn thousands of years ago. As maize spread, popcorn became very popular in North America. In the 20th century it became the typical **cinema** snack. At funfairs (Chilbis) and fairs in Switzerland, too, popcorn is freshly made in large machines. However, popcorn is not suitable for small children, because they can easily choke on it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of maize with a hard shell that bursts when heated.
A nutrient in cereals and potatoes made of many sugar building blocks.
Water in the form of a gas, which needs much more space than liquid water.
How strongly something presses on a surface from inside or outside.

gewusst: A popped piece of popcorn can be many times bigger than the original grain.
When it bursts, the grain jumps up because the starch pushes against the bottom of the pan like a little leg.
Depending on how the grain bursts, you get a butterfly shape or a round mushroom shape.

teile.einleitung: A pipette is a thin tube with which you can take up small amounts of liquid, measure them and release them drop by drop. It is an important tool in the laboratory, but also for experimenting at home, and it works thanks to air pressure.
wichtigste: With a pipette, you can drip liquid very precisely.
If you close the top of a filled tube, the air pressure from below holds the water in it.
If you take your finger away, air flows in and the liquid runs out.
With a dropping pipette, the outside air pressure pushes the liquid into the tube.
A volumetric pipette measures exactly one fixed volume.
Micropipettes measure from a few microlitres up to about one millilitre.
The simple glass pipette with a rubber bulb is named after Louis Pasteur.

abschnitte.text: A **pipette** is a narrow tube of glass or plastic with a fine tip at the bottom. You use it to suck up liquid and release it again. The word comes from French and means something like little tube or little pipe. Pipettes are needed in chemistry, biology and medicine, but also for simple experiments.

If you fill a tube with water and put your finger over the top, the water stays in. **Air pressure** pushes against the water from below and holds it in place. If you take your finger away, air flows in at the top, the pressure evens out and the water runs out. With a **dropping pipette**, you first squeeze the rubber bulb. When you let go, there is low pressure inside, and the outside air pressure pushes the liquid in.

The **Pasteur pipette** is a simple glass tube with a rubber bulb, named after the French scientist Louis Pasteur. With a **volumetric pipette**, you measure exactly one fixed amount, for example 10 millilitres. A graduated pipette has a scale and allows different amounts. The **micropipette** works with a plunger and replaceable plastic tips and measures tiny amounts from a few microlitres to about one millilitre.

In a narrow glass tube, water forms a downward curve at the surface, the **meniscus**. You read the level at the bottom of this curve. Your eyes must be at the same height, or you will read it wrongly. This rule also applies to measuring cylinders at school.

A big relative of the pipette is the **wine thief**, a long glass tube used to take wine or cider out of a barrel. Eye drops and nose drops are also measured out with small pipettes. In school experiments, you drip water onto a coin with a pipette to count how many drops fit on it. This shows nicely how **surface tension** shapes the water into a hill.

In the past, liquid was often sucked into the pipette by mouth. That is dangerous, because you could swallow poisonous or corrosive substances. That is why a **pipette bulb** or pipetting aid is always used today. In laboratories, care is also taken to change the plastic tips after each use so that no samples get mixed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow tube.
A millionth of a litre, that is a thousandth of a millilitre.
Pressure that is lower than the air pressure around it.
A long tube for taking samples out of a barrel.

gewusst: A single drop of water from a pipette has a volume of roughly 0.05 millilitres.
A surprising number of drops of water often fit on a coin before the water hill overflows.
The micropipette with a plunger was invented in Germany in the 1950s.

teile.einleitung: A string is a thin, tightly stretched thread of metal, nylon or gut that vibrates and makes a note when it is plucked, bowed or struck. From the violin to the hammered dulcimer, many instruments are based on this simple physics.
wichtigste: A thick string sounds lower than a thin one.
If you tighten a string more, the note gets higher.
If you make a string shorter with your finger, the note also gets higher.
The harp has a great many strings and is plucked with both hands.
On the hammered dulcimer of Swiss folk music, you strike the strings with beaters.
Strings today are often made of metal or nylon; in the past many were made of animal gut.
The zither is also a stringed instrument.

abschnitte.text: A **string** is held firmly at two points and is under tension. When it is plucked, it vibrates back and forth many hundreds of times a second. These vibrations make the air quiver, and we hear a **note**. The number of vibrations per second is called the **frequency** and decides the pitch.

Three things decide how high a string sounds: its length, its tension and its thickness. A shorter string vibrates faster and sounds higher, which is why guitar players press the strings onto the fingerboard. If it is tightened more, it also sounds higher, which is how an instrument is tuned with the **tuning pegs**. Thick, heavy strings vibrate more slowly and sound lower, which is why the bass strings are thick.

The Greek scholar **Pythagoras** is said to have used a single string, the monochord, to study how string length and pitch are related. If you halve the length, the note sounds an octave higher. In the past, strings were often made of dried and twisted **animal gut**, usually from sheep. Today they are mostly made of steel, nylon or other plastics, often wound with metal wire.

Stringed instruments are played in three ways. The guitar, **harp** and zither are plucked, and the violin, viola, cello and double bass are bowed. In the piano, small felt hammers strike the strings; on the hammered dulcimer, the musician does it with two beaters. In all of them, a wooden **sound box** amplifies the sound.

The **hammered dulcimer** is a typical instrument of string band music, especially in Appenzell and the Toggenburg. It has many strings stretched over a trapezium-shaped wooden box. The zither was also popular in mountain regions. In Ländler music, the double bass also often plays, and sometimes violins.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of vibrations per second; it decides the pitch.
A hollow wooden body that vibrates along and amplifies the sound.
A pin that can be turned to tighten and tune a string.
The distance between two notes in which the higher one vibrates twice as fast.

gewusst: A concert grand piano has over 200 strings, because many notes sound on two or three strings at the same time.
A concert harp usually has 47 strings; some of them are coloured so that the harpist can find her way.

teile.einleitung: A rocket is a flying machine that moves forwards by pushing hot gases out backwards with great force. Because it carries its own fuel and oxygen, it can also fly in airless space. Rockets carry satellites, space probes and people into space.
wichtigste: Rockets fly on the principle of recoil.
They push hot gases out backwards and are pushed forwards as a result.
A balloon rocket works on the same principle as a space rocket.
Because there is no air in space, rockets carry their own oxygen.
To orbit the Earth, a rocket needs about 28,000 km/h.
Large rockets have several stages, which are dropped when empty.
In 1961, Yuri Gagarin was the first person to fly into space.

abschnitte.text: If you blow up a balloon and let it go, it shoots off because the air streams out backwards. A rocket works in exactly the same way. According to Newton's **third law**: when one object pushes another away, it is itself pushed in the opposite direction. The rocket pushes hot gases backwards, and they push the rocket forwards. This is called **recoil**.

In the engine, fuel burns with oxygen to form very hot gases. Because there is no air in space, the rocket has to carry its own **oxygen**, usually deep-frozen and liquid. Some rockets burn liquid hydrogen, others kerosene or solid fuels. The gases stream out at high speed through a bell-shaped **nozzle**.

Most of a rocket at launch is fuel. So that it does not have to drag empty tanks along, it is made of several **stages**. When one stage is empty, it is dropped and the next one fires. This way the rocket gets lighter and lighter and can go faster. For an orbit around the Earth it needs about 28,000 km/h, and to leave the Earth completely even around 40,000 km/h.

Many centuries ago, people in China were already building rockets with gunpowder. In 1926, the American Robert Goddard launched the first rocket with liquid fuel. In 1957, the Soviet Union put the first satellite, Sputnik, into space, and shortly afterwards the dog **Laika** orbited the Earth. In 1961, **Yuri Gagarin** was the first person to fly into space, and in 1969 the giant Saturn V took astronauts to the Moon.

Today, rockets mainly carry **satellites** for weather, navigation, the internet and television into space. The European Ariane is launched from the space centre in French Guiana in South America. Some companies land their first stages again after launch and use them several times, which saves money. Before launch, it is traditional to count backwards to zero; this is called the **countdown**.

You can build a **water rocket** from a plastic bottle. You fill it partly with water and pump air into it with a bicycle pump. When it is released, the air pressure forces the water out downwards, and the bottle shoots up into the air. The first Swiss person in space was Claude Nicollier, who flew on the Space Shuttle in 1992.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that pushes an object forwards when it pushes something out backwards.
A part of a rocket with its own tanks and engines, which is dropped after use.
The path along which a satellite circles the Earth.
Counting backwards to zero before the launch.

gewusst: The Saturn V was over 100 metres tall, higher than a church tower.
The idea of counting backwards before launch comes from a silent film of 1929.
A rocket is slowest and heaviest just after launch; later it gets lighter and faster and faster.

teile.einleitung: The tyre tread is the pattern of grooves and blocks on the running surface of a tyre. It makes sure that a vehicle finds grip even on a wet or snowy road. Depending on the vehicle and the surface, the tread looks quite different.
wichtigste: The tyre tread is the grooves and blocks in the tyre.
In rain, the grooves channel the water away from under the tyre.
When a car slides on a film of water and can no longer be steered, this is called aquaplaning.
Winter tyres have a special tread for snow and cold.
On snowy mountain roads, snow chains are put on the tyres.
Mountain bikes have chunky knobs, racing bikes almost smooth tyres.
When the tread is worn down, the tyre must be replaced.

abschnitte.text: A tyre only touches the road over an area about the size of a postcard. Grooves, blocks and fine cuts are moulded into this **running surface**: the **tread**. It decides how well the tyre grips, how it pushes water away and how quietly it rolls. Over time the tread wears down and becomes flatter and flatter.

In rain, there is a film of water on the road. The grooves in the tread take in the water and channel it away to the side and backwards. If the tread is too shallow or you drive too fast, the tyre can no longer manage this. Then it floats up on the water, and the car can neither be steered nor braked. This dangerous state is called **aquaplaning**.

**Winter tyres** are made of a softer rubber mixture that stays grippy even in the cold. Their tread has many fine cuts, the **sipes**, which dig into the snow like little teeth. In Switzerland there is no general obligation to use winter tyres, but anyone who holds up traffic with unsuitable tyres can be fined. On steep, snowy mountain roads, **snow chains** are also put on the drive wheels; sometimes a road sign makes them compulsory.

Every vehicle has a tread that suits its use. **Mountain bikes** have chunky, knobbly tyres that grip in earth and gravel. Racing bikes have narrow, almost smooth tyres so that they roll easily on the road. Tractor tyres have especially chunky and deep lugs for soft fields. In Formula 1, completely smooth tyres, the **slicks**, are even used in dry weather, because more rubber then touches the road.

In Switzerland, the tread of car tyres must by law be at least 1.6 millimetres deep. But experts recommend clearly more, especially in winter. Many tyres have small bars in the grooves, the **wear indicators**: when the tread is worn down to these bars, the tyre must be replaced. The depth can also be checked with a simple tread depth gauge.

A car does not slide because of the **static friction** between tyre and road. Rubber changes shape and fits itself to the small bumps in the tarmac. A good tread makes sure this contact stays even with water or snow. With worn tyres, the braking distance on a wet road becomes clearly longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: The depth of the grooves in the tyre, measured in millimetres.
A tyre floating up on a film of water, so that the vehicle can no longer be steered.
Fine cuts in the tread of winter tyres.
The force that stops two surfaces from sliding on each other.

gewusst: A tyre with a full tread can push away several litres of water per second in the rain.
Formula 1 racing cars change to tyres with a deep tread when it rains.
The typical M+S on the side of the tyre stands for mud and snow.

teile.einleitung: Snow chains are steel chains that are put round the tyres of a car in winter. They help stop the car from skidding on snow and ice. Especially on steep mountain roads in Switzerland, they can make the difference between a car getting up or not.
wichtigste: Snow chains improve the grip of the tyres on snow and ice.
They are fitted to the drive wheels, the wheels that the engine turns.
In Switzerland, a round blue sign with a tyre and a chain means: snow chains are compulsory.
Even with good winter tyres, snow chains are still needed when this sign is shown.
On roads clear of snow, the chains are taken off, because they damage the road and the tyres.
It is best to practise fitting them at home before driving into the mountains.
Snow socks made of fabric are a light alternative for less difficult conditions.

abschnitte.text: A snow chain consists of many **links** of hardened steel. It is stretched like a net over the tread of the tyre and fastened on the inside and outside. There are simple ladder chains and chains with a diamond pattern, which runs even more smoothly. For lorries, buses and tractors there are especially heavy versions.

A car can only brake, steer and pull away if there is enough **friction** between the tyre and the ground. On ice this friction is very small, because the smooth surface gives the rubber hardly any grip. The links of the chain press into the snow and ice and **interlock** with the ground. This creates a kind of positive locking, similar to crampons on mountain boots.

Snow chains go on the **drive wheels**: at the front for front-wheel drive, at the back for rear-wheel drive. For four-wheel-drive vehicles, follow the car's owner's manual. After driving a few metres, you stop and tighten the chain again. With chains you drive slowly; manufacturers usually recommend no more than 50 km/h.

On pass roads and in mountain valleys there may be a round blue **mandatory sign** showing a tyre with a chain. From this sign onwards, snow chains are compulsory, and winter tyres alone are not enough. Anyone who drives on without chains risks a fine and puts others in danger. That is why chains belong in the boot for winter trips into the mountains.

**Snow socks** are fabric covers pulled over the tyres that improve grip. They are light and quick to fit, but do not last as long as steel chains. It is important to practise fitting them at home in daylight, because at the roadside it is often cold, dark and wet. Gloves and a mat to kneel on make the job more pleasant.

begriffe.erklaerung: How well the tyre holds on the ground without slipping.
The wheels that are turned by the engine and move the car forwards.
A round blue traffic sign that tells you what you must do.
Fabric covers for car tyres, a light alternative to chains.

gewusst: As early as 1904, the American Harry Weed patented a tyre chain.
There are also snow chains for bicycles and for prams.
On a dry road, snow chains wear out badly within a few kilometres.

teile.einleitung: A photon is the smallest packet of light, a particle of light. All light, and also radio waves, X-rays and heat radiation, consists of photons. They have no rest mass and always travel at the speed of light in a vacuum.
wichtigste: A photon is a packet of energy of electromagnetic radiation.
Photons have zero rest mass.
In a vacuum they move at around 300,000 kilometres per second.
The higher its frequency, the greater the energy of a photon.
Photons are bosons.
The antiparticle of the photon is the photon itself.
The name photon was coined by Gilbert Newton Lewis in 1926.

abschnitte.text: A **photon** is an elementary particle and at the same time part of an electromagnetic wave. That sounds contradictory, but it is a basic idea of quantum physics: light sometimes behaves like a wave and sometimes like a stream of particles. This is called **wave-particle duality**. Photons have no electric charge and no rest mass.

The energy of a photon is calculated with E = h · f, where h is **Planck's constant**. Blue light has a higher frequency than red and therefore consists of photons with more energy. Visible light has wavelengths of about 380 to 780 nanometres. A photon with an energy of 1 electronvolt has a wavelength of around 1240 nanometres and so lies in the invisible infrared. X-ray photons carry a thousand times more energy than visible light.

Even though a photon has no rest mass, it has **momentum**, a kind of impact. The momentum is p = h / λ, where λ is the wavelength. A green photon of 500 nanometres has a momentum of around 1.3 · 10 to the power of minus 27 kg·m/s. That is tiny, but enough to drive a thin solar sail through space with sunlight.

In 1900, Max Planck introduced the idea that radiation is only given off in portions. In 1905, **Albert Einstein** used it to explain the photoelectric effect and spoke of light quanta. Around 1923, Arthur Compton showed that photons collide with electrons like little balls. The word **photon** comes from the Greek word for light and was introduced in 1926 by Gilbert Newton Lewis.

A red laser with a power of just 1 milliwatt sends out around 3 · 10 to the power of 15 photons per second, that is three quadrillion. Single photons can be detected with a **photomultiplier**, which multiplies a freed electron like an avalanche. When a photon flies outwards from the gravitational field of a star, it loses energy and its frequency gets lower. This is called **redshift**.

Photons are the **force carriers** of the electromagnetic force. When two magnets attract each other or electric charges repel, according to today's understanding photons act as go-betweens. Without photons there would be no seeing, no photosynthesis in plants and no mobile phone network. Fibre-optic cables for the internet also carry information with photons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that, as far as we know today, is not made of smaller parts.
A kind of particle that includes, for example, the force carriers of the fundamental forces.
The distance between two crests of a wave.
The constant of nature h, which links the energy of a photon with its frequency.

gewusst: Light from the Sun takes a little over eight minutes to reach the Earth.
Because of many collisions, a photon from the inside of the Sun takes a very long time to reach the surface.
Under very good conditions, the human eye can detect just a few photons.

teile.einleitung: A sledge is a vehicle that glides over snow or ice on runners. In Switzerland, sledging is called “schlitteln”, and it is one of the most popular winter pastimes. In physics, the sledge is interesting because there is only a little friction on snow.
wichtigste: A sledge glides over the snow on narrow runners.
There is little friction on snow and ice, which is why a sledge glides so well.
The steeper the slope, the faster the sledge goes down.
On a simple wooden sledge you usually brake and steer with your feet.
The Davoser is a well-known wooden sledge named after the town of Davos in Graubünden.
In cold countries, dogs often pull sledges over the snow.
In a bobsleigh, two or four people race down an ice channel.

abschnitte.text: A sledge consists of a seat and two **runners**, long, narrow gliding rails. On a classic wooden sledge the runners are often covered with metal, so that they glide better and wear less. You have to pull the sledge up the slope on a cord. The **Davoser sledge** made of ash wood is especially common in Switzerland. There are also luges, plastic bobs and horn sledges, which were used in the past to bring wood or hay down into the valley.

On snow and ice, **friction** is very low. The rubbing of the runners produces a wafer-thin layer of water on the surface, which acts like a lubricant. Narrow runners only press a little into the snow and therefore glide more easily than a wide surface. At very low temperatures a sledge glides less well, because less water film forms.

On a slope, gravity pulls the sledge down. Part of this force, the **downhill force**, pushes it down the slope. The steeper the slope, the greater this force and the faster you go. You are slowed down mainly by friction and air resistance. If you lie flat instead of sitting upright, you offer the air less surface and go faster.

Switzerland has many marked **sledge runs**, often with a train or chairlift to the top. One well-known example is the run from Preda to Bergün in Graubünden on the old Albula Pass road. As early as 1883, one of the first international sledge races took place between Davos and Klosters. **Bobsleigh** and the Cresta Run, a famous ice channel for skeleton riders, began in St. Moritz in the late 19th century. The bob run from St. Moritz to Celerina is built anew from natural ice every year.

In cold countries such as Canada, Alaska, Greenland or Scandinavia, sledges have been an important means of transport for centuries. There, **sledge dogs** such as huskies often pull loads over snow and ice. In Lapland, the Sami also harness reindeer to their sledges. Today there are dog sledge races over hundreds of kilometres. At the Winter Olympics, bobsleigh, luge and skeleton are among the fastest sports.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, narrow gliding rail under the sledge.
The Swiss German word for sledging.
A racing sledge with steering, in which two or four people race down an ice channel.
The part of gravity that pulls a body down a slope.
A racing sledge on which you ride on your tummy, head first.

gewusst: In bobsleigh, the sledges reach speeds of over 130 km/h.
The natural ice run from St. Moritz to Celerina is the oldest bob run in the world still in use.
In the past, mountain farmers used horn sledges to carry heavy loads such as hay or wood down into the valley.

teile.einleitung: A rainbow is a coloured arch in the sky that forms when sunlight is split into its colours in raindrops. It shows the colours red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet, always in the same order. You only see it when the Sun is behind you and rain is falling in front of you.
wichtigste: A rainbow forms when sunlight is refracted and reflected in raindrops.
In the process, white light is split into its colours.
In the primary rainbow, red is on the outside and violet on the inside.
You only see a rainbow with the Sun at your back.
Sometimes a fainter secondary rainbow appears above it, with the colours in reverse order.
A small rainbow also forms in the spray from a garden hose or a waterfall.

abschnitte.text: A rainbow is a **light phenomenon** and not an object, which is why you can never reach it. It consists of many colours that blend smoothly into each other. Usually seven colours are counted: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. This sequence of colours is called the **spectrum**.

Sunlight looks white but contains all the colours. When it enters a round raindrop, it is bent as it goes in; this is called **refraction**. Inside, it is reflected off the back of the drop and refracted again as it comes out. Because each colour is bent by a slightly different amount, the light fans out into its colours; this is **dispersion**.

For a rainbow you need sunshine and raindrops in the air at the same time. The Sun must be behind the observer, and the rain must be falling in front of her. It works best in the morning or late afternoon, when the Sun is low. The arch always appears at an angle of about **42 degrees** around the point opposite the Sun.

Sometimes you see a second, paler arch above the primary rainbow. This **secondary rainbow** forms when the light is reflected twice inside the drop. Its colours are in reverse order, with red on the inside and violet on the outside. Between the two arches the sky is noticeably dark; this is called **Alexander's dark band**.

On a sunny day, you can make your own rainbow with a garden hose. Stand with your back to the Sun and spray a fine mist into the air. At waterfalls such as the **Rhine Falls** near Schaffhausen or the Staubbach Falls in Lauterbrunnen, you also often see rainbows. With a glass prism you can also split light into its colours, as **Isaac Newton** did around 1666.

begriffe.erklaerung: Light changing direction as it passes from air into water or glass.
The series of all the colours that white light is made of.
A piece of glass that splits light into its colours.
A second, fainter rainbow with the colours reversed.

gewusst: From an aeroplane, you can sometimes see a whole, circular rainbow.
Every person sees their own rainbow, because the light reaches their eyes from different drops.
On bright full-moon nights, a pale moonbow can form.

teile.einleitung: A phase diagram is a kind of map that shows whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas at a particular pressure and temperature. It can explain, for example, why water boils below 100 °C in the mountains.
wichtigste: In the typical phase diagram of a pure substance, pressure and temperature are on the axes.
Lines separate the solid, liquid and gas regions.
The boundary between liquid and gas is called the vapour pressure curve.
The boundary between solid and gas is called the sublimation curve.
At the triple point, all three phases exist at the same time.
The melting curve of water has a negative slope, which is unusual.
At the Jungfraujoch, water boils at around 88 °C.

abschnitte.text: A **phase diagram** is a chart with temperature on the horizontal axis and pressure on the vertical axis. Every point on the diagram stands for a state. If the point lies in the solid region, the substance is solid, for example ice. The states solid, liquid and gas are called **phases**.

The **vapour pressure curve** separates liquid and gas; on it, the substance boils. The **melting curve** separates solid and liquid. The **sublimation curve** separates solid and gas; here a substance goes directly from the solid to the gaseous state. How steep these lines are is described by the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.

All three lines meet at the **triple point**, where solid, liquid and gas occur at the same time. For water it is at 0.01 °C and a very low pressure of about 6 millibars. The vapour pressure curve ends at the **critical point**, for water at around 374 °C and about 221 bar. Above it, liquid and gas can no longer be told apart. According to Gibbs' phase rule, a pure substance on a boundary line has only one degree of freedom: if you choose the temperature, the pressure is fixed.

For almost all substances, the solid form is denser than the liquid. For water it is the other way round, which is why ice floats. That is why the melting curve of water has a **negative slope**: under higher pressure, ice melts at a slightly lower temperature. The ordinary ice on Earth is called **ice Ih**, where the h stands for hexagonal. At very high pressure there are many other forms of ice.

The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure gets. According to the vapour pressure curve, water then boils at a lower temperature. At the **Jungfraujoch**, at around 3500 metres, it boils at about 88 °C, which is why cooking pasta takes longer. In a **pressure cooker** it is the other way round: the higher pressure means the water only boils above 100 °C, and the food cooks faster.

**Dry ice** is frozen carbon dioxide. Its triple point is at about 5 bar, which is above normal air pressure of around 1 bar. That is why CO2 cannot become liquid here. Dry ice does not melt but sublimes directly into gas at about minus 78 °C. You see this in the theatre as fog, and it is used to keep food cold during transport.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state of a substance, for example solid, liquid or gas.
The point at which solid, liquid and gas exist side by side at the same time.
The direct change from solid to gas, without becoming liquid.
The end point of the vapour pressure curve, beyond which liquid and gas can no longer be told apart.

gewusst: For a long time, the triple point of water was the basis for defining the temperature unit kelvin.
Scientists today know of almost twenty different forms of water ice.
On Mount Everest, water boils at around 70 °C.

teile.einleitung: A pulley is a wheel that can turn, with a groove for a rope to run over. It is one of the simple machines and has helped people lift heavy loads for thousands of years, at wells, on building sites and on flagpoles.
wichtigste: A pulley is a wheel with a groove for a rope.
A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the force.
With a single fixed pulley, you save no force at all.
A movable pulley that moves with the load roughly halves the force needed.
On a flagpole, you pull down on the rope at the bottom to raise the flag.
On construction cranes and chairlifts, the ropes run over pulleys.
Several pulleys together make a block and tackle.

abschnitte.text: A **pulley** is a disc mounted so that it can turn, with a groove around the edge in which a rope, chain or belt runs. Like the lever, the inclined plane and the wheel, it is one of the **simple machines**. Its job is to redirect forces or make them smaller. Because the wheel turns, the rope hardly slides and there is little friction.

A **fixed pulley** is attached to a beam, scaffold or mast and does not move with the load. It only changes the direction of the force; you need just as much force as without the pulley. Even so, it is practical, because pulling down is more comfortable and you can use your body weight. This is how the flagpole on which the Swiss flag is raised works, or the pulley over an old draw well.

A **movable pulley** hangs in the rope and moves upwards with the load. The load now hangs from two pieces of rope, which share the weight. That is why you only need about half the force. But you have to pull twice as much rope to lift the load the same height.

If you combine several fixed and movable pulleys, you get a **block and tackle**. With four supporting pieces of rope, you only need about a quarter of the force but have to pull four times as much rope. This is called the **golden rule of mechanics**: what you save in force, you have to add in distance. Construction cranes, sailing ships and breakdown trucks use blocks and tackles.

On chairlifts, ski lifts and cable cars, the steel cables run over sets of pulleys on the masts. Large **return wheels** in the stations drive the cable and guide it back. Lifts in houses also hang from cables that run over pulleys. In ancient times, Greek scholars such as Archimedes are said to have moved heavy loads with blocks and tackles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic tool such as a lever, pulley or inclined plane that changes forces.
A pulley that is attached in one place and only changes the direction of the force.
A pulley that moves with the load and halves the force.
A combination of several pulleys with which heavy loads can be lifted easily.

gewusst: Climbers use small pulleys to pull injured people out of crevasses with little force.
According to tradition, Archimedes is said to have pulled a loaded ship ashore on his own with a block and tackle.

teile.einleitung: Deposition, also called desublimation, is the direct change of a substance from a gas into a solid without becoming liquid in between. You see it every winter when hoar frost forms on branches or ice flowers grow on windows.
wichtigste: Deposition is the direct change from gas to solid.
Another technical term for it is desublimation.
Hoar frost forms when water vapour turns directly into ice.
Ice flowers on cold windowpanes also form through deposition.
Snow crystals grow in the clouds as water vapour attaches directly as ice to tiny seeds.
During deposition, the gas gives off heat to its surroundings.
The opposite, the change from solid directly to gas, is called sublimation.

abschnitte.text: Substances can be solid, liquid or gas; these are called their **states of matter**. Normally, water vapour first turns into liquid water and this then into ice. But if it is cold enough, the water vapour skips the liquid stage and turns straight into ice. This jump is called **deposition** or desublimation.

On cold, clear winter nights, blades of grass, branches and fences cool below zero degrees. The water vapour from the air settles directly on them as fine ice crystals; this is **hoar frost**. On cold windowpanes, branching patterns grow in the same way: the **ice flowers**. In modern houses with well-insulated windows, you rarely see them today.

In the clouds, water vapour attaches directly as ice to tiny dust particles or ice seeds. This is how **snow crystals** grow, which usually have six arms or a hexagonal shape. The reason is the arrangement of the water molecules in ice, which form a hexagonal lattice. Depending on temperature and humidity, plates, stars or needles form.

When a gas turns into a solid, the particles arrange themselves firmly and give off energy as **heat**. In sublimation, the reverse process, the same heat has to be added again. A well-known example of sublimation is dry ice, frozen carbon dioxide, which turns straight into gas without melting. Snow can also slowly disappear in dry, sunny weather without melting.

In a **freezer** that is opened often, a layer of ice forms because the moisture from the room air turns directly into ice on the cold walls.
