That is why older freezers have to be defrosted now and then. In technology, deposition is used to coat spectacle lenses, tools or computer chips with wafer-thin layers. In the chemistry laboratory, some substances are purified by vaporising them and letting them turn solid again on a cold surface.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form in which a substance exists: solid, liquid or gas.
The direct change from solid to gas.
Fine ice crystals that grow directly from water vapour on cold objects.
Another word for deposition.

gewusst: From 1885, the American Wilson Bentley photographed thousands of snow crystals and found no two alike.
The frost on a car on an autumn morning is often deposition, even though the air is still above zero degrees.

teile.einleitung: Quarks are tiny elementary particles that make up the protons and neutrons in the atomic nucleus. You can never observe them on their own, because they are always tightly bound in groups. Even so, they are among the most important building blocks of all matter.
wichtigste: There are six kinds of quark: up, down, strange, charm, bottom and top.
A proton consists of two up quarks and one down quark.
A neutron consists of two down quarks and one up quark.
Quarks have charges of +2/3 or minus 1/3 of the elementary charge.
Quarks never occur freely on their own; this is called confinement.
The top quark is the heaviest quark and was discovered at Fermilab in 1995.
The name quark comes from the novel “Finnegans Wake” by James Joyce.

abschnitte.text: As far as we know today, **quarks** are elementary particles that cannot be divided further. Together with the leptons, which include the electron, they make up matter. There are six kinds, called **flavours**: up, down, strange, charm, bottom and top. The ordinary matter around us is made only of up and down quarks.

abschnitte.titel: Building blocks of the proton and neutron
abschnitte.text: A **proton** consists of two up quarks and one down quark. An up quark has a charge of +2/3, a down quark minus 1/3 of the elementary charge. For the proton, this adds up to +1. A **neutron** consists of two down quarks and one up quark and so has a charge of zero. The delta particle Δ++, made of three up quarks, has a charge of +2.

Quarks have a special property called **colour charge**, labelled red, green and blue. This has nothing to do with real colours; it is just a name. The quarks are held together by the strong force, whose force carriers are called **gluons**, from the English word glue. Particles made of three quarks are called baryons, and particles made of a quark and an antiquark are called **mesons**.

If you try to pull two quarks apart, the force between them does not get weaker but stays strong. At some point the energy is enough to create new quarks, and new particles are formed instead of free quarks. That is why quarks are never found on their own. This phenomenon is called **confinement**.

In 1964, **Murray Gell-Mann** and, independently, George Zweig suggested that many known particles are made of smaller building blocks. Gell-Mann took the name quark from a line in the novel “Finnegans Wake” by James Joyce. At the end of the 1960s, experiments in California showed that protons really do have small components. Gell-Mann received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1969.

The **top quark** was discovered in 1995 at Fermilab near Chicago. It is the heaviest known elementary particle and about as heavy as a whole gold atom. But it decays so quickly that it cannot form particles. Today, quarks are studied mainly at **CERN**'s LHC particle accelerator near Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest electric charge found freely, for example that of the proton.
The force carrier of the strong force, which holds quarks together.
The fact that quarks never occur alone but only in groups.
A particle made of a quark and an antiquark.

gewusst: The mass of the three quarks makes up only about one per cent of the mass of a proton; the rest is in the binding energy.
Gell-Mann also chose the name because Joyce mentions exactly three quarks, and protons really are made of three quarks.
Shortly after the Big Bang, there were free quarks for a moment in a hot soup of particles.

teile.einleitung: A pendulum is an object that hangs from a thread or rod and swings back and forth. Swings, pendulum clocks and wrecking balls are examples. With a pendulum, you can see wonderfully how energy changes from one form into another.
wichtigste: A pendulum swings back and forth around its lowest position.
At the lowest point it is fastest and has the most kinetic energy.
At the turning points the speed is zero, and the energy is all potential energy.
For small swings, the period depends mainly on the length.
A pendulum about 1 m long takes about 2 seconds for a whole swing.
Christiaan Huygens invented the pendulum clock in 1656.
In 1851 in Paris, Léon Foucault used a pendulum to show the rotation of the Earth.

abschnitte.text: A **pendulum** is an object that can swing on a thread, rope or rod around a point it hangs from. If you pull it to the side and let go, gravity pulls it back down. Because it has momentum, it swings past the lowest point to the other side. The outermost points, where it stands still for a moment, are called **turning points**.

At the turning points, the pendulum is at its highest and stands still for a moment; its energy is all **potential energy**. As it swings down, the potential energy turns into **kinetic energy**, and at the lowest point it is fastest. Then it rises again, and the kinetic energy turns back into potential energy. If a pendulum is raised 20 cm, it travels at about 1.98 m/s at the bottom, without friction.

For small swings, the time of one swing depends almost only on the **length** of the pendulum. How heavy the bob is, on the other hand, makes no difference. A pendulum about 1 m long takes about 2 seconds to go there and back once. A pendulum four times as long swings only half as fast, so it takes twice as long.

According to legend, around 1583 Galileo Galilei watched a swinging lamp in Pisa Cathedral and noticed that every swing took the same time. The Dutchman **Christiaan Huygens** invented the pendulum clock in 1656, which was much more accurate than earlier clocks. In 1851, **Léon Foucault** set a long pendulum swinging in Paris whose plane of swing seemed to turn slowly. This proved that in reality the Earth is turning beneath the pendulum.

A swing is a pendulum too. To keep it from stopping, you have to add energy in the right rhythm, for example by swinging your legs. A real pendulum always gets slower, because air resistance and **friction** turn energy into heat. Without a drive, it eventually comes to rest.

In old grandfather clocks and cuckoo clocks, the pendulum sets the rhythm. A metronome helps musicians play evenly. On building sites, houses used to be knocked down with a heavy **wrecking ball** that swings like a pendulum. Some very tall skyscrapers have huge pendulums hanging inside that damp the swaying in the wind.

begriffe.erklaerung: The outermost point where the pendulum stands still for a moment and turns back.
The time for one whole swing, there and back.
Energy an object has because it is high up.
Energy an object has because it is moving.

gewusst: A pendulum whose half swing lasts exactly one second is called a seconds pendulum; it is just under a metre long.
Pendulum clocks were the most accurate clocks in the world for around 250 years.
On the Moon, the same pendulum would swing much more slowly than on Earth, because gravity is weaker there.

teile.einleitung: Recoil is the force that pushes an object forwards when it pushes something out backwards with force. If you let go of a blown-up balloon, it whizzes through the air because the air streams out at the back. Rockets fly into space and squid swim away in a flash on the same principle.
wichtigste: Recoil happens when an object pushes mass away in one direction and is moved in the opposite direction itself as a result.
The principle of recoil is based on the conservation of momentum.
It is closely linked to Newton's third law: every force has an equal opposing force.
A light object that is pushed away gets a higher speed than the heavy object that moves back.
Rockets and jet engines use recoil to produce thrust.
Animals such as squid and cuttlefish also use recoil to move when escaping.
A rocket needs no air to push against and so works in space too.

abschnitte.text: If you blow up a balloon and let go, the air streams out of the opening at the back. The balloon itself is pushed in the **opposite direction** and flies off. This effect is called **recoil**. It always occurs when an object pushes something away from itself, whether air, water, gas or a solid object.

In physics, recoil is explained by **momentum**, the product of mass and velocity. If two objects are at rest at first, their total momentum is zero, and it stays that way after they push apart. So mass times velocity is the same on both sides, just in opposite directions. If two ice skaters of 60 kg and 40 kg push off from each other and the heavier one glides away at 2 m/s, the lighter one moves off at 3 m/s. Isaac Newton described this in the 17th century in his **third law**, the principle of action and reaction.

A rifle with a mass of 4 kg fires a 10 g bullet at 800 m/s. The rifle recoils at 2 m/s, because it is 400 times heavier than the bullet. An astronaut of 100 kg floating in space who throws away a 2 kg tool at 5 m/s then drifts at 0.1 m/s in the other direction. In space there is no friction, so she would keep gliding on and on. That is why astronauts have to be well secured when working outside the space station.

A **rocket** burns fuel and pushes the hot gases out backwards at very high speed. This pushes it forwards, even in the airless vacuum of space. An aircraft's **jet engine** sucks in air at the front, compresses it, burns it with kerosene and pushes the gas out fast at the back. Around 1903, the Russian scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky described mathematically how rockets can reach space using recoil.

abschnitte.titel: Recoil in nature and everyday life
abschnitte.text: **Squid** and cuttlefish fill their body mantle with water and, when in danger, squirt it out suddenly through a funnel. This shoots them away in a flash. Jellyfish also move with small spurts of water. Firefighters have to hold a hose nozzle with a high water flow firmly, because the jet of water coming out produces a strong recoil. **Segner's water wheel** from the 18th century turns because water squirts out sideways from bent pipes, much like a garden sprinkler.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that pushes an object in the opposite direction when it pushes something away.
Mass times velocity, that is the impact of a moving object.
The total momentum stays the same as long as no force acts from outside.
The force with which an engine or rocket is pushed forwards.
An aircraft engine that pushes out hot gas backwards at high speed.

gewusst: Around 2000 years ago, Hero of Alexandria described a ball that turned because of steam streaming out of it.
A garden sprinkler that turns by itself uses exactly the same recoil principle as Segner's water wheel.
If you throw a heavy object backwards from a rowing boat, the boat moves forwards a little.

teile.einleitung: The wheel is a round disc that turns around an axle. It is one of the most important inventions of humankind, because it makes things much easier to move. Without wheels there would be no bicycles, cars, trains or clocks.
wichtigste: A wheel turns around a rod, the axle.
The invention of the wheel made it much easier to move things.
The oldest wheels are about 5000 to 5500 years old.
A bicycle wheel has thin rods, the spokes.
On a bicycle, the chain connects the pedals to the back wheel.
Gear wheels have teeth that mesh with each other.
Rack railways such as the Pilatus Railway have a toothed rack between the rails.

abschnitte.text: A **wheel** is a round object that turns around an **axle**. Instead of dragging a heavy object along the ground, you can roll it on wheels. This creates much less friction. That is why the wheel is one of the most important inventions of humankind.

The first wheels appeared about 5500 years ago, at roughly the same time in Mesopotamia and in Europe. They were heavy wooden **disc wheels**. In Switzerland, wooden wheels around 5000 years old have been found in lake dwelling settlements on Lake Zurich. Later, lighter wheels with spokes were invented, for example for fast chariots.

A bicycle wheel consists of a hub, a rim, a tyre and many thin **spokes**. The spokes make the wheel stable and still light. The **chain** connects the pedals to the back wheel and so passes on your force. With the gears, you choose whether to pedal more easily or ride faster.

**Gear wheels** have teeth around the edge that mesh with each other. This lets one wheel drive another. A small gear wheel turns faster than a large one connected to it. Gear wheels are found in clocks, mixers, bicycles and machines.

On steep mountain lines, normal wheels would spin on the rails. That is why there are **rack railways** with a **toothed rack** between the rails. A gear wheel under the train meshes with this rack. With gradients of up to 48 per cent, the Pilatus Railway near Lucerne is the steepest rack railway in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rod around which a wheel turns.
A thin rod connecting the hub and rim of a wheel.
A wheel with teeth that can drive another wheel.
A rail with teeth that a gear wheel meshes with.

gewusst: The Pilatus Railway has been running since 1889 and uses a special rack system with teeth on the sides.
In Central America, old toy figures on wheels have been found, but the wheel was not used there for carts.
The giant Ferris wheel in Vienna's Prater has been turning since 1897.

teile.einleitung: Luge is a fast winter sport in which you lie on your back and race feet first down an ice channel. The athletes reach speeds of over 120 km/h, and physics such as air resistance and friction decides between victory and defeat.
wichtigste: In luge, you lie on your back with your feet pointing forwards.
In the related sport of skeleton, on the other hand, you lie on your front, head first.
You steer by pressing on the sled with your legs and shoulders.
Lugers lie completely flat so that air resistance is as small as possible.
In the ice channel they reach speeds of over 120 km/h.
At the start, they push themselves off with their hands on the ice.
In the doubles, two people ride on one sled.

abschnitte.text: Luge takes place on an artificially frozen **track** with banked curves. The sled has two runners with sharp steel blades and no brake or steering. There are the **singles** events for women and men, the doubles and a team relay. The time counts, usually added up over several runs, and thousandths of a second often decide the result.

At the start, the luger sits on the sled and pulls hard forwards on two handles. Then they paddle with their hands on the ice, for which they have small **spikes** on their gloves. Then they lie down flat and steer only with gentle pressure of the calves on the runner tips and by shifting the weight of their shoulders. Every unnecessary movement costs time.

Gravity pulls the sled down the track, while mainly **air resistance** and the friction of the runners on the ice slow it down. That is why the athletes lie as flat as possible and wear smooth, tight-fitting suits. In the banked curves, the centrifugal force presses them onto the sled with many times their body weight. The highest speeds ever measured are over 150 km/h.

Sledging as a sport has an important root in Switzerland. In 1883, an international sledge race from **Davos** to Klosters took place, which is considered one of the first of its kind. Luge has been an Olympic sport since the 1964 Winter Games in Innsbruck. Athletes from Germany, Austria and Italy have been especially successful since then.

In **skeleton**, you lie on your front and ride head first; the Cresta Run in St Moritz is world-famous for this. In bobsleigh, two or four people sit in a bob with steering. There is also natural track luge on icy mountain paths without banked curves. Luge, bobsleigh and skeleton often use the same artificial ice tracks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A channel of ice with high walls and banked curves in which luge is ridden.
A long, narrow gliding part under the sled.
The force with which the air slows down a moving object.
A sled sport in which you ride face down, head first.

gewusst: A luge sled has no brake; in the run-out at the end of the track, the athletes brake with their feet.
Because the time is measured to a thousandth of a second, luge is one of the closest sports of all.

teile.einleitung: A puddle is a small pool of water that forms in hollows in the ground after rain. For children, puddles are a playground for jumping into; for birds, a bathtub; and for physicists, a place full of things to observe. After a while a puddle disappears again, because the water soaks away or evaporates.
wichtigste: Puddles form after rain in hollows where the water cannot soak away fast enough.
After a thunderstorm there are especially many puddles, because a lot of rain falls in a short time.
A puddle disappears by soaking away and evaporating, often leaving dry mud behind.
A small still body of water that is bigger than a puddle is called a pond.
Birds like to bathe and drink at puddles.
For puddle jumping, it is best to wear wellington boots.
On a bike, you ride slowly through large puddles, because you cannot see how deep they are.

abschnitte.text: When it rains, part of the water soaks into the ground. But if the ground is hard, compacted or covered with tarmac, the water cannot get in fast enough. It then flows downhill and collects in the lowest **hollow**. In a **thunderstorm**, a lot of rain falls in a short time, which is why there are especially many puddles afterwards.

A puddle gets smaller over time. Part of the water seeps into the ground; this is called **infiltration**. Another part turns into invisible water vapour at the surface; this is **evaporation**. Sun, warmth and wind speed it up. If the puddle was muddy, a layer of dry mud is left at the end, which often cracks into plates.

The still surface of the water acts like a **mirror**; you can see houses, trees and the sky in it. If a thin film of oil floats on the puddle, it shimmers in rainbow colours because light waves overlap. If you jump in, you hear a splash and the water sprays in all directions. If a car drives through, the wheels push the water away and it sprays up to the side.

Birds such as sparrows and blackbirds bathe in puddles to care for their feathers, and drink from them. Swallows collect damp earth for their nests at puddles. In Switzerland, the rare **yellow-bellied toad** uses water-filled wheel ruts and puddles to lay its eggs. Mosquito larvae and tiny water creatures also live in puddles that last for a longer time.

Puddle jumping is fun, best with **wellington boots** and waterproof trousers. On a bike, you ride slowly through large puddles, because you cannot see how deep they are or whether there is a hole underneath. Cars can start sliding on a lot of water; this is called **aquaplaning**. In winter, puddles can freeze and form very slippery patches.

begriffe.erklaerung: When water soaks into the ground.
When water slowly turns into invisible water vapour.
A small, still body of water, bigger than a puddle.
When a car slides on a layer of water and can no longer be steered.

gewusst: Puddle jumping is a popular game in many children's books and cartoons.
Puddles that keep forming in the same place can be vital for the survival of rare amphibians.
On Mars, researchers have found traces showing that water once stood in hollows there.

teile.einleitung: In physics, shear is a deformation in which forces act parallel to a surface and shift the layers of a body against each other. You can imagine it like a stack of playing cards that you push sideways at the top. Shear plays an important part in scissors, screws, buildings and even earthquakes.
wichtigste: In shear, forces act parallel to a surface.
Shear stress is the force parallel to the surface divided by the area.
The angle by which the body is deformed is called the shear angle.
The shear modulus links shear stress and shear angle.
Liquids at rest have no shear modulus; they simply flow away.
Seismic S waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core of the Earth.
A shear pin breaks on purpose when overloaded and so protects a machine.

abschnitte.text: If you put your hand on a stack of playing cards and push it sideways, the cards slide against each other. Seen from the side, the rectangle turns into a slanting parallelogram. That is exactly what **shear** is: the force does not press or pull, but acts parallel to the surface. The angle by which the body slants is called the **shear angle**.

**Shear stress**, shortened to the Greek letter τ (tau), is the force parallel to the surface divided by the area. If a bolt with a cross section of 100 mm² is loaded in shear with 5,000 newtons, the shear stress is 5,000 divided by 100, which is 50 N/mm². Engineers use calculations like this to check whether screws, rivets and bolts will hold. If the stress is too great, the part is sheared off.

How much a material deforms under shear is described by the **shear modulus** G. It links shear stress and shear angle: the larger G, the stiffer the material. It can be calculated from the elastic modulus E and Poisson's ratio. For steel, with E equal to 210 GPa and a Poisson's ratio of 0.3, this gives about 81 GPa. Rubber, on the other hand, has a very small shear modulus and is easy to shear.

A solid body resists shear, but a liquid at rest does not: it gives way to any sideways force by flowing. That is why liquids have no shear modulus. Researchers make use of this with earthquakes: **S waves** are shear waves and cannot cross the liquid outer core of the Earth. From the “shadow” where no S waves arrive, scientists concluded that the outer core is liquid.

Scissors, punches and tin snips separate material on purpose by shear. A **shear pin** in a drive is deliberately so thin that it breaks when overloaded, before expensive parts such as the gearbox are damaged. You find this, for example, in snow blowers and boat engines. With bridges, beams and glued joints, too, engineers have to calculate the shear forces exactly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force parallel to a surface, divided by the size of that surface.
The angle by which a body slants under shear.
A material constant that tells you how strongly a substance resists shear.
An earthquake wave in which the rock vibrates across the direction of travel.

gewusst: When you spread butter on bread, you shear it: the layers of butter are shifted against each other.
A shear pin is a deliberately built-in weak point that saves a machine from greater damage.

teile.einleitung: The period is the time an oscillation takes for one complete cycle. For a pendulum, it is the time to go there and back once. It can be used to build clocks, describe sounds and compare many processes in nature.
wichtigste: The period is the time for one complete back-and-forth movement.
It is given the letter T and is measured in seconds.
Frequency is the reciprocal: frequency equals 1 divided by the period.
A tuning fork at 440 hertz has a period of about 2.3 milliseconds.
In experiments, you usually time ten oscillations and divide by ten so that reaction time matters less.
The period of a pendulum depends mainly on its length.
Going from one turning point to the other takes only half a period.

abschnitte.text: Many movements repeat themselves again and again, for example a pendulum, a swing or a guitar string. Such a movement is called an **oscillation**. The time for one complete cycle, until everything is exactly the same again, is called the **period** T. If a swing goes from right at the front to right at the back in 0.8 seconds, the period is 1.6 seconds, because it also has to come back again.

The **frequency** tells you how many oscillations happen per second, measured in hertz. It is the reciprocal of the period. If a pendulum makes exactly 20 swings in 36 seconds, one swing lasts 1.8 seconds and the frequency is about 0.56 hertz. For the note A of a tuning fork at 440 hertz, one oscillation lasts only about 2.3 milliseconds.

Timing a single swing with a stopwatch is inaccurate, because we press about a tenth of a second too late. This **reaction time** matters less if you time ten swings and divide the result by ten. It is best to start timing when the pendulum passes through its lowest point. Swinging in step is interesting too: two pendulums with periods of 2.0 and 2.1 seconds are at the same point at the same time again after 42 seconds.

For a **simple pendulum**, the period depends almost only on the length and hardly on the mass or how far it swings. Galileo Galilei is said to have noticed this from a swinging chandelier in Pisa Cathedral. The Dutchman Christiaan Huygens built the first **pendulum clock** in 1656. A pendulum just under a metre long has a period of about 2 seconds, so it swings from one side to the other once a second.

In heat, a metal pendulum rod expands a little, the pendulum gets longer and swings more slowly. The clock then loses time. If a pendulum clock gains time, you move the **pendulum bob** down a little so that the pendulum gets longer. Clockmakers used to build special pendulums from different metals that balanced each other out.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement that repeats itself regularly.
The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.
The unit of frequency; 1 hertz is one oscillation per second.
The point where a pendulum stands still for a moment and turns back.
The time we need to react to something.

gewusst: The Earth has periods too: it turns on its own axis in about a day and goes round the Sun in about a year.
A pendulum on the Moon would swing much more slowly than on Earth.
The quartz crystals in wristwatches usually oscillate more than 32,000 times a second.

teile.einleitung: Planck's constant is a tiny constant of nature with the symbol h. It shows that energy is not passed on in amounts as small as you like, but only in small packets. That is why it is fundamental to all of quantum physics.
wichtigste: Planck's constant is a constant of nature with the symbol h.
Its value is exactly 6.62607015 · 10⁻³⁴ joule seconds.
Max Planck introduced it in 1900.
It shows that energy is only passed on in small packets.
The energy of a particle of light is E = h · f.
Planck's constant is fundamental to quantum physics.
Since 2019, the kilogram has been defined with the help of h.

abschnitte.text: **Planck's constant** is one of the most important **constants of nature**. It is written with the letter h. Its value is unimaginably small, about 6.626 · 10⁻³⁴ joule seconds. That is a zero, a decimal point and then another 33 zeros before the first digit.

**Max Planck** was a German physicist who lived from 1858 to 1947. He studied how hot objects give off light and heat. In 1900 he found a formula that only worked if energy is given off in small portions. He called these portions **quanta**, and in 1918 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this.

Before Planck, people thought energy flowed evenly like water from a tap. Planck showed that it comes more like marbles, in separate pieces. The energy of such a packet is E = h · f, where f is the **frequency**. Blue light has a higher frequency than red, which is why its photons carry more energy.

**Quantum physics** began with Planck's constant. Einstein used it in 1905 to explain the photoelectric effect. Niels Bohr used it in 1913 for his model of the atom. Werner Heisenberg's **uncertainty principle** also contains the constant h.

Since 20 May 2019, h has had an exactly fixed value. It is used to define the **kilogram**, which is no longer defined by a metal cylinder near Paris. With a special measuring device, the **Kibble balance**, a mass can be determined through electrical measurements. The Swiss Federal Institute of Metrology, METAS, has also built such a balance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number in nature that never changes.
A smallest, indivisible packet of energy.
How often a wave oscillates per second.
A precision instrument that measures mass through electrical quantities.

gewusst: At first, Planck himself thought his quanta were just a calculating trick.
Because h is so small, in everyday life we do not notice that energy comes in packets.
The Max Planck Society, a large research organisation in Germany, is named after him.

teile.einleitung: A projector is a device that uses light and lenses to throw a small picture, greatly enlarged, onto a wall or screen. From the slide projector and the overhead projector to the digital projector, projectors come in many forms. But the principle is always the same: a bright lamp, a picture and a lens.
wichtigste: A projector throws an enlarged picture onto a wall or screen.
It consists of a light source, a condenser, a picture and a lens.
The condenser directs the lamp light evenly through the picture.
A slide must be put in upside down and reversed left to right.
The further the projector is from the wall, the larger the picture becomes.
In Swiss schools, the projector for transparencies is called a Hellraumprojektor.
An early projector from the 17th century was the magic lantern.

abschnitte.text: Every classic projector has a bright **light source**: in the past a light bulb, today often LEDs or lasers. The **condenser** consists of converging lenses and directs the light evenly through the picture, for example a slide. Behind it is the **lens**, which enlarges the picture and throws it sharply onto the wall. You focus the picture by moving the lens.

For a converging lens to form an enlarged, sharp image, the slide must be between one and two **focal lengths** away. The picture on the wall is then upside down and reversed left to right. That is why you put a slide in the wrong way round; then it appears the right way on the wall. If the projector moves further from the wall, the picture gets bigger but also darker, because the light is spread over a larger area.

abschnitte.titel: How big does the picture get?
abschnitte.text: The **magnification** tells you how many times bigger the picture is than the original. A slide is 36 millimetres wide. If it appears 1.8 metres, that is 1800 millimetres, wide on the wall, it is 1800 divided by 36, so 50 times enlarged. The picture does not only get wider but also taller, which is why its area even grows 2500 times.

The **overhead projector**, called a Hellraumprojektor in Switzerland, was found in every Swiss classroom for decades. You laid transparent sheets on a lit glass plate, and a mirror sent the picture onto the wall. The slide projector showed holiday photos from 35 mm slides, and the film projector brought moving pictures onto the screen in the cinema. Today mostly **digital projectors** are used, which project pictures directly from a computer or mobile phone.

As early as the 17th century there was the **magic lantern**, which used a candle or oil lamp to throw painted glass pictures onto the wall. It is often credited to the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens. Later, showmen used it for spooky shows and stories. In 1895, the **Lumière** brothers showed films publicly for the first time in Paris with their cinematograph, and that was the beginning of the age of cinema.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lens or group of lenses that throws the picture onto the wall.
Converging lenses that direct the lamp light evenly through the picture.
The distance between the lens and the point where it brings light together.
A small, transparent photo in a frame that can be projected.
A projector that throws pictures from a computer onto the wall.

gewusst: The German word “Beamer” for a digital projector is a pseudo-anglicism; in English it is simply called a projector.
In the cinema, usually 24 single pictures are projected every second, and our eyes see them as smooth movement.
Twice as far from the wall, a picture becomes twice as wide but four times as dark.

teile.einleitung: A converging lens is a transparent object, usually made of glass, that is thicker in the middle than at the edge. It brings rays of light together at one point, the focal point. Magnifying glasses, glasses for long-sighted people, cameras and even our eyes use converging lenses.
wichtigste: A converging lens is thicker in the middle than at the edge.
It brings parallel rays of light together at one point, the focal point.
The distance from the lens to the focal point is called the focal length.
A magnifying glass is a converging lens that shows things enlarged.
Glasses for long-sighted people have converging lenses.
In our eye, the lens of the eye acts as a converging lens.

abschnitte.text: A **converging lens** is also called a convex lens, because it curves outwards. It is made of glass or transparent plastic. Its opposite is the **diverging lens**, which is thinner in the middle and makes light spread out. Even a round drop of water acts like a small converging lens.

Light is bent when it passes from air into glass and out again; this is called **refraction**. Because of the curved shape, the rays at the edge are bent more strongly towards the middle. That is why parallel rays meet behind the lens at the **focal point**. The more strongly curved the lens, the shorter the **focal length**.

If an object is further away than the focal length, the converging lens forms an upside-down image behind it. This image can be caught on a sheet of paper or a camera sensor. If the object is closer than the focal length, you see an enlarged, upright image through the lens. This is exactly how a magnifying glass works.

Long-sighted people see things close up blurred; converging lenses in their **glasses** help them to read. In cameras, mobile phone cameras and projectors, lenses make sure the pictures are sharp. Microscopes and telescopes combine several converging lenses. The **lens of the eye** is also a converging lens, which forms an image on the retina.

With a magnifying glass, you can concentrate sunlight so strongly that paper starts to burn. That is why it is also called a **burning glass**. In rare cases, a glass bottle in dry grass can act in the same way. You must never look straight at the Sun through a magnifying glass or binoculars, because this seriously damages the eyes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point where the concentrated rays of light meet.
The distance between the lens and the focal point.
Curving outwards, like the back of a spoon.
The unit for the strength of a spectacle lens.

gewusst: The oldest known reading glasses come from 13th-century Italy.
A glass full of water in front of a text acts like a magnifying glass and makes the letters look bigger.

teile.einleitung: Projectile motion describes a throw in which an object is thrown at an angle upwards or forwards. Without air resistance it flies along an evenly curved path, the trajectory parabola. Whether football, shot put or the jet of water from a garden hose: you come across this movement everywhere.
wichtigste: Without air resistance, a body thrown at an angle flies along a parabola.
Projectile motion is split into a steady horizontal movement and an evenly accelerated vertical movement.
Throughout the whole flight, only the gravitational acceleration g acts vertically downwards, even at the top point.
At the top point the speed is smallest, because the vertical speed is zero there.
Without air resistance, a ball thrown horizontally and a ball dropped from the same height land at the same time.
Without air resistance, on level ground you get the greatest distance with a launch angle of 45 degrees.
In the 17th century, Galileo Galilei was the first to realise that the path of a throw is a parabola.

abschnitte.text: In **projectile motion**, a body is sent off at a starting speed at an angle to the horizontal. After that, if you leave out air resistance, only gravity acts on it. The body first rises, slowing down as it does, reaches its highest point, the **apex**, and then falls again. The flight path has the shape of a **trajectory parabola**. A special case is the horizontal throw, in which the launch angle is zero degrees.

The trick to understanding it is to split the movement into two parts that do not disturb each other. Horizontally, the body flies at a **constant speed**, because no force acts sideways. Vertically, it is **evenly accelerated** by gravitational acceleration of about 10 m/s², first slowed down and then accelerated downwards. That is why a ball thrown horizontally and a ball dropped from the same height land at the same time. The first one just also flies forwards.

The starting speed is split up using sine and cosine. If a ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 60 degrees, the horizontal component is 10 m/s. If you throw at 30 m/s at 30 degrees, the vertical starting speed is 15 m/s. A ball at 20 m/s at 30 degrees rises at 10 m/s and reaches the apex after 1 s. A ball at 40 m/s at 30 degrees flies for 4 s in total before it lands again at launch height.

If a ball rolls horizontally at 2 m/s over the edge of a platform 1.8 m high, it falls for 0.6 s. In that time it flies 1.2 m horizontally, which is how far from the edge it lands. The faster the ball rolls over the edge, the further it flies, but the fall time stays the same. This also applies to **jets of water**: a jet coming out horizontally forms a beautiful parabola that is easy to watch.

In reality, the air slows the body down, so the path is steeper and shorter at the front than a parabola; this is called a **ballistic curve**. For light balls this difference is large, for a heavy shot it is small. In the **shot put**, the best launch angle is below 45 degrees, because the shot is released above head height. In 1638, the Italian scientist **Galileo Galilei** described projectile motion in his book on two new sciences as a combination of two movements.

begriffe.erklaerung: The curved path of a thrown body without air resistance.
The highest point of the flight path.
The acceleration with which bodies fall towards the Earth, about 9.81 m/s².
One part of a speed, for example only the horizontal or only the vertical part.
The braking force of the air on a moving body.

gewusst: Without air resistance, a ball thrown at 30 degrees or at 60 degrees at the same speed lands the same distance away.
At the apex a ball is never completely still, because it keeps flying horizontally.
The path of a jet of water from a fountain shows a trajectory parabola almost perfectly.

teile.einleitung: Circuit symbols are small, standardised symbols used to show electrical components in a circuit diagram. A lamp, for example, is drawn as a circle with a cross, a motor as a circle with an M. If you know these symbols, you can read circuits like a secret code.
wichtigste: Circuit symbols are simplified, standardised symbols for electrical components.
A lamp is drawn as a circle with a cross inside it.
For a battery, the longer line stands for the positive terminal.
Under the European standard, a resistor is a small rectangle.
An electric motor is a circle with a large M.
A filled-in dot shows that two wires are electrically connected.
Circuit symbols are simple, clear and understood everywhere.

abschnitte.text: Real components look very different depending on the manufacturer. If you drew them as they are, a diagram would be cluttered and hard to understand. That is why **circuit symbols** are used, which are easy to draw and clear. They are laid down in international **standards**, so that experts all over the world speak the same language.

A battery or a cell is drawn as two parallel lines, one long and one short. The long line is the **positive terminal**, the short one the negative terminal. Several cells one after the other make a battery and are drawn as several such pairs of lines. A mains socket or alternating voltage can often be recognised by a small wavy line.

The light bulb is a circle with a cross inside it. An electric motor is a circle with a large M, a generator a circle with a G. In Europe, the **resistor** is drawn as a small rectangle, but in the USA as a zigzag line. A meter for current is a circle with an A for ampere, and one for voltage a circle with a V for volt.

A **diode** only lets current through in one direction. Its symbol is a triangle pointing like an arrow in the direction of the current, with a line across its tip. For a **light-emitting diode**, LED for short, two small arrows pointing outwards are added. They mean that the component gives out light.

An open switch is drawn as a line sticking out at an angle and leaving a gap. In a closed switch, the line lies on the wire, so the path is unbroken. If two wires cross without a dot, they are not connected to each other. A filled-in **junction**, on the other hand, shows that they are electrically connected.

begriffe.erklaerung: A binding rule for how something is made or drawn, so that it is the same everywhere.
The connection of a battery with the higher electrical potential.
A component that slows down the flow of current.
An electronic component that lights up when current flows through it in the right direction; LED for short.

gewusst: A resistor looks quite different in an American circuit diagram than in a European one, namely like a zigzag line.
The circuit symbol for earth looks like a small rake pointing upside down into the ground.

teile.einleitung: The sound level tells you how loud a noise is and is measured in decibels (dB). Because our ears can detect very quiet and extremely loud sounds, a special scale is used. Just a few decibels more mean clearly more sound energy.
wichtigste: The sound level is given in the unit decibel, shortened to dB.
The decibel scale is logarithmic: 10 dB more means ten times the sound intensity.
A noise is felt to be twice as loud when the level rises by about 10 dB.
If you double the distance from a point source in the open, the level falls by about 6 dB.
A-weighting in dB(A) takes into account that the ear does not hear all pitches equally well.
Loudness level, which refers to a 1 kHz tone that sounds equally loud, is given in phon.
Constantly high sound levels can damage your hearing.

abschnitte.text: The **sound level** is a measure of how strong a sound is. Our ears hear a huge range of sound strengths, from quietly rustling leaves to a jet engine. So that you do not have to calculate with awkwardly large numbers, the **decibel** is used. The unit is named after the inventor Alexander Graham Bell; one decibel is a tenth of a bel. 0 dB corresponds roughly to the threshold of hearing, the quietest sound a healthy young ear can only just hear.

For the **sound intensity level**, the intensity is compared with 10^-12 W/m², the threshold of hearing. A sound of 10^-6 W/m² is a million times stronger and therefore has 60 dB. If ten equally loud, independent sources run instead of one, the level rises by 10 dB. Two sources of 90 dB and 80 dB together only give about 90.4 dB, because the louder one decides almost everything. For the **sound pressure level**, doubling the sound pressure gives about 6 dB more, and a sound pressure of 0.2 Pa gives 80 dB.

Our ears hear middle pitches better than very low or very high notes. That is why measurements are often made in **dB(A)**, where A-weighting imitates this sensitivity of the ear. The loudness level in **phon** tells you how loud a tone is felt to be, compared with a 1 kHz tone. We only feel a noise is twice as loud when the level rises by about 10 dB.

Whispering is about 30 dB, a normal conversation about 60 dB. Heavy road traffic reaches around 80 dB, a rock concert 100 dB or more. From about 120 to 130 dB, sound starts to hurt the ears; this is called the **threshold of pain**. If you move away from a source of noise, it gets quieter: at double the distance, the level of a point source in the open falls by about 6 dB.

Anyone exposed to loud noises for a long time can permanently damage their hearing. Typical results are hearing loss or a constant whistling in the ear called **tinnitus**. In Switzerland, the Sound and Laser Ordinance sets how loud concerts and parties may be. At loud events, earplugs help, and when listening to music with headphones you should not turn the volume right up. You can measure the level with a **sound level meter** or an app.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit for sound level, shortened to dB.
The quietest sound a person can only just hear.
A scale on which each equal step means multiplying.
The unit for loudness as people experience it.
A constant whistling or rushing sound in the ear, often after too much noise.

gewusst: A level of 0 dB does not mean silence, just sound at the threshold of hearing.
Two equally loud lawnmowers together are only 3 dB louder than one alone.
A noise of 100 dB has ten times more sound intensity than one of 90 dB.

teile.einleitung: The Rutherford scattering experiment is one of the most famous experiments in physics. In it, tiny alpha particles were fired at a wafer-thin gold foil. The surprising result showed that every atom has a tiny, heavy nucleus and is otherwise almost empty.
wichtigste: The experiments took place from 1909 in Manchester in England.
Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden carried them out under the direction of Ernest Rutherford.
Alpha particles were fired at a very thin gold foil.
Most particles flew through almost undisturbed, so the atom consists mostly of empty space.
A few particles were strongly deflected or even bounced back, which points to a small, positively charged nucleus.
The experiment disproved Thomson's model of the atom.
In 1911, Rutherford presented his model of the atom with a nucleus and a shell.

abschnitte.titel: How the experiment was set up
abschnitte.text: A radioactive source sent out **alpha particles**, which are positively charged, fast particles. They flew towards a **gold foil** thinner than a thousandth of a millimetre. Gold was well suited because it can be hammered very thin. Around the foil stood a screen that flashed briefly every time a particle hit it. The researchers counted these tiny flashes of light in the darkened room through a microscope.

**Ernest Rutherford** was a physicist from New Zealand who worked at the University of Manchester. He had already received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1908 for his research on radioactivity. The actual measurements were carried out by his colleague **Hans Geiger** and the young student Ernest Marsden. Hans Geiger later became known for the Geiger counter tube, which is used to measure radiation.

The vast majority of alpha particles flew almost straight through the foil. Only very few were strongly deflected, and some even bounced back. Rutherford later compared this to a cannonball bouncing back off a sheet of tissue paper. He concluded that the positive charge and almost the whole mass of the atom are in a tiny **atomic nucleus**. The electrical repulsion between the positive nucleus and the positive alpha particles deflected them.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the plum pudding
abschnitte.text: Before this, **Thomson's model of the atom** by Joseph John Thomson was accepted. He pictured the atom as a pudding of positive mass with the electrons stuck in it like plums or raisins. With this model, no particle should have been strongly deflected. So Rutherford developed a new model: a small nucleus in the middle and electrons in a wide shell around it. With his scattering formula he calculated that the scattering rate depends on the scattering angle as 1/sin⁴(θ/2), and the measurements confirmed this.

The diameter of an atom is around 10,000 to 100,000 times larger than that of its nucleus. If the nucleus were as big as a pea, the whole atom would be as big as a huge football stadium. Even so, almost all the mass is in the nucleus. In 1913, Niels Bohr built his well-known model of the atom with electron orbits on Rutherford's model.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle made of two protons and two neutrons, produced in radioactive decay.
The tiny, heavy, positively charged centre of an atom.
The deflection of particles from their straight path.
A simplified picture of how an atom is built.

gewusst: The researchers had to count the flashes of light by eye for hours, because there were no electronic counters yet.
The chemical element rutherfordium is named after Ernest Rutherford.
So almost everything you can touch consists mostly of empty space.

teile.einleitung: A suction cup is a soft, bowl-shaped disc, usually made of rubber or plastic, that sticks to smooth surfaces. It does not hold with glue but because air pressure presses it on from outside. Suction cups are found on bathroom hooks, mobile phone holders and also in nature, for example on the arms of octopuses.
wichtigste: A suction cup sticks to smooth surfaces such as glass or tiles.
When you press it on, air is squeezed out from under the suction cup.
Underneath, low pressure is created.
The outside air pressure presses the suction cup firmly against the surface.
On rough surfaces, air gets in and the suction cup falls off.
Octopuses, squid and some fish have natural suction cups.

abschnitte.text: A **suction cup** looks like a small, flat bell made of soft material. You find them on towel hooks, soap holders, sat navs in cars or toy arrows. It can be fixed without screws or glue and removed again. That makes it especially practical for bathrooms and windows.

If you press the suction cup onto a smooth surface, the air underneath is squeezed out. The soft rim seals it, so that no new air can get in. Under the cup there is now **low pressure**, that is less air pressure than outside. The normal **air pressure** of the surroundings then presses the suction cup firmly against the tile from outside.

At sea level, the air above us presses on every surface with about **1 bar**. That corresponds roughly to the weight of 10 kilograms per square centimetre. That is why a large suction cup can carry a surprising amount. Glaziers use special **suction lifters** to carry heavy panes of glass safely.

On rough or porous surfaces such as wood or roughcast plaster, air gets in through small cracks. Then the pressure evens out, and the suction cup falls off. Over time, air also slowly seeps in under the rim, which is why some hooks come loose after a few days. A damp rim seals better, so it helps to moisten the suction cup a little first.

An **octopus** has hundreds of suckers on each of its eight arms, with which it holds on to prey and can also taste. The remora, a fish, attaches itself to sharks and whales with a sucking disc on its head. Leeches also have suckers at both ends of their bodies. Researchers copy such models from nature; this is called **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pressure that is lower than the air pressure around it.
The force with which air presses on all surfaces.
Technology that copies ideas from nature.

gewusst: In space, a suction cup would not hold, because there is no air pressure there.
On a high mountain, a suction cup holds a little less strongly, because the air pressure is lower there.
Octopuses can open jars with screw lids using their suckers.

teile.einleitung: A lubricant is a substance that you put between two parts that rub against each other, so that they slide more easily. Oil on a bicycle chain, grease in a ball bearing or wax on a drawer are all lubricants. They make things run quietly, wear less and last longer.
wichtigste: Lubricants reduce the friction between two parts.
A dry bicycle chain needs a few drops of oil.
A squeaky door becomes quiet again with a little oil on the hinges.
A car engine needs engine oil so that its parts run well.
Grease is a thick, sticky lubricant like a paste.
A pencil lead helps with a zip that sticks.
In our joints, the joint fluid acts like a lubricant.

abschnitte.text: Even surfaces that look smooth have tiny hills and valleys under the microscope. When two such surfaces rub against each other, these bumps catch on each other and **friction** is produced. A lubricant lies between them as a thin layer and keeps the surfaces apart. So they slide more easily, get less hot and wear more slowly; this is called less **wear**.

A **bicycle chain** should be cleaned and oiled regularly. If it is never looked after, it runs stiffly, squeaks, rusts and quickly wears out together with the cogs. If a door squeaks, a few drops of oil on the hinges help. A wooden drawer that sticks slides better if you rub the runners with candle wax, and for a zip, the graphite of a pencil lead helps.

Lubricants come in different forms. **Oils** are liquid and get into narrow gaps too. **Grease** is thick and sticky like a paste and stays where you spread it, for example in ball bearings. Solid lubricants such as graphite, wax or Teflon work as a thin, slippery layer. Even water or soap can lubricate in some cases.

A **car engine** needs engine oil, which is constantly pumped through the engine. Without oil, the metal parts would get so hot that they would seize up. Gearboxes, factory machines, the cogs of cable cars and clocks are also lubricated. In food factories, special lubricants are used that are harmless if they come into contact with food.

Our body has its own lubricant too. In the joints, for example in the knee, the **joint fluid** makes sure that the cartilage surfaces slide over each other with almost no friction. Tear fluid keeps the eyelids moving, and saliva helps with swallowing. Thousands of years ago, people were already greasing cart axles with animal fat so that the wheels turned more easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force produced when two surfaces rub against each other, which slows movement down.
The slow wearing away of a part through friction and use.
A thick, paste-like lubricant that stays in place.
A thick fluid in the joints that keeps them supple.

gewusst: Thanks to their lubrication, the joints in the human body often slide better than many technical bearings.
Too much oil on a bicycle chain is not good either, because dust and dirt stick to it.

teile.einleitung: A prism is a transparent object, usually made of glass, with surfaces set at an angle to each other. If you send white light through it, the light is bent and split into the colours of the rainbow. Using prisms, Isaac Newton discovered that white light is made up of many colours.
wichtigste: A prism for light experiments is usually made of glass.
A prism bends the direction of a ray of light.
In a prism, white light is split into spectral colours.
Red light is bent the least, violet the most.
If you bring the colours back together, white light forms again.
Red laser light stays red in a prism and is only bent.
Diamonds, glass crystals and glasses of water also split light like a prism.

abschnitte.text: In optics, a **prism** is an object made of transparent material, usually **glass**. The best known is the triangular prism, which looks like a little roof. What matters is that its surfaces are not parallel to each other. That is why light is bent in the same direction both when it enters and when it leaves.

Light is slower in glass than in air. So when a ray of light hits the glass surface at an angle, it changes direction; this is called **refraction**. In a prism, the ray is refracted twice and bent clearly overall. How much depends on the angle of the prism and the kind of glass.

The different colours are refracted by different amounts; this is called **dispersion**. **Red** is bent the least, **violet** the most. So white sunlight fans out into a coloured band, the **spectrum**. If you bring the colours back together with a lens or a second prism, white light forms again. Red laser light, on the other hand, consists of only one colour and stays red; it is only bent.

In the 1660s, the English physicist **Isaac Newton** studied sunlight with prisms. He let a sunbeam fall through a hole in the window shutter and split it with a prism. Then he showed that a single colour cannot be split any further with a second prism. This proved that white light is a mixture of all the colours.

A cut **glass crystal** in the window throws colourful patches onto the wall. A **diamond** sparkles in many colours because it splits light especially strongly. A glass full of water in the sun can also produce a small rainbow. In nature, the **rainbow** forms because many raindrops split sunlight much like little prisms.

In **binoculars**, prisms redirect the light and turn the image the right way up, using total internal reflection. In single-lens reflex cameras, a prism makes sure you see the correct image through the viewfinder. In science, **spectrometers** split light into its colours. This makes it possible, for example, to find out what substances distant stars are made of.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bending of a ray of light as it passes into another material.
The different amounts by which the various colours are refracted.
The coloured band produced when light is split into its colours.
The pure colours of the spectrum, from red through yellow and green to violet.

gewusst: Newton counted seven colours in the spectrum, probably partly because the number seven was thought especially important at the time.
Light is about a third slower in glass than in air.
The famous Pink Floyd album cover “The Dark Side of the Moon” also shows a prism splitting light.

teile.einleitung: Stride length is the length of one step when walking. It is a handy built-in measuring tool that lets you estimate distances roughly without a tape measure. Even the ancient Romans measured long distances in paces.
wichtigste: Stride length is the distance you cover with one step when walking.
A normal step of an adult is about 70 centimetres long.
Adults usually take longer steps than children, because their legs are longer.
If you count your steps, you can roughly measure a distance without a tape measure.
Measuring with steps is not exact, because steps are not always the same length.
A pedometer counts how many steps you walk.
In the past, body measurements such as the pace, foot and ell were used as units of length.

abschnitte.text: **Stride length** is the distance you cover with one step when walking. It is usually measured from the heel of one foot to the heel of the other. For adults walking at a comfortable pace it is about 70 centimetres; for children it is shorter. If you walk faster or run, you take bigger steps. Your height plays a part too: people with longer legs usually take longer steps.

You can find out your own stride length. Walk 10 steps quite normally along a straight stretch and mark the start and end. Measure the distance with a tape measure and divide the result by 10. For a distance of 5 metres, your stride length is 50 centimetres. If you repeat the measurement several times and take the **average**, the result becomes more accurate.

If you know your stride length, you can **pace out** distances. If you count your steps and multiply them by your stride length, you get the rough distance. With 10 steps of 50 centimetres, for example, you get 5 metres. This is useful at scout camp, in orienteering or for marking out a flower bed in the garden. It is not exact, though, because steps turn out different lengths uphill, on soft ground or when you are tired.

In the past there were no standard units such as the metre. People measured with their own bodies: with the **foot**, the width of a hand, the ell, which was about as long as a forearm, and the pace. The Romans used the **double pace**, in Latin passus, of about 1.5 metres. A thousand double paces made a Roman mile, which is where the word mile comes from. Because every person is built differently, fixed units were introduced later, the metre in France in 1799.

A **pedometer** detects each step with a motion sensor and counts along. Many mobile phones and sports watches have one built in. If you enter your own stride length, the device works out the distance covered. You often hear the advice to walk about 10,000 steps a day to stay fit. This number, however, comes from an advert for a Japanese pedometer and is not a fixed rule.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length of one step when walking.
Measuring a distance by walking it and counting the steps.
An old unit of length, about as long as a forearm.
A device that counts the number of steps walked.
The mean value of several measurements.

gewusst: The word mile comes from the Latin mille, which means a thousand.
When running fast, top sprinters can cover over 2 metres with one stride.
Anyone who walks 10,000 steps of 70 centimetres each covers about 7 kilometres.

teile.einleitung: Reflection means throwing back: light bounces off a surface, rather like a ball off a wall. That is why you can see yourself in the mirror and can make out things in the dark with a torch. Sound and water waves can also be reflected.
wichtigste: A mirror throws light back.
You see yourself in the mirror because the light travels from you to the mirror and back into your eyes.
With a torch, you see things because they throw the light back to your eyes.
Smooth, shiny surfaces reflect especially well.
Light colours throw back more light than dark ones.
Sound is thrown back too; you hear it as an echo.

abschnitte.text: If you throw a ball at an angle against a wall, it bounces off at an angle in the other direction. Light behaves very similarly at a mirror. This process is called **reflection**. The word comes from Latin and means to bend back.

In a dark room, you can see almost nothing. If you switch on a **torch**, its light falls on things such as a chair or a cuddly toy. They throw back part of the light, and it reaches your **eyes**. Only then can your brain make a picture of them.

A **mirror** is usually made of glass with a thin layer of metal on the back. This smooth layer throws the light back in a very orderly way. That is why a clear **mirror image** forms, in which you can see yourself. A still mountain lake can also act like a mirror, for example when the Matterhorn is reflected in the Riffelsee.

White and light-coloured things reflect a lot of light, which is why they look bright. Black things swallow almost all the light; this is called **absorption**. That is why a black T-shirt gets warmer in the sun than a white one. In winter, the snow dazzles you because it throws back a great deal of sunlight.

High-visibility vests and **reflectors** on your bike and school bag throw back the light from car headlights. This means drivers can see you at night from a long way off. Dark clothes, on the other hand, can only be seen very late in the dark. That is why light-coloured clothes and reflectors are worth it on the way to school in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The throwing back of light or sound from a surface.
The image of an object that a mirror shows.
Light being swallowed by a material instead of thrown back.

gewusst: With two mirrors at an angle to each other, you can see yourself from behind.
A kaleidoscope uses three mirrors to make ever new colourful patterns.
Bats use the reflection of sound to find insects in the dark.

teile.einleitung: The speed of sound tells you how fast sound travels. In air at 20 °C, sound covers about 343 metres per second, which is roughly 1,235 km/h. In water and in solid materials such as steel, sound is much faster still.
wichtigste: In air at 20 °C, sound travels at about 343 m/s.
In water, sound moves at about 1,500 m/s, more than four times as fast as in air.
In steel, sound is especially fast at around 5,000 m/s.
In warm air, the speed of sound is higher than in cold air.
If an aircraft flies exactly as fast as sound, we say it is flying at Mach 1.
If an aircraft is faster than sound, a loud sonic boom can be heard on the ground.
In 1947, Chuck Yeager in the Bell X-1 was the first person proven to break the sound barrier in level flight.

abschnitte.titel: What is the speed of sound?
abschnitte.text: Sound is a vibration that is passed on from particle to particle. The **speed of sound** tells you how many metres this vibration travels per second. In air at 20 °C it is about 343 m/s, which works out at roughly 1,235 km/h. That is fast, but much slower than light, which is almost a million times faster. That is why you see a flash of lightning at once but only hear the thunder later.

How fast sound is depends on the material it travels through. In **water** it travels at about 1,500 m/s, in **steel** at as much as about 5,000 m/s. If a hammer blow travels 1,000 m through a steel rail in 0.2 seconds, its speed is 5,000 m/s. That is why people used to be able to hear a train coming by putting an ear to the rail. In empty space there is no sound at all, because there are no particles that could vibrate.

In warm air, the air particles move faster and pass the vibration on more quickly. That is why the speed of sound rises when the air gets warmer. At 0 °C it is about 331 m/s, at 20 °C about 343 m/s. High up where aircraft fly, the air is very cold, so sound is slower there than on the ground.

Speed compared with sound is given as the **Mach number**, named after the Austrian physicist Ernst Mach. Mach 1 means exactly the speed of sound, Mach 2 twice as fast. If an aircraft flies faster than sound, the sound waves crowd together into a pressure wave that can be heard on the ground as a **sonic boom**. On 14 October 1947, the American pilot Chuck Yeager, flying the rocket plane **Bell X-1**, became the first person proven to break the sound barrier in level flight. Until 2003, the passenger aircraft Concorde flew across the Atlantic at about twice the speed of sound.

You can use the speed of sound to work out distances. If you see a woodcutter strike and hear the blow 2 seconds later, at 340 m/s he is about 680 m away. In a **thunderstorm**, count the seconds between lightning and thunder and divide by 3; that gives you roughly the distance in kilometres. An **echo** also gives distances away: bats and ships with echo sounders use this principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The speed at which sound travels through a material.
Tells you how many times faster than sound something is moving.
The point at which an aircraft becomes faster than sound.
A loud bang produced by an aircraft flying faster than sound.
A device that measures the depth of water using sound and echoes.

gewusst: You only hear the thunder of a storm 10 kilometres away about 30 seconds after the lightning.
Whales can communicate with sounds over very great distances in the sea, because sound travels fast and far in water.
The crack of a whip happens because its tip moves faster than sound for a moment.

teile.einleitung: Resonance is the strong vibrating along of an object when it is pushed in time with its own natural vibration. You come across it on a swing, in musical instruments and sometimes, unfortunately, with swaying bridges.
wichtigste: Resonance is strong vibrating along at the natural frequency.
A swing goes higher if you push it in time with its own swing.
The hollow wooden body of a guitar vibrates along and makes the sound louder.
Soldiers are not supposed to march in step across bridges, because these could vibrate dangerously.
The Millennium Bridge in London was closed in 2000 shortly after it opened because it swayed strongly.
A very loud note at the natural frequency of a wine glass can make it shatter.
Vibration dampers stop resonant vibrations in buildings and bridges from becoming too strong.

abschnitte.text: Almost every object has a **natural frequency**, a rhythm in which it prefers to vibrate. If it is pushed again and again in exactly this rhythm, the vibration grows each time. This effect is called **resonance**, from the Latin word for to echo. If it is pushed in a different rhythm, the vibration stays small.

The best-known example is the **swing**. If you push it every time exactly when it comes back, it swings higher and higher. Even small pushes at the right moment are enough. If you push at the wrong moment, on the other hand, you actually slow it down.

Guitars, violins and pianos have a built-in **soundboard or sound box**. The thin string on its own moves only a little air and sounds quiet. The wooden body vibrates along and passes the sound on to the air much more loudly. In the same way, a tuning fork sounds much louder if you stand it on a suitable wooden box.

When the **Millennium Bridge** in London opened in June 2000, it began to sway sideways under the many pedestrians. People unconsciously adjusted their steps to the swaying and so made it stronger. After dampers were fitted, it reopened in 2002. Tall buildings such as the Taipei 101 skyscraper have huge pendulums as **vibration dampers**, which weaken vibrations in wind and earthquakes.

Resonance is often wanted too. A radio tunes in to a station by bringing an electrical oscillating circuit into resonance with its frequency. In medicine, magnetic resonance imaging uses a form of resonance of atomic nuclei to make pictures of the inside of the body. Quartz clocks also work with a crystal that vibrates very evenly at resonance.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rhythm in which an object prefers to vibrate by itself.
The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
The hollow part of an instrument that vibrates along and amplifies the sound.
Anything that takes energy from a vibration and makes it smaller.

gewusst: The opera singer who makes a wine glass shatter with her voice is not a fairy tale, but it takes a very loud and exactly matching note.
The pendulum in the Taipei 101 skyscraper weighs several hundred tonnes and can be seen by visitors.
The humming noises of a car at a certain speed are often caused by individual parts resonating too.

teile.einleitung: Snails are molluscs that creep slowly over the ground on a broad foot. In Switzerland, almost every child knows the Roman snail with its round shell and the slugs without a shell. From the point of view of physics, it is especially interesting how snails move with the help of slime.
wichtigste: A Roman snail creeps about 7 centimetres per minute.
Snails glide over the ground on a trail of slime.
The Roman snail has four tentacles; the eyes sit at the tips of the long tentacles.
The shell of the Roman snail is made of lime.
A snail without a shell is called a slug.
In German, someone going “im Schneckentempo” is moving at a snail's pace, very slowly.
The Roman snail is a protected species in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Snails belong to the **molluscs**, like mussels and squid. Their body consists of the head, the broad **foot** and the visceral mass, which in snails with shells sits inside the shell. The Roman snail has four tentacles: the two long upper ones carry the eyes at their tips, and the two short lower ones are used for feeling and smelling. Its **lime** shell grows with it and can become up to about 5 centimetres wide.

A Roman snail creeps about 7 centimetres per minute, which is a good 4 metres in an hour. A person out for a walk is about a thousand times faster. That is why we say something goes “at a snail's pace” when it is very slow. If a snail first creeps 10 centimetres and then another 5 centimetres, it has covered 15 centimetres altogether.

Under the foot, wave-like muscle movements run from back to front. Between the foot and the ground lies a thin layer of **slime**, which has a special property: under strong stress it becomes liquid, and at rest it becomes firm and sticky again. In this way the snail can stick at one point and glide forwards at another. Thanks to this slime, it can even creep up vertical walls and over a sharp knife blade without hurting itself.

Snails scrape off their food with a **radula**, a tongue covered with thousands of tiny teeth. Roman snails mainly eat wilted plant parts, while slugs such as the Spanish slug also like lettuce in the garden. Snails are active in damp weather and at night, because otherwise they dry out. In winter, the Roman snail seals its shell with a lid of lime and rests in the ground.

Well over 200 species of land and water snails live in Switzerland. The **Roman snail** is the largest native land snail and is protected, so you are not allowed to simply collect it. Snails are important recyclers, because they break down dead plants, and they are food for hedgehogs, birds and slow worms. You should be careful with slug pellets, because they can also harm other animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of soft-bodied animals without bones, including snails and mussels.
The muscular underside of the snail with which it moves.
A tongue with many tiny teeth that snails use to scrape off their food.
A snail without a visible shell.

gewusst: A Roman snail can pull itself so deep into its shell that nothing of it can be seen from outside.
The radula of some snails carries several tens of thousands of tiny teeth.

teile.einleitung: A pirouette is a fast spin on one foot, as seen in figure skating and ballet. Behind the elegant whirl there is exciting physics. When you pull your arms in, you suddenly spin much faster, without any extra push.
wichtigste: A pirouette is a spin around your own axis on one leg.
The faster spin when pulling in the arms is explained by the conservation of angular momentum.
The moment of inertia tells you how hard it is to set an object spinning.
If a skater halves her moment of inertia, her spinning speed doubles.
If you spread your arms out, the pirouette gets slower.
Friction from the blade and the air slows every pirouette down over time.
The Biellmann spin is named after the Swiss figure skater Denise Biellmann.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from French and means something like spinning top. In **figure skating**, the skater spins quickly on the blade of one skate. There are also pirouettes in **ballet**, where you spin on the tip or ball of your foot. Spins are compulsory elements in competitions and are marked by the judges.

Every spinning object has **angular momentum**. It depends on the spinning speed and the **moment of inertia**. The moment of inertia is large when the mass is far from the axis of rotation and small when it is close to the axis. Because angular momentum is conserved, the spin has to get faster when the moment of inertia gets smaller. If you halve it, you spin twice as fast.

At the start, the skater spreads her arms and leg out wide and builds up momentum. Then she pulls her **arms** in close to her body and whirls away. To slow down, she stretches her arms out again without putting her foot down. Over time, every pirouette still gets slower, because **friction** between the blade and the ice and air resistance cost energy.

In an **upright spin**, you spin standing straight on one leg. In a **sit spin**, you go down into a deep crouch on one leg and stretch the other forwards. In a camel spin, the upper body is horizontal and one leg is stretched out behind. The **Biellmann spin** is especially difficult: you pull your free foot from behind up over your head.

**Denise Biellmann** from Zurich made the spin named after her famous in the 1970s and 1980s. In 1981 she became world champion. The Swiss skater Lucinda Ruh also became known for her extremely fast and long spins. Later, **Stéphane Lambiel** won the world title twice and was also a master of spins.

A high diver spins faster in a somersault in a tucked position than in a straight one, because his moment of inertia is smaller. Cats use similar tricks to turn onto their paws when they fall. An **office chair** is also good for trying it out: spin with your arms stretched out and then pull them in. You will notice how you suddenly get faster.

begriffe.erklaerung: The momentum of a spin, which stays the same without any outside influence.
A measure of how hard it is to set an object spinning.
A law of physics that says a certain quantity stays the same.
The narrow metal runner under an ice skate.

gewusst: Very good figure skaters manage several turns per second in a spin.
To avoid getting dizzy, figure skaters train their sense of balance for years.
Planets and stars also follow the conservation of angular momentum: when a star shrinks, it spins faster.

teile.einleitung: An hourglass, or sand timer, is a simple device that measures a certain length of time. Sand trickles from one glass bulb through a narrow neck into a second one. It needs neither electricity nor a battery, because gravity does all the work.
wichtigste: An hourglass usually consists of two glass bulbs connected by a narrow neck.
Gravity pulls the sand down, which is why it needs no battery.
When all the sand is at the bottom, you turn the hourglass over and can measure again.
An hourglass does not tell the time of day, only a certain duration.
In the kitchen, small sand timers are used for boiling eggs.
In board games, a sand timer limits the time for a round.
If you lay a running hourglass on its side, the sand stops trickling.

abschnitte.text: An hourglass has two glass **bulbs** standing one above the other. In the middle they are connected by a narrow opening, the **neck**. A frame of wood or metal holds the bulbs and protects them. Inside, an exactly measured amount of very fine, dry sand is sealed in.

**Gravity** pulls the grains of sand down through the neck. Because only a few grains fit through at the same time, the sand trickles evenly. When the top bulb is empty, the set time is over. What is amazing is that the sand always flows at about the same speed, however much is still at the top. This is because the grains support each other and the pressure on the opening hardly rises.

When all the sand is at the bottom, you simply turn the hourglass over, and the measurement starts again. If you lay a running hourglass flat on its side, the sand stops trickling because it can no longer fall downhill. If you stand it up again, it carries on. How long an hourglass runs depends on the **amount of sand**, the grain size and the width of the neck.

Hourglasses have been known in Europe since the **Middle Ages**. An early picture of an hourglass can be found on a 14th-century wall painting in Siena. On sailing ships, sailors used hourglasses to time the watches and, together with a line, to measure the ship's speed. Preachers in churches also sometimes had an hourglass on the pulpit.

Today, sand timers are used mainly in everyday life and in games. The **egg timer** in the kitchen often runs for about three to five minutes, depending on how soft the egg should be. In board games, a small sand timer limits the time for a round. Some families use a sand timer for brushing teeth, so that you brush for long enough.

Hourglasses do not always contain real sand. Finely ground marble, tiny glass beads or, in the past, even crushed eggshells are also used. What matters is that the grains are the same size, round and completely **dry**. Damp grains would stick together and block the neck.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the Earth pulls everything down towards it.
The narrow opening between the two glass bulbs.
A rounded glass container, here at the top and bottom of the hourglass.
A particular duration, for example three minutes.
