gewusst: In an hourglass, the sand flows almost equally fast whether the top bulb is full or nearly empty.
The hourglass is still a symbol of passing time, for example as the waiting symbol on computers.
Because sand does not slosh about, hourglasses worked better than water clocks on rocking ships.

teile.einleitung: A lock is a structure on rivers and canals that raises or lowers ships from one water level to another. It works like a lift made of water: the ship sails into a chamber, and then the water in it rises or falls. This lets ships get past barrages, weirs and power stations.
wichtigste: A lock raises or lowers ships to a different water level.
The ship waits in the lock chamber, which is closed at the front and back by gates.
If the ship wants to go up, water flows into the chamber.
If it wants to go down, water is let out.
No pump is needed for filling; the water flows in from the higher side.
The gates are only opened when the water is at the same height on both sides.
On the way to Basel, large cargo ships pass through several locks on the Rhine.

abschnitte.text: In many places, rivers are held back by weirs and hydroelectric power stations. This creates steps in the water that a ship cannot simply sail up or down. A **lock** solves this problem. It is a kind of staircase for ships, in which each step is a chamber.

The ship sails from the lower water into the **lock chamber**, and the lower **gate** closes. Then sluices are opened so that water flows into the chamber from the upper side. The water rises, and the ship is lifted with it. When the water in the chamber is as high as above, the upper gate opens and the ship sails out.

Going down works the other way round. The ship sails into the chamber at the high water level, and the upper gate closes. Now the water is let out to the lower side until the water level is as low as below. No **pump** is needed for this, because water always flows downhill by itself.

abschnitte.titel: Why the water must be level
abschnitte.text: If the water is higher on one side, it presses against the gate with great force. In large locks, this **water pressure** is so strong that the gate could not be opened or would be damaged. Only when the water levels are equal do the forces on both sides cancel out. Many lock gates are built as mitre gates, whose two leaves brace against the current at an angle and are pressed together by the water.

abschnitte.titel: Locks in Switzerland and the world
abschnitte.text: On the Rhine, large cargo ships sail from the North Sea to Basel and on to Rheinfelden. On the way they pass through locks at the power stations, for example at **Birsfelden** and Augst. There is also a lock on the Jura waters, at Port near Biel. The famous **Panama Canal** lifts ocean ships with several locks to around 26 metres above sea level and down again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The space in a lock in which the ship is raised or lowered.
A large, watertight gate that closes the chamber at the front or back.
A place on a river where the water is held back by a weir.
The force with which water presses on a surface; it increases with depth.

gewusst: Locks with two gates and one chamber, as we know them today, have existed in Europe since the Middle Ages.
In the Panama Canal, a great deal of fresh water from a reservoir is used up for every ship that passes through.

teile.einleitung: The rocket equation describes how fast a rocket can go when it burns and pushes out its fuel. It shows why rockets are so huge and consist almost entirely of fuel. It was published by the Russian scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in 1903.
wichtigste: The rocket equation is Δv = v e · ln(m0 / m1).
Konstantin Tsiolkovsky published it in 1903.
The change in speed depends on the exhaust velocity and the mass ratio.
The mass ratio is the launch mass divided by the empty mass.
The natural logarithm links the mass ratio and the change in speed.
Above a mass ratio of about 2.72, a rocket becomes faster than its own exhaust velocity.
Multi-stage rockets improve the mass ratio, because empty tanks are dropped.

abschnitte.text: The **rocket equation** is Δv = v e · ln(m0 / m1). Here Δv is the rocket's change in speed and v e the **exhaust velocity** of the gases. m0 is the mass at launch with full tanks and m1 the mass after the fuel has been burned. The ratio m0 / m1 is called the **mass ratio**. The equation applies when no outside forces such as gravity or air resistance act.

**Konstantin Tsiolkovsky** lived from 1857 to 1935 and was a teacher in Russia. As a child, an illness left him almost deaf, and he taught himself a great deal. In 1903 he published a paper on exploring space with reaction devices, which contains the equation. He also already described multi-stage rockets and space stations and is considered one of the fathers of space travel.

If a rocket has an exhaust velocity of 3000 metres per second and a mass ratio of 4, that gives 3000 · ln 4, around 4.2 kilometres per second. With a mass ratio of e, about 2.72, the rocket becomes exactly as fast as its gases stream out. For twice the exhaust velocity it already needs a mass ratio of about 7.4. The **logarithm** means that every further gain in speed costs a great deal more fuel.

The force with which the rocket is pushed forwards is called **thrust**. It is calculated as the mass pushed out per second times the exhaust velocity. If a rocket pushes out 100 kilograms of gas per second at 2500 metres per second, the thrust is 250,000 newtons, that is 250 kilonewtons. For it to lift off at all, the thrust must be greater than its weight.

Taking gravity and air resistance into account, you need about 9 to 10 kilometres per second for an orbit around the Earth. Even the best chemical engines with hydrogen and oxygen only reach an exhaust velocity of around 4.5 kilometres per second in a vacuum. So a single-stage rocket would have to consist almost entirely of fuel. With **multi-stage rockets**, empty tanks are dropped, which improves the mass ratio of each stage.

Space engineers calculate with the rocket equation for every mission. It shows that a high exhaust velocity is very valuable. **Ion engines** push out charged particles much faster than chemical engines but have only a tiny thrust. That makes them suitable for space probes that accelerate gently for months.

begriffe.erklaerung: The speed at which the gases leave the back of the rocket.
A rocket's launch mass divided by its mass without fuel.
The function ln, which tells you to what power the number e must be raised.
The driving force of an engine.

gewusst: In large rockets, around nine tenths of the mass at launch is often fuel.
Tsiolkovsky also wrote science fiction stories about life in space.
The number e, about 2.718, is one of the most important numbers in mathematics.

teile.einleitung: A ramp is a sloping surface that makes it easier to move things or people up or down. In physics it is called an inclined plane and is one of the simplest machines. The ancient Egyptians probably used ramps to move huge stones up for the pyramids.
wichtigste: In physics, a ramp is called an inclined plane.
On a long, gentle ramp, you need the least force to push a trolley up.
Ramps at entrances help people in wheelchairs and with prams.
Removal workers often push heavy furniture up a ramp onto the lorry.
On a steep ramp, a marble rolls down faster.
A U-shaped ramp for skateboarders is called a halfpipe.
A ramp on a lakeshore for launching boats into the water is called a slipway.

abschnitte.text: A **ramp** is a sloping surface between two heights. In physics it is called an **inclined plane** and counts as one of the simple machines. Instead of lifting a load straight up, you push it up the slope. In doing so, you only have to overcome part of its weight.

The **gentler** a ramp is, the less force you need. But the distance gets longer. Without friction, the work, that is force times distance, stays the same; this is called the **golden rule of mechanics**. A steep ramp is short but tiring, a gentle one is long but easy.

Ramps at entrances help people in **wheelchairs**, with walking frames or with prams. In Switzerland, the **Disability Discrimination Act** requires new public buildings to be accessible without obstacles. Ramps for wheelchairs should be as gentle as possible; a gradient of at most about 6 per cent is recommended. That is why stations and buses are also getting more ramps and raised kerbs at stops.

When building the pyramids, the ancient **Egyptians** probably moved the heavy stone blocks up over long ramps made of mud bricks and rubble. Exactly what these ramps looked like is disputed among researchers. Castles and fortresses also often had ramps up which cannons and carts were pulled. Today, **loading ramps** are used at warehouses so that lorries can be loaded easily.

Skateboarders ride in the **halfpipe**, a U-shaped ramp, and jump over small ramps called kickers. On a steep ramp, a marble rolls down faster because a larger part of its weight drives it. A **ski jump** is also a huge ramp. On the lakeshore, boats are launched into the water over a **slipway**.

Motorway slip roads and multi-storey car parks have ramps so that cars can change height. Steep mountain roads in the Alps wind up the slope in **hairpin bends**, which is like a very long, gentle ramp. Screws and wedges also work on the principle of the inclined plane. A screw is basically a ramp wrapped around a pin.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sloping surface on which loads can be moved up with less force.
How steeply a surface rises, often given as a percentage.
A U-shaped ramp for skateboarding, snowboarding or BMX.
A ramp on the shore for launching boats into the water or pulling them out.

gewusst: A gradient of 100 per cent does not mean vertical but an angle of 45 degrees.
Many multi-storey car parks have spiral ramps on which cars drive up floor by floor in a circle.
In halfpipe snowboarding competitions, professionals jump several metres above the edge.

teile.einleitung: A real image is an image formed when light rays really do meet at a point behind a lens or in front of a concave mirror. It can be caught on a screen or a sheet of paper. Projectors, cameras and even our eyes produce real images.
wichtigste: In a real image, the light rays really do cross.
A real image can be caught on a screen.
The real image from a single converging lens is upside down and reversed left to right.
A converging lens forms a real image when the object is further away than the focal length.
A real, upside-down and smaller image forms on the retina.
A pinhole camera and a concave mirror can also produce real images.
The opposite is the virtual image, which cannot be caught on a screen.

abschnitte.text: Light rays go out from every point of a lit object. A **converging lens** bends these rays so that they meet again at a point on the other side. There a **real image** forms, an actual image made of real light. If you hold a **screen** at that spot, you see the image sharply on it.

The real image from a single converging lens is **inverted**: it is upside down and reversed left to right. Whether it is bigger or smaller depends on how far away the object is. An object that is far away gives a small image near the **focal point**. As the object moves closer to the focal length, the image gets bigger and lies further away.

The relationship is described by the **lens equation**: 1 divided by the focal length equals 1 divided by the object distance plus 1 divided by the image distance. A real image only forms if the object is further from the lens than the **focal length**. An example: a lens with a focal length of 12 cm forms a sharp image 36 cm behind the lens. Then the object is 18 cm in front of the lens, and the image is twice as big.

A **projector** throws a greatly enlarged real image onto the screen. A **camera** produces a smaller real image on the image sensor, or in the past on the film. The **pinhole camera** even manages a real image without any lens, because only a narrow beam of light from each point falls through the small hole. A **concave mirror**, as in large telescopes, can also produce real images.

The human **eye** works like a camera. The cornea and the lens of the eye together act as a converging lens and form a real, upside-down and smaller image on the **retina**. We still see the world the right way up because the brain interprets the signals correctly. If the image is not sharp, glasses or contact lenses help.

The opposite of a real image is the **virtual image**. It forms when the light rays only seem to cross, that is when they are traced backwards. One example is your reflection in the bathroom mirror, which seems to stand behind the mirror. A **magnifying glass** also produces a virtual image, which cannot be caught on a screen.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lens that is thicker in the middle and brings light rays together at one point.
The distance between the lens and the focal point.
The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.
An apparent image that cannot be caught on a screen.

gewusst: In ancient times, people already noticed that light through a small hole throws an upside-down image into a dark room.
You can build a pinhole camera yourself from a shoebox, baking paper and a pin.
Newborn babies first have to learn to see; their brain gets used to the images on the retina in the first months.

teile.einleitung: The pascal is the unit of pressure, abbreviated Pa. One pascal is a very small pressure, roughly as much as a sheet of paper lying flat on a table exerts. That is why larger units such as hectopascals are often used in everyday life, for the weather.
wichtigste: One pascal equals 1 newton per square metre.
The unit is named after the French scholar Blaise Pascal.
Blaise Pascal lived in the 17th century and built a mechanical calculating machine when he was still a young man.
1 hectopascal is 100 Pa, 1 kilopascal 1000 Pa and 1 megapascal 1,000,000 Pa.
At sea level, the average air pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.
One pascal is roughly the pressure of a sheet of paper lying flat.
The pascal is the official unit of pressure in the International System of Units, SI.

abschnitte.text: **Pressure** tells you how strongly a force presses on an area. It is calculated as force divided by area. If a force of 1 newton presses evenly on an area of 1 square metre, the pressure is 1 **pascal**. That is very little, because 1 newton is roughly the weight of a small 100-gram bar of chocolate.

Because a pascal is so small, prefixes are usually needed. 1 **hectopascal** (hPa) is 100 Pa, 1 kilopascal (kPa) is 1000 Pa and 1 megapascal (MPa) is a million Pa. The **bar** is also very common: 1 bar equals 100,000 Pa. Bicycle and car tyres are usually pumped up to a few bar.

Weather reports give the **air pressure** in hectopascals. At sea level it averages about 1013 hPa. Higher up it is lower; at the Jungfraujoch, at around 3500 metres, it is only about two thirds of that. High air pressure often brings fine weather, low air pressure more likely clouds and rain.

Blaise Pascal was born in France in 1623 and died in 1662. At about 19 he built a **calculating machine** to help his father with tax calculations; it is called the Pascaline. He researched air pressure and in 1648 had measurements taken on the Puy de Dôme mountain showing that air pressure decreases with height. He was also an important mathematician and thinker.

In everyday life, we come across pressures from tiny to enormous. A sheet of paper lying flat presses on the table with about 1 Pa. The air pressure around us is about 100,000 Pa; we just do not feel it, because it presses equally from all sides. In engineering, the strength of steel or concrete is measured in **megapascals**, and at the deepest point of the ocean there is a pressure of over 100 megapascals.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a certain area.
The unit of force.
100 pascals, the unit for air pressure in the weather report.
A unit of pressure; 1 bar is 100,000 pascals.
The International System of Units, which applies to measurements worldwide.

gewusst: The programming language Pascal is also named after Blaise Pascal.
Air pressure used to be given in millibars in the weather report; one millibar is exactly one hectopascal.
The pressure under a pointed stiletto heel can be greater than under an elephant's foot.
